title: Faithful in Exile
subtitle: Pastoral Leadership and the Church's Witness in a Post-Christian Age
blurb: The church in the West has lost the cultural power it held for sixteen centuries, and most of us are treating the loss like a catastrophe to be reversed. It isn't a catastrophe. It's a homecoming, a return to the church's oldest and most faithful condition, the condition of exile, where the people of God have always done their truest work. This book traces how Christendom rose and how it fell, and it argues that the long stretch of years in front of us is not a sentence. It's an assignment.

chapters.title: The Map We Were Handed Is Wrong
chapters.summary: The church in the West is grieving a lost cultural power, mistaking the end of Christendom for the end of the faith. The map we were handed assumed Christianity was the home team, and that map no longer matches the country we live in.
chapters.body:
There's a particular kind of grief that has settled over the pastors I serve, and it took me a long time to name it right. It looks like exhaustion. It sounds like complaint. A man will sit across from me at a diner, his coffee going cold while he turns the mug around in his hands, and he'll tell me the numbers are down, the young people are gone, the school board doesn't return his calls anymore, the mayor stopped coming to the prayer breakfast, the funeral home calls him less than it used to because half the families don't want a pastor now. And underneath all of it, every time, is the same sentence. It didn't used to be this way.

He's right. It didn't.

For most of American history the church operated with a tailwind. The culture handed us the basic furniture for free. That there's a God. That he has spoken. That the Bible carries weight. That a pastor is somebody you can trust with your daughter and your secrets and your deathbed. That Sunday is set apart, that you don't schedule the big game against it, that the stores close, that the town slows down. We didn't argue for any of that. We inherited it. A pastor in 1955 could stand up in a pulpit and assume the whole room already agreed with his foundations. His job was application, not foundation. He was speaking the home language to people who'd grown up in the home.

That world is gone. I want to be careful with that word, so let me say it slowly. Not declining. Not under threat. Gone. And the grief in that diner is the grief of a man who was handed a map of a country that no longer exists, who keeps following the roads it shows him, and who keeps driving into the lake.

I've done it myself. I want to be honest about that up front, because this is not a book I'm writing from a clean distance. I've stood in my own pulpit at First Baptist and felt the pull of the old map, felt myself reaching for an agreement in the room that wasn't there anymore, talking like the whole town still shared my starting points when half of them had never heard them. I drove into the lake plenty of times before I understood it was a lake.

Now, the first thing the wrong map does is make you reach for the wrong word. And the wrong word, in our circles, is persecution. I have to push back on that, gently but firmly, because it matters. The church in the West is not being thrown to lions. We're being ignored. We're being treated as one option among many, and not a particularly interesting one, and that stings worse in some ways because there's no glory in being ignored. A martyr gets a story. A man nobody listens to just gets quieter. But ignored is not persecuted. The loss is real, and I'm not going to minimize it. But it's the loss of privilege, not the loss of life. Those are two different sufferings, and a leader who confuses them is going to lead his people into self-pity instead of into faithfulness. I've watched it happen. A congregation that believes itself persecuted when it's merely been demoted gets mean. It gets scared. It starts looking for enemies, and it finds them, and the looking eats it alive.

So let me try to say what actually happened, because naming it right is most of the work.

A philosopher named Charles Taylor wrote a big, dense book called A Secular Age, and it's one of the few books I keep coming back to when I'm trying to understand the ground under my feet. His point, stripped down, is this. We used to live in a world where belief in God was the default. It was the air. It was the assumption underneath all the other assumptions. A man might be a bad Christian, a lazy one, even a wicked one, but the question of whether God existed simply wasn't live for most people. It was the water. Now we live somewhere else. Belief is one option among many, and often not the easiest one to hold. The change isn't mainly that fewer people believe, though fewer do. The change is in the conditions. Faith now takes a decision, a swimming against the current, where it used to take no decision at all. Taylor has a phrase for the new situation. He calls it the immanent frame, which is just a fancy way of saying that most of our neighbors experience the world as closed, as self-contained, as needing no reference to anything above it. The sun comes up because the earth turns, the baby gets well because the antibiotics worked, the marriage survives because they went to counseling, and at no point does the explanation reach for heaven. Most of the people in your town live inside that frame without ever having chosen it. They just breathe it. The way we once breathed faith.

Let me tell you how I learned this in my own body, because I didn't come to the faith inside the believing world. I came to it from the other side. I was an atheist. Not a soft, cultural, never-thought-about-it atheist, but a real one, a young man who had looked at the whole apparatus of religion and concluded it was a crutch for the weak and a lie for the frightened, and who felt some contempt for the people who needed it. I grew up without a father, and I'll talk more about what that did to me later in this book, but one of the things it did was make me suspicious of any authority that asked me to trust it, and God was the biggest authority of all, the Father with a capital F, and I wanted nothing from him because I'd learned early that fathers leave. So when I tell you the immanent frame is real, that you can live inside a closed world where God is simply not a live option, I'm not describing my neighbors. I'm describing myself at nineteen. I lived in that frame. I breathed it. It felt not like unbelief but like clarity, like waking up from a story other people were still asleep in.

And here's why that matters for this book. When God broke into that frame for me, and he did, though that's a longer story, I came up out of atheism and into the church at the tail end of Christendom, and I noticed something almost immediately that the lifelong churchgoers couldn't see, because they'd never been outside it. They assumed everyone basically knew the story and just needed to come back to it. I knew that wasn't true, because I hadn't known the story, I'd known a cartoon of it, and most of my old friends knew even less. The church was preaching to a country it thought was full of prodigals who'd wandered off and needed to come home, and the country was actually filling up with people who'd never been in the house at all, who didn't know there was a house, who'd have to be told the story from the very beginning as though it were brand new, because to them it was. I could see it because I'd been one of them. The church couldn't see it because it had never not been Christian. So in a strange way my atheism was a gift to my pastoring, because it meant I was never operating from the old map. I'd never had it. I came in already knowing the room didn't agree with me, because I remembered not agreeing.

I find it helps to make it concrete. My grandfather's doubts, if he had any, happened inside a believing world. He could doubt the way a man inside a house doubts whether the roof will hold. My sons' doubts, if they have them, happen inside an unbelieving world. They have to decide to believe, and the deciding never stops, because every day the frame closes around them again and they have to choose again. That's a different kind of faith than I was handed. Harder. And I think, if it holds, deeper. But different, and the difference is the whole story.

So the map is wrong. And here's what makes a wrong map so dangerous. A wrong map doesn't feel wrong. It feels like the territory betrayed you. The pastor who assumes cultural support and doesn't find it won't conclude that his assumptions are out of date. He'll conclude that the country went evil, that an enemy did this, that the institutions were captured by forces hostile to God. And some of that is even partly true. There are forces, and some of them are hostile. But the conclusion produces a posture, and the posture is the problem. Defensive. Embattled. Aggrieved. Always looking over the shoulder for the next attack. And that posture is one the New Testament simply never models and the gospel cannot carry. You cannot preach the love of enemies from a bunker. You cannot wash feet while you're checking the perimeter.

Because here's what the wrong map hides from us, and it's the thing this whole book turns on. The church did not begin in Christendom. The church began in exile.

Look at who Peter is writing to in his first letter. He calls them elect exiles of the dispersion (1 Peter 1:1). Sit on both of those words a second. Elect. Chosen, beloved, secure, held. And exiles. Displaced, foreign, scattered, without standing in the empire that surrounded them. Both at once, with no contradiction, no tension Peter feels any need to resolve. The earliest Christians had no cultural power at all. No Constantine. No Christian magistrate. No Sunday protected by law. No chaplain at the emperor's table, no prayer at the inauguration, no cross on the courthouse lawn. What they had was a crucified Lord, a borrowed upstairs room, and a witness that got a lot of them killed. And out of that, not in spite of it, out of it, the faith spread across the whole Roman world in three centuries.

We've spent sixteen hundred years forgetting that. We took a long, strange, unusual stretch of cultural establishment and mistook it for the normal condition of the people of God. It was never normal. It was the exception. And now the exception is ending, and we're being returned to the condition we were born in, and we're treating the return like a death.

I keep coming back to Jeremiah, and I'll come back to him a lot in this book, so let me set him down here at the start. When Babylon hauled the people of Judah off into exile, the natural thing, the human thing, was to assume God had failed and to plan the quickest possible return. Jeremiah sent them a letter that told them to do almost the opposite. Build houses and live in them. Plant gardens and eat what they grow. Marry, have children, let your children marry. And then the line that should stop a Christendom church cold. Seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare (Jeremiah 29:5-7). He didn't tell them to mount a campaign to recover Jerusalem. He told them to settle in and serve the city that had conquered them and did not want their God. Because the exile was going to be long, and faithfulness would not be measured by how fast they got their power back. It would be measured by how well they loved a city that never asked for them.

That's our assignment. Not the recovery of a country. The cultivation of a witness, from a position of weakness, over a long time, in a place that did not send for us.

Let me stay with that diner a little longer, because I don't want this to drift into the abstract too fast, and because that diner is where I actually do most of my real pastoral work. The man across from me, let's call him a composite of a dozen real men, came up in ministry the same way I did. He was told that if he preached the Word and loved the people and worked hard, the church would grow, because that's how it worked for his father and his father's mentor. And he did all of it. He preached the Word. He loved the people. He worked himself half to death. And the church shrank anyway, slowly, a family at a time, the young ones first, and now he's fifty-six years old and the thing he gave his whole life to is smaller than when he started, and nobody told him this was possible, let alone likely, and he has concluded, in the quiet of his own heart where he'd never say it out loud, that he must have failed. That's the wound under the complaint. He thinks he failed, because he was handed a map that said faithfulness produces growth, and he was faithful and didn't get growth, so the only conclusion the map allows is personal failure. And I have to spend the rest of that cup of coffee, and usually several more conversations after it, trying to hand him a different map, one on which a man can be entirely faithful and still watch his church shrink, because the shrinking isn't mainly about him. It's about the draining of the pond. He's not a failed pastor. He's a faithful one who was handed the wrong measuring stick, and the wrong measuring stick is killing him as surely as any sin would.

I labor that point because the wrong map doesn't just confuse our strategy. It condemns our souls. A whole generation of pastors is walking around under a low-grade sense of failure that they did not earn, because they measured themselves by Christendom's metrics in a post-Christendom world, and Christendom's metrics will tell a faithful man he's a failure every single time the culture stops cooperating. The first gift of the right map is that it lifts a false guilt off of good men. You did not fail. The country changed. Those are different things, and a man who can tell them apart can breathe again.

Now, I can already hear the objection, because I've heard it from men I respect. Isn't this just an excuse? Isn't this just a comfortable way for declining churches to feel good about declining, a theology of failure dressed up as faithfulness, a permission slip to stop trying? And I take that objection seriously, because there's a real danger in it. Yes, there are lazy pastors who would love a theology that excuses their laziness, and a man can absolutely hide his sloth or his sin behind the language of exile and blame the culture for fruit that's missing because he never planted anything. So let me be clear. The exile is not an excuse to stop working. Jeremiah didn't tell the exiles to sit down and feel theological about their displacement. He told them to build and plant and multiply and seek the welfare of the city, which is a tremendous amount of work, harder work in some ways than maintaining an establishment. The exile changes what we work for and how we measure the work. It does not cancel the work. A faithful exile is exhausted at the end of the day, just not from chasing a census that isn't coming. So when I tell that pastor he didn't fail, I am not telling him to do less. I'm telling him to stop measuring his enormous, faithful labor against a number that was always going to lie to him.

I'm not going to pretend the rest of this book resolves all that into something you can run on Monday morning. Exile doesn't resolve. It gets endured, and in the enduring it turns into the place where God is most plainly with his people. What I'm going to try to do is walk the ground with you. How we got here, beginning with one edict in the fourth century and a long establishment after it and a fast collapse in our own time. What the Bible knows about exile that we forgot. What it does to a pastor's soul to lead without the borrowed power, and what kind of church can actually witness when the power is gone. What it asks of our worship, our children, our suffering, our friendships with other pastors who are drowning in the same water we are.

Before I close this opening chapter, I want to say a word about the tone of everything that follows, because tone is going to matter as much as content in a book like this. There are a lot of books right now about the decline of the church, and most of them fall into one of two registers, and I want to avoid both. The first register is panic, the alarm-bell book, the everything-is-collapsing-and-here-is-the-enemy book, written in a key of fear and often of anger, and I understand why those books sell, because fear sells, but I don't think fear has ever produced faithfulness, and I'm not going to try to frighten you into the exile. The second register is the breezy, optimistic, it's-all-going-to-be-fine book, the one that pats you on the head and tells you the next revival is coming and you just need to stay positive, and I find that register dishonest, because it refuses to look at the actual numbers and the actual loss, and you can't be comforted by someone who won't tell you the truth about your situation.

I'm trying for a third register, and I'll probably miss it sometimes, but I want to name the aim. The register I want is the one a good doctor uses when the news is serious but not hopeless, the register of someone who looks you in the eye and tells you the truth, the whole truth, including the hard parts, and who is also, somehow, not afraid, because he knows something about the larger situation that lets him be honest without panic and hopeful without lying. That's the register of Jeremiah's letter, when you read it carefully. It does not minimize the exile, seventy years, you'll die here, and it does not despair of it, build, plant, seek the welfare, I have plans for you. Honest and unafraid at the same time. That's hard to pull off, and the only way to pull it off is to actually believe the thing that makes it possible, which is that the God who is sovereign over the rise of Christendom is just as sovereign over its fall, that he is not wringing his hands in heaven over the secularization of the West, that the collapse did not catch him off guard, and that he is up to something in it that we can trust even when we can't see it. If I believe that, I can tell you the truth without panic. If I don't, I'll either minimize the loss to comfort you or exaggerate it to frighten you. The whole book stands or falls on whether God is actually sovereign over the exile, and I'm staking it on the conviction that he is.

The map we were handed is wrong. But there's an older map. It was drawn by people who never expected the empire to love them, and it has not failed yet. We're going to learn to read it again.

We are not losing. We are being returned.
chapters.verdict: We are not losing. We are being returned.

chapters.title: How Christendom Was Born
chapters.summary: The arrangement we mistook for normal Christianity began with Constantine's vision in 312 and Theodosius making the faith the official religion in 380. What was won in those decades, protection and status and power, came with a cost the church has never fully reckoned.
chapters.body:
To understand what's ending, you have to know how it began, and it began on a specific day, with a specific man, who saw a specific sign. In October of the year 312, Constantine marched on Rome to fight his rival Maxentius at a crossing called the Milvian Bridge. The story comes down to us through Eusebius and Lactantius, tangled up with legend the way these things always are, and it goes like this. Constantine saw a cross of light in the sky, with words attached to it. In this sign, conquer. He had his soldiers mark their shields. He won the battle, threw Maxentius into the Tiber, and the most powerful man in the world began to identify the God of the crucified Galilean as the God who gives you victory in war.

I want you to sit with that sentence, because everything that followed grows out of it. The God who was executed by the empire became the God who helped the empire win.

The next year, in 313, Constantine and his co-emperor Licinius issued what we've come to call the Edict of Milan, which granted toleration to Christians, returned confiscated property, and ended the persecutions. You have to feel what that meant to the people who received it. The church had spent the better part of three centuries as an illegal minority, hunted in waves, sometimes left alone for a generation and then suddenly, under Decius or under Diocletian, dragged back into the arenas. There were Christians still alive in 313 who had watched friends die under Diocletian's persecution just a decade earlier, the worst one, the one that tried to burn the Scriptures and level the church buildings. And then, almost overnight, it stopped. The killing stopped. The pastor who could have been arrested last year could build openly this year. The bishops who'd hidden could meet in daylight. To a mother who'd feared for her sons, this was not an abstraction. It was the difference between dread and breath. I will not be cynical about that. The end of the persecutions was a mercy, and a mother's relief is a real thing.

Then it kept going. In 325 Constantine summoned the Council of Nicaea and presided over it, and the church hammered out the doctrine of Christ's full divinity against Arius, who taught that the Son was a created being, the highest creature but a creature still. Nicaea gave us the words we still confess, that the Son is of one substance with the Father, begotten not made. Good words. True words. The church needed them and I'm glad we have them. But notice who called the council and sat at its head. Not a bishop. The emperor. A man who, as far as anyone can tell, was not yet baptized and did not fully grasp the theology he was refereeing. That should have alarmed us more than it did.

The whole arrangement got finished in 380, when the emperor Theodosius issued the Edict of Thessalonica and made Nicene Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire. Within a few years the old pagan sacrifices were banned outright. The faith of the catacombs had become the faith of the throne. Inside of one long lifetime, the church went from a body the empire killed to a body the empire enforced. That's fast. Less than seventy years, which I find a haunting number given how this book ends, from Diocletian's fires to Theodosius's establishment. The people who lived through it could be forgiven for calling it a miracle.

And in some ways it was. I'm not going to flatten this into a simple story about the church selling out, because real goods came with the change, and a man who can't see the goods can't be trusted to weigh the costs. The persecutions ended. The slow Christianizing of Roman law softened some of its cruelties; the games grew less bloody, infants got a little more protection, the slave a few more rights. The church gained the stability to think, to build, to send missionaries north into the forests. The cathedrals and the universities and the hospitals that came centuries later all grew in soil that Constantine cleared. I've stood in those cathedrals. I've felt what they were built to make you feel. You don't get Chartres out of the catacombs in one generation. Establishment gave the church room, and the church did beautiful things with the room.

The clearest-eyed man of that whole era saw both sides at once, and his name was Augustine. He wrote The City of God a century after Constantine, as the empire was coming apart at the seams, after Rome itself was sacked in 410 and pagans were blaming the Christians for abandoning the old gods who'd supposedly kept the city safe. Augustine refused to take the bait. He would not make Christianity the guarantor of Rome's fortunes. He drew a line down the middle of all human history, two cities, the City of God and the City of Man, built by two loves, the love of God to the point of contempt for self and the love of self to the point of contempt for God. And the two cities, he insisted, are tangled together in this age, never to be collapsed into each other, never to be identified with any earthly kingdom, not even a Christian one. The City of God is a pilgrim here. It's passing through. It doesn't own the empire and the empire doesn't own it. Augustine saw the danger of the fusion even as the fusion was being built around him. He saw it. And then we forgot it, almost completely, for over a thousand years.

Because the cost was real, and it got paid slowly, in a currency nobody noticed they were spending. When the empire stopped killing the church, it started owning it. The pastor who used to answer to God and to a small frightened flock now answered, partly, to the magistrate who protected him and signed his salary and expected his loyalty. The faith that had been a costly decision against the grain became, in a generation or two, the unremarkable condition of being born inside the empire. You were a Christian the way you were a Roman, by location, by inheritance, by default, the way you'd be a Buckeye if you grew up in Columbus. The category of the convert started to fade. The category of the citizen-believer took its place, and the citizen-believer doesn't have to repent of anything to belong, because belonging is automatic.

I want to name the deep structure here as plainly as I can, because the word Christendom gets thrown around and most people don't stop to define it. Christendom is the arrangement where Christian faith and cultural belonging get fused together, so that to be a member of the society is presumed to be a member of the church, and the institutions of faith get braided into the institutions of power. It is not the same thing as Christianity. Let me say that again, because it's the hinge of this whole book. Christendom is not Christianity. It's a particular, historically conditioned settlement between the gospel and a civilization. It happened in time and it can end in time, and it is ending in our time, and the gospel will outlive it the way the gospel outlived the catacombs. When you grieve, grieve the right thing. We are losing Christendom. We are not losing Christ.

And like every settlement, it traded something away to get what it got. What it traded was the church's clarity about its own strangeness. Stanley Hauerwas has been pressing this point his whole career, sometimes too sharply, but he's right at the center of it. The church in Christendom forgot that it was supposed to be a contrast society, a colony of heaven, a people whose common life was itself the argument. When everybody is a Christian, nobody has to be. The distinction between the church and the world, which the New Testament treats as the whole point, gets sanded down until the church is just the spiritual department of the broader culture, there to bless the harvest and marry the young and bury the dead and put a sheen of the sacred over the social order. The salt loses its bite. Not because anyone decided to throw it out, but because it got dissolved into so much soup that you could no longer taste it.

Let me bring this home, because it's easy to keep it safely back in the fourth century. I have benefited from this arrangement my entire ministry, and so have you. When I tell a stranger I'm a pastor, the leftover residue of Christendom still buys me a half-second of respect I did not earn and could not have earned in three centuries of Rome. When my church files its paperwork, the state still treats us with a deference that quietly assumes our usefulness. When there's a tragedy in town, somebody still thinks to call a pastor, even somebody who hasn't darkened a church door in twenty years. We've been swimming in this water so long that we mistake it for the ocean. It is not the ocean. It's a pond the empire dug for us in the fourth century, and the pond is drying up, and we are going to have to learn to live as fish that were always meant for the sea.

I want to slow down on one figure from that era, because he's become a kind of patron saint of mine for thinking about all this, and that's Augustine, and not just the famous bishop but the man underneath the office. Augustine had been a pagan, a brilliant and dissolute one, chasing prestige and pleasure and the next intellectual fashion, and he came to Christ as an adult, dramatically, in a garden in Milan, hearing a child's voice chanting take up and read and opening the Scriptures to a verse in Romans that broke him open. So Augustine, like me, came to the faith from outside it, which I think is part of why he could see the danger of the establishment so clearly while everyone around him was celebrating. A convert never quite loses his outsider's eyes. He remembers what it was like to not believe, and that memory keeps him from assuming that the surrounding Christian culture is the same thing as the kingdom of God. Augustine had watched Rome from the inside as a pagan and from the inside as a Christian, and he knew the city of man too well to mistake it for the City of God, even when it had a cross on its standards.

And the thing he saw, that I keep coming back to, is that the danger of establishment is not mainly that the church might become wicked, though it might. The danger is subtler and harder to fight. The danger is that the church might become comfortable, that it might fuse with the social order so thoroughly that it loses the ability to imagine itself as anything other than the social order's spiritual department. Augustine wanted to keep the two cities distinct not because he hated Rome but because he loved the church and knew that a church which forgot it was a pilgrim, a church which settled down and got comfortable and started thinking of the empire as home, would lose the very thing that made it the church. The City of God is always packing its bags. It's always on the way somewhere. The moment it unpacks and hangs pictures and decides it has arrived is the moment it forgets what it is. Christendom was the church unpacking its bags and hanging pictures and forgetting it was a pilgrim, and it took sixteen centuries and a collapse to remind us that we were never supposed to settle.

There's an objection I should handle here, because thoughtful people raise it and they're not wrong to. Aren't you being ungrateful? All those goods you just listed, the hospitals and the universities and the end of the persecutions and the softening of the law, those were real, they helped real people, and they came through the establishment you're critiquing. Isn't there something precious and ungracious about a comfortable American pastor in the twenty-first century, who has benefited from every one of those goods, sitting back and second-guessing the arrangement that produced them? And I feel the weight of that, I do. Here's my answer. I'm not saying Constantine was a disaster or that the establishment produced nothing good. I'm saying that the goods came with a hidden cost, that the cost was paid in a currency we didn't notice, the currency of the church's clarity about its own strangeness, and that the time to count the cost is now, when the arrangement is ending anyway and we have to decide what we're actually grieving. You can be grateful for the cathedral and still see that the cathedral taught us to mistake grandeur for faithfulness. Gratitude and critique are not opposites. A son can be grateful for his inheritance and still see that the inheritance made him soft. That's not ingratitude. That's growing up.

Here's the question that should keep us up at night. Jesus said his kingdom was not of this world (John 18:36). He refused the crowd that wanted to make him king by force, and he slipped away from them up the mountain by himself (John 6:15). He told us that whoever wants to be great among us has to become a servant, and that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, but it shall not be so among you (Mark 10:42-43). Every one of those sentences cuts against the logic of Constantine. And yet for sixteen centuries we built our common life on the assumption that the empire's favor was a gift from God instead of a temptation to resist.

There's a question that comes up whenever I teach this material to pastors, and it's a good one, so let me put it here. If Christendom was such a compromise, are you saying Constantine should have refused the toleration, that the church should have wanted to keep being persecuted, that the establishment was simply a mistake the church should have rejected? And my answer is no, and the no matters, because I'm not trying to make us feel guilty for an arrangement our ancestors couldn't have foreseen the costs of. The end of the persecutions was a mercy, full stop, and no Christian should have wanted the killing to continue for the sake of some theological purity. The toleration was good. The problem was never the toleration. The problem was the fusion that came after, the slow slide from being tolerated to being established to being identical with the culture, and that slide happened over generations and nobody chose it as a whole, each step seemed reasonable in its moment, and the people who took the steps could not have seen where the road led any more than we can see where ours leads.

So I'm not condemning Constantine, and I'm not saying the church should have stayed in the catacombs. I'm saying that the church, having gained its freedom, failed to stay vigilant about the difference between freedom and fusion, between being tolerated and being established, between the gospel and the culture that carried it. It accepted the gift, which was right, and then it forgot that the gift was not the Giver, that the empire's favor was not the same as God's favor, that being respectable was not the same as being faithful. The failure was not in accepting the toleration. The failure was in falling asleep, in letting the centuries of favor lull the church into mistaking its cultural home for its true home, into forgetting that it was a pilgrim, into building the establishment as though it would last forever and was the point. We can't go back and tell Constantine to leave us in the arena. But we can refuse, now, on the way out of the establishment, to repeat the church's deepest mistake, which was never accepting the favor but forgetting what the favor was, and letting it put us to sleep.

Maybe it was both. Augustine would say it was both, and that the whole of wisdom lay in never confusing the gift with the Giver, the City of Man with the City of God. We did confuse them. We spent the inheritance and called it blessing, and now the inheritance is gone, and we are finding out what we actually have left.

There's one more thing I want to draw out of the Constantine story before we leave the fourth century, because it's the thing that most directly mirrors our moment, only in reverse. The early church, the persecuted church, the church before Constantine, knew exactly who it was. It had no choice. When following Jesus could get you killed, nobody joined the church by accident, nobody was a Christian by inheritance or social convenience, because there was no social convenience in it, there was only cost. So the pre-Constantinian church was, by necessity, a converted church, a church of people who had counted the cost and paid it, a church with a sharp edge and a clear boundary and a vivid sense of its own difference from the world. It didn't have to work to be a contrast society. The persecution did that work for it, by ensuring that only the serious stayed. And then Constantine removed the cost, and within a few generations the church filled up with people who had paid nothing, who were Christians because everyone was, and the edge dulled and the boundary blurred and the contrast faded, not because anyone decided to compromise but because the absence of cost let in the uncommitted by the thousands.

Now run that in reverse and you have our moment exactly. The cost is coming back. Not the cost of death, not here, not soon, but the cost of inconvenience, of lost status, of being one of those people, and that returning cost is going to do to our churches what its absence undid. It's going to clear out the merely cultural Christians, the ones who were here for the social benefit, because the social benefit is gone and soon there'll be a mild social cost instead, and people don't pay even a mild cost for something they never really believed. And what's left, after the clearing, will be a smaller, sharper, more converted church, a church that more closely resembles the church before Constantine than the church after him, a church with an edge again because the cost has restored the edge. That's the strange symmetry of it. The thing Constantine started by removing the cost, the exile is undoing by restoring it. We are being handed back, by the loss of our privilege, the very clarity that the gaining of our privilege took away. The pond is draining, and the fish that can only live in the pond are leaving, and what remains will be fish that were always meant for the sea.

The day the empire stopped killing us, it started owning us. We are only now learning what we sold, and at what price, and whether we want it back.
chapters.verdict: The day the empire stopped killing us, it started owning us.
reflect: What did your church gain by being respectable, and what did it quietly lose to keep that respectability?
Can you tell the difference in your own ministry between the authority of the gospel and the authority of social status?
If the state withdrew every favor it has ever shown the church, what in your work would actually stop?

chapters.title: The Long Establishment
chapters.summary: For more than a thousand years, Christendom shaped Europe and then America, the calendars and laws and schools and the felt sense that to be civilized was to be Christian. The arrangement carried real goods and real corruptions, and it trained the church to mistake cultural dominance for faithfulness.
chapters.body:
What Constantine began and Theodosius established, the next thousand years built into the bones of a civilization. This is the part of the story we tell ourselves with the most affection and the least suspicion, because it's genuinely the era of the cathedral and the chant, of Aquinas and Dante and Bach a bit later, of the monastery copying out manuscripts by candlelight through centuries when almost no one else could read, of the university that grew up out of the cathedral school. I don't want to spit on it. There's a reason a Baptist pastor from Fenton, Michigan, can stand in a French cathedral he didn't build and doesn't theologically endorse and feel his throat tighten. Christendom made beautiful things. The medieval church fed the poor and ransomed captives and built the first hospitals and kept Europe from forgetting how to read. Credit where it's owed.

It also made the one assumption that would eventually undo us, and it made it so thoroughly that we stopped being able to see it. The assumption was simple. To be a member of European society was to be a Christian, and to be a Christian was to be a member of European society. The two were one thing. The calendar was the church's calendar, feast days and fast days and saints' days, Advent and Lent and Easter organizing time itself, so that you couldn't tell a farmer's year from the liturgical year because they were the same year. The law absorbed the church's moral vocabulary. Kings were crowned by bishops, and the crowning was a sacrament of legitimacy, a way of saying God put this man here. The village organized itself around the parish, and the parish boundaries simply were the social boundaries, the map of belonging. You were baptized into a faith and a polity in the same moment, usually as an infant who got no say, and you couldn't tell where the one ended and the other began. There was no line, because the whole achievement of Christendom was the erasing of the line.

Now you'd think the Reformation would have broken this. It didn't. It rearranged it. Luther needed the German princes to survive, and they needed him, and the principle that came out of the religious wars was this Latin tag, cuius regio, eius religio, whose realm, his religion. The prince's confession decided the people's confession. If your prince was Lutheran, you were Lutheran; if he turned, you turned, or you moved. The map of Europe became a map of established churches, each one fused to its state. Lutheran here, Reformed there, Anglican across the channel, Catholic to the south. The fusion of faith and power was never questioned. Only the denomination on the letterhead changed.

There was one group that did question it, and I want to dwell on them because they were treated as heretics for proposing exactly what we are now being forced into. The Anabaptists. They said the church should be a gathered body of believers, people who chose the faith as adults and were baptized on their confession, separated from the surrounding society, holding the faith by conviction rather than by birth, expecting no protection from the magistrate and wielding no sword. In the sixteenth century that was not an interesting alternative ecclesiology. It was a death sentence. Protestants and Catholics, who agreed on almost nothing else, agreed on drowning Anabaptists, and they did, by the hundreds, sometimes mockingly, since you want a baptism, here's your baptism, holding them under in the rivers and lakes of Switzerland and the Low Countries. They burned them too. Because the Anabaptists had touched the one nerve that no one in Christendom would let be touched. They had suggested that the church might not need the state's arm to survive. For suggesting that, they died.

I dwell on them because history has a grim way of vindicating the people it murders. What got an Anabaptist drowned in 1527 is, in 2026, simply a description of where the Western church is headed. A gathered people, distinct from the surrounding culture, holding the faith by conviction because there's no longer any cultural reward for holding it by inheritance, expecting nothing from the magistrate. The thing they died for is becoming our ordinary condition. I'm not saying their whole program was right. I'm a Baptist, not an Anabaptist, and there are real differences. But on this one nerve, the nerve of whether the church needs the state to prop it up, they saw something five hundred years early, and they paid for the seeing.

America complicated the picture without breaking the pattern, and this part matters because it's the air most of my readers were raised in. The founders, having watched Europe tear itself apart in religious wars, declined to establish a national church. The First Amendment said Congress would make no law respecting an establishment of religion. That was genuinely new and genuinely good, and I'll defend it. But here is what people miss. Disestablishment in law did not mean disestablishment in culture. What grew up in America instead was a softer, more durable Christendom. Not a state church, but a civil religion, a broad Protestant consensus that soaked the whole public square.

A sociologist named Robert Bellah named it in a famous essay back in 1967. He called it American civil religion, a set of shared beliefs and rituals that gave the nation a sacred self-understanding without naming any particular church. God on the currency. God in the pledge, added in the 1950s precisely to distinguish us from the godless Soviets. God invoked at every inauguration, by presidents who may or may not have meant it. The sense that America was a nation under a deity, accountable to him, blessed by him, a city on a hill. The church didn't run the state. But the church and the state agreed about enough that the pastor stayed a public figure, Sunday stayed protected, the high school moved the football game so it wouldn't conflict with church, and the basic Christian story stayed the water the culture swam in. You could be a thoroughgoing secularist in 1960 and still know the story, still feel its pull, still get married in a church because that's what you did.

That's the Christendom my generation of pastors was trained inside, and it shaped how we measured absolutely everything. We learned to count. We measured the kingdom by attendance, by buildings, by budgets, by the standing of the pastor in the Rotary Club, by how many came to the Easter service, by whether the new family in town visited us first or the church down the road. We took the deference of the culture as evidence of the favor of God. When the numbers were up we assumed we were faithful. When a church grew we assumed it was blessed. We built a whole apparatus of success, books and conferences and metrics and best practices, and underneath all of it was a machine for measuring one thing. How thoroughly the surrounding culture still agreed to carry us.

We learned to measure the kingdom by the census, and the census lied to us.

I want to confess how deep this goes in me, because it's not just a strategic error I can fix by adopting better metrics, it's a hunger in my own heart that the better metrics don't touch. Even now, knowing everything I've written here, I still feel the pull on a Sunday morning when I look out at the room. If it's full, something in me lifts, feels validated, feels successful, even though I know better. If it's thin, something in me sinks, feels like a failure, takes it personally, even though I know the thinness is mostly the draining of the pond and not the verdict on my faithfulness. The census got into me, down deep, in the years I was formed by it, and it didn't leave just because I figured out it was lying. The idol doesn't leave when you discover it's an idol. It leaves slowly, painfully, as God pries your fingers off it one at a time, and the prying hurts because the thing felt like life to you, felt like the source of your worth, and letting go feels like dying. The exile is the prying. Every thin Sunday is God working another finger loose, and it hurts, and it's mercy, because the census was never going to be able to bear the weight I put on it, and a man whose worth rests on the census is a man who'll be destroyed by a draining pond, and God loves me too much to let my worth rest there.

Here's why it lied. Cultural Christianity and converted Christianity produce the exact same statistics for a long, long time before they diverge. A nation full of people who are Christian by inheritance looks, on paper, identical to a nation full of people who are Christian by conviction. The pews are full either way. The census counts heads, not hearts. It cannot tell the difference between a man who'd die for Jesus and a man who shows up because his wife makes him and the boss expects it. And so for centuries the church mistook the breadth of nominal belief for the depth of real discipleship, because nothing forced the difference out into the open. That's one way to understand Christendom, honestly. It's a machine for hiding the difference between the crowd and the church. As long as the machine ran, you could never tell how many of the people in the building actually wanted Jesus, because there was no cost to being there and every social reward, so of course they were there.

And the corruptions ran deeper than just miscounting. When faith is the price of belonging, faith gets coerced, and coerced faith is a contradiction the New Testament will not allow. You cannot make a disciple at the point of a sword; you can only make a hypocrite. When the church holds the sword, it uses the sword. The Inquisition. The wars of religion that killed a third of Germany. The conquered peoples of the Americas baptized at swordpoint, their old gods smashed and their new God offered with a musket. When the bishop sits at the king's table, the bishop learns to flatter the king, and the prophetic voice goes quiet. The voice that's supposed to say to power, thus says the LORD, you have done evil, that voice gets domesticated by the very arrangement that gave the man his platform. Walter Brueggemann has a name for this. He calls it the royal consciousness, the way established religion, fused to established power, slowly loses the ability to imagine the world being any different than it is, loses its nerve, and settles down into managing the status quo and blessing the king. Christendom was, among other things, a thousand-year exercise in the royal consciousness. We forgot how to grieve, and we forgot how to hope, because both of those require a distance from power that we no longer had.

Let me make the census problem concrete, because it's easy to nod along with the critique while still being trapped inside it, and I was trapped inside it for years without knowing it. Early in my ministry I went to a conference, the kind we all went to, where a very successful pastor of a very large church told a few thousand of us how he'd done it, and I sat there with a notebook taking it all down, the systems and the strategies and the principles, and I drove home electrified, certain I'd been handed the keys. And I went to work applying it, and some of it even worked in the sense that the numbers ticked up for a season, and I felt the rush of that, the validation, the sense that I was finally doing ministry right. And it took me an embarrassingly long time to notice that nothing in that whole conference, not one session, had been about whether the people coming in were actually becoming disciples of Jesus. It was all about getting them in the door and keeping them in the building. The entire apparatus was a machine for improving the census, and I had received it as a machine for advancing the kingdom, and I never questioned the equation because the equation was the water I swam in. More people in the building equals more kingdom. That was the unstated axiom under everything, and it's false, and Christendom is what made it feel true.

Because here's what the axiom hides. You can grow a church to thousands and disciple no one. You can fill a building with people who are, every one of them, exactly as enslaved to the spirit of the age on the way out as they were on the way in, who've added a religious accessory to an essentially unconverted life, and the census will glow and the kingdom will not have advanced one inch. And the reverse is also true and even harder to swallow. You can pastor a church that shrinks for ten years and disciple a handful of people so deeply that they become unshakable, that they raise children who follow Jesus, that they bless their city in ways that ripple for generations, and the census will show decline the whole time. Christendom could not see the difference between those two churches, because Christendom only counted heads, and on a headcount the first church is a triumph and the second is a tragedy. The exile is teaching us to see the difference, and seeing it is painful, because some of our biggest success stories are going to turn out to have been the first kind of church, and some of our quiet failures are going to turn out to have been the second.

I think about the prophet Samuel at Jesse's house, sent to anoint a king, looking at the tall impressive sons and being sure each one was the one, and the LORD telling him, do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). The census is man looking on the outward appearance. It counts what's tall and visible and impressive, and it cannot see the heart, which is the only thing God counts. Christendom trained us to be Samuel looking at the tall sons, certain that the impressive thing was the anointed thing, and the exile is the voice saying, you're measuring the wrong thing, you've always been measuring the wrong thing, look lower, look at the heart, look at the one nobody bothered to call in from the field.

And here's my confession, and I think it's the confession of a whole generation of American pastors. I was formed to want the census. I wanted the full sanctuary. I wanted the respected name, the seat at the table, the call from the newspaper when something happened. I read the books on growth and I went to the conferences on influence, and I measured my faithfulness by the very metrics that Christendom invented to hide its own hollowness. I am not pointing at someone else here. I did this. We did this. The man writing this book spent years counting the things the census counts and calling the count a calling.

I want to be fair to the long establishment, because I've been hard on it and a wise reader will sense that I'm tilting the scales, and I don't want to do that. So let me say the genuinely good thing it did, the thing we'll miss most and should. The establishment carried the faith across centuries and continents in a way that a perpetually persecuted church might not have managed. It built the institutions that preserved and transmitted the Scriptures, copied them by hand through the dark centuries, translated them, eventually printed them. It created the conditions for theology to develop, for the great creeds and confessions to be hammered out, for the church to think long and hard about God across generations of relative peace. It produced art and music and architecture that have lifted human hearts toward God for a thousand years and still do. It established the assumption, now eroding, that human beings have dignity because they're made in God's image, an assumption our whole civilization still runs on even as it forgets where it came from. These are not small things. A man who can't see them is as blind as the man who can't see the corruptions. The establishment was a mixed bag, like every human arrangement, carrying real treasure and real poison in the same vessel, and the honest reckoning has to hold both.

But consider what happens to treasure carried in a corrupt vessel. The treasure does not need the vessel. That's the whole point, and it's the point Christendom made it hard for us to see. The Scriptures do not need an established church to survive; they survived in Babylon, they survived in the catacombs, they survive right now in places where owning a Bible is a crime, smuggled and memorized and copied by hand all over again. The dignity of the human person does not need a Christian civilization to be true; it was true before Constantine and it'll be true after the last Christian nation forgets it. The deep theology, the great worship, the love of neighbor, none of it requires the establishment, because none of it came from the establishment. It came from God, and the establishment was just one vessel that carried it for a while, and now the vessel is cracking, and the treasure is rolling out onto the ground, and our job is not to mourn the vessel but to gather up the treasure and find a new way to carry it. The exile church will carry the same treasure the establishment carried. It'll just carry it the way the exiles carried it, the way the catacomb church carried it, in earthen vessels, on foot, at cost, without the protection of the empire. And the treasure will be just as real. It was always the treasure that mattered. We just couldn't tell, while the vessel was so grand, how little the treasure depended on it.

The long establishment is ending now, and the ending is not the tragedy. Hear me. The ending is not the tragedy. The tragedy is how thoroughly the establishment taught us to count the wrong things, so that now, when the census finally tells the truth, we mistake the truth for a disaster. The gift hidden inside the loss is that the census is finally being taken honestly. We're about to learn how many of us there really are. And I'll be honest, that number frightens me, because I suspect it's smaller than our buildings suggested, smaller than our records claim, smaller than we want it to be. The pews that emptied were partly the pews of people who were never converted in the first place, who came because it was expected and left when it stopped being expected, and their leaving makes the building feel like a defeat when it's actually just the truth becoming visible. But a true small number is worth more than a false large one, because you can shepherd a true number, can disciple it, can build something real on it, and you can do nothing lasting on a false count except mistake it for health. I would rather pastor forty real disciples than four hundred names on a roll, half of whom I've never met and most of whom would not notice if the doors closed. The honest census is a hard gift. It's still a gift. You cannot heal what you will not diagnose, and the emptying is, among other things, a diagnosis we badly needed and were never going to get as long as the culture kept the buildings full of people who didn't believe.

That's a frightening number to wait for. It's also the most useful number the church could possibly receive, because you cannot shepherd a flock you've never actually counted.
chapters.verdict: We learned to measure the kingdom by the census, and the census lied to us.
reflect: What habits of measurement in your church assume that bigger and more respected means more faithful?
Where has your tradition baptized a cultural arrangement and called it biblical?
What would it mean to separate the gospel from the civilization that carried it without despising either?

chapters.title: The Collapse
chapters.summary: The Christendom settlement that took sixteen centuries to build came apart in roughly one, through war and secularization and the sexual revolution and the rise of the nones and the digital reordering of authority. The collapse is not coming. It has happened.
chapters.body:
A thing that takes sixteen centuries to build can come apart in one, and ours did. If you want a rough span to hold in your head, take the hundred-some years from 1914 to now, and watch the water drain out of the pond.

The First World War broke something in the Christian West that never healed. Think about what it actually was. A civilization that called itself Christian spent four years feeding its own young men into machine guns operated by other young men who also called themselves Christian, and the bishops on both sides blessed the slaughter from their cathedrals. German chaplains told German boys that God was with the Kaiser. English chaplains told English boys that God was with the King. They couldn't both be right and they were probably both wrong, and the boys in the mud started to suspect it. The civil religion that had wrapped the nation in the sacred got exposed, at the Somme and at Verdun, where men died by the tens of thousands for a few hundred yards of ruined ground, as a god that demanded children and gave nothing back. The cheerful liberal Christianity of the prewar years, the kind that assumed history was a gentle upward climb and the kingdom of God was more or less the same thing as progress and good manners, that died in the trenches and never came back.

Then the Second World War, and the death camps built in the heart of the most educated, most musical, most theologically sophisticated Christian nation in Europe. That finished the demolition of the old confidence. A church fused to a culture gets carried wherever that culture goes, and the German culture, with its great universities and its Bach and its Luther, went to Auschwitz, and most of the German church went along, or kept quiet, or worse. Dietrich Bonhoeffer saw it from the inside and named the cost and paid it. He wrote about a world come of age, a humanity that had learned to run its own affairs without God as a working hypothesis, and he refused the cheap grace of a church that wanted to bless the world without dying to it. He went home to Germany when he could have stayed safe in New York. He joined the conspiracy against Hitler. They hanged him at Flossenbürg in April of 1945, naked at the gallows, a few weeks before the camp was liberated. The clearest-eyed German pastor of the century died because he understood, before almost anyone, that Christendom's god and the gospel's God were not the same god, and that when the test came, the people who'd been formed by Christendom would mostly bow to the wrong one.

After the war came the long secularization, and this is where the numbers start to move fast. Europe emptied its churches with stunning speed. The great cathedrals became museums where tourists shuffle through with audio guides; the parish became a postal address; in some English cities the Sunday attendance is now a fraction of one percent. America held on longer, propped up by the religious boom of the 1950s, the Eisenhower years, the new churches in the new suburbs, Billy Graham filling stadiums. But the 1960s loosened the grip, and the place it loosened first was sex. The sexual revolution detached the culture's moral imagination from the church's, and once sex got renegotiated without any reference to the church, everything downstream of sex followed. Marriage, divorce, the family, the meaning of the body, what we owe each other, who gets to say. The church's authority to define the good life simply evaporated, not by argument but by erosion. People stopped asking the church what to do. And then, and this is the part that's easy to miss, they stopped even noticing that they had stopped. The church became, for most of our neighbors, not wrong, just irrelevant. Not the enemy. The furniture. The old building on the corner that you drive past.

Then came the numbers no pastor in my generation can unsee. For most of American history the religiously unaffiliated were a rounding error, two or three percent, the village atheists and the genuinely lost. Starting in the early 1990s the line began to climb, and it has not stopped. The nones, the people who check no religious affiliation, are now roughly a third of American adults, and among the young they're approaching half. I'm not going to pretend to precision the surveys don't have, but the shape of it is beyond dispute and it's the fastest religious change in the country's history. Here's the part that should reorder how you preach. The generation coming up was not, for the most part, raised in the faith and then lost it. Many were never raised in it at all. They're not lapsed. They're unevangelized, in a country that used to assume everyone had at least heard the story once. I've sat with young men in their twenties who could not have told you who Moses was, not because they rejected it but because no one ever told them. That's not the back end of Christendom. That's the front end of a mission field.

And the alliance with power, the thing that once protected the church, has turned into the thing most often held against it. When the church spent its accumulated credibility blessing a political order, defending its own institutions through cycle after cycle of abuse and cover-up, trading its prophetic voice for a seat at the table and a photo with the powerful, the watching culture drew the obvious conclusion. And I have to be honest with my own people here, because we want to call the conclusion unfair, and a lot of it isn't. The scandals were not incidental. They were structural. They are what happens when an institution accumulates more power than accountability, which is precisely the condition Christendom created. We taught a generation to associate the name of Christ with hypocrisy and the lust for power and the protecting of predators, and then we stood in our empty buildings and wondered why they wouldn't come. Some of the contempt we're receiving is contempt for the gospel. But a lot of it is the bill coming due for sins we actually committed, and a church that can't tell the difference will repent of the wrong things.

The last piece is the one happening in everyone's pocket right now, the digital reordering of authority. For most of Christendom's history the church was one of the very few sources of meaning a person ever encountered. The pastor was a gatekeeper of knowledge; for a lot of people he was the most educated man they knew. Now every person in your sanctuary carries a device that offers a thousand rival sources of meaning every hour, custom-fitted to their desires by an algorithm that knows them better than their spouse does, with no Sabbath and no gatekeeper and no closing time. The plausibility structures Christendom maintained, the felt sense that of course there's a God and of course the church matters, have been replaced by a structure that makes a thousand other things feel more plausible than the resurrection at three in the morning when you can't sleep. The church no longer competes with the village atheist down the street. It competes with the entire attention economy, and the attention economy never closes and never rests and is engineered by some of the smartest people alive to be impossible to put down. I have felt it in my own hand, the pull of the phone in the quiet moment that used to belong to prayer. We're not fighting unbelief. We're fighting a thousand small enchantments that leave no room for it.

I want to pause on the digital piece, because I think it's the part we understand least and it's reshaping everything underneath us in real time. We tend to think of the phone as a delivery system for bad content, and so we fight it on the level of content, we worry about what our kids are looking at, and that worry is legitimate. But the deeper thing the phone does isn't about content at all. It's about formation, about what kind of people we're becoming by the shape of how we spend our attention. The phone trains us, every hour, to expect novelty, to be unable to tolerate boredom, to want our desires met instantly, to compare ourselves endlessly to curated images of other lives, to perform a self for an audience, to consume rather than to dwell. And every one of those trained instincts is corrosive to the life of faith, which requires exactly the opposite, the ability to stay, to wait, to be bored in prayer, to be unseen, to be content, to dwell long with one text and one God instead of skimming a thousand things. We are forming, at scale, the first generation in human history that has never known sustained silence, never known a quiet that wasn't immediately fillable, and you cannot easily disciple a person who has lost the capacity to be quiet, because the knowledge of God comes to the quiet. Be still, and know that I am God (Psalm 46:10). We have built a civilization that is never still, and then we wonder why so few of us know God.

So when I say the church now competes with the attention economy, I don't mean the church needs a better app or a slicker presence on the platforms, though I'm not against those things. I mean the attention economy is forming people into a shape that makes the gospel hard to receive, not because they've heard it and rejected it, but because they've been trained out of the very capacities the gospel requires. The soil itself has changed. The seed of the word falls now onto ground that's been compacted by constant stimulation, packed hard like the path in the parable where the birds come and snatch the seed before it can root (Matthew 13:4, 19). It's not that people are more wicked than they used to be. It's that the ground is harder, and the sower has to reckon with the hardness of the ground, and a lot of our evangelistic methods assume a softer soil than actually exists out there now.

I'll be honest about my own complicity here too, because I'm not standing above the attention economy lecturing the kids about their screens. I check my phone in the bathroom. I reach for it in the quiet moment that used to be prayer, the moment in the car before I go in to the hospital visit, the moment in bed before sleep that I used to give to God and now give to a glowing rectangle that gives nothing back. I have felt my own attention shatter over the last fifteen years, felt my capacity to read a long book or sit in long silence erode, felt the pull of the thing in my pocket compete with and often beat the pull of the God I've given my life to serve. If it's doing that to me, a man whose whole vocation is attention to God, what is it doing to the sixteen-year-old who's never known anything else? I'm not the doctor diagnosing a disease I'm immune to. I've got it too. We've all got it. And a church that doesn't reckon honestly with what the attention economy is doing to its own people, starting with its pastors, is going to keep wondering why the word seems to land so shallow, when the answer is that the soil's been compacted by the thing we're all still holding in our hands.

So here's the verdict, and I won't soften it. The water we were swimming in has drained, and too many of us are flopping on the rocks calling it an attack. The collapse is not coming. It is not a storm on the horizon that a better strategy might steer us around. It has already happened. The country the old map described does not exist, and it is not coming back, and the energy we spend grieving its loss or scheming its return is energy stolen straight out of the assignment in front of us.

I say this as a man who has flopped on the rocks with the rest of them. I've preached the sermons that treated the collapse as an enemy assault instead of a homecoming. I've rallied my people to defend a cultural position instead of to inhabit an exile. I've wanted the device in the teenager's pocket to lose, as though the gospel needed the iPhone to fail in order to succeed. We did this. We read the collapse through the eyes of Christendom, which could only ever see in it a defeat, because Christendom had no other category for the loss of power than catastrophe.

But the Bible has another set of eyes, and that's where we're going next. The Bible was largely written by exiles, for exiles, out of the experience of having watched a settlement collapse. Jerusalem fell in 587 BC. The temple, the place God's own name was said to dwell, burned to the ground. The king was forced to watch his sons killed and then had his eyes put out and was dragged in chains to Babylon, the last thing he ever saw being the slaughter of his children (2 Kings 25:7). Everything the people had assumed about God's permanent favor and their permanent security came apart in a single brutal season. And out of that collapse came some of the deepest theology the world has ever received, because the collapse forced a question that prosperity never asks. Who is the LORD when the temple is ash and the empire holds the whip?

I want to name a particular grief inside the collapse, the one I think pastors feel most sharply and talk about least, which is the grief of watching it happen to people you love. The collapse is not a statistic to a pastor. It's a girl you baptized when she was eight who's twenty-four now and texts you, kindly, that she just doesn't believe it anymore, that she's grateful for how you loved her but she's moved on, and there's no anger in it, which is somehow worse, because anger would mean it still mattered to her and the kindness means it doesn't. It's the family that was the backbone of the church for three generations, whose grandkids you can't get in the door no matter what you do. It's the funeral where the adult children stand awkwardly at the back because they don't know when to stand or what to say, because their parents' faith never reached them and now their parents are gone and the faith went into the ground with them. That's what the collapse actually is, on the ground, in a pastor's week. It's not an abstraction about secularization. It's a hundred specific faces of people you love walking out of a story you'd have given your life to keep them in, and you can't make them stay, and the powerlessness of it is one of the heaviest things I carry.

And I have to be careful what I do with that grief, because it can go bad. It can turn into resentment of the people who left, which is poison, or into a frantic redoubling of effort to win them back through methods that won't work because the problem was never method, or into a quiet despair that makes me a worse pastor to the ones who stayed. What I'm slowly learning to do with it instead is to let it drive me to my knees over the specific names, to pray for the girl who texted me and the family whose grandkids won't come, by name, year after year, with no visible result, trusting that the God who pursued me when I was a hardened atheist with contempt for the whole thing is more than able to pursue them, that no one is past his reach, that I was past everyone's reach and he reached me anyway. The collapse, held in prayer over specific names, becomes intercession instead of resentment. That's the only redemptive thing I've found to do with it. I can't make them come back. I can carry their names to the only One who can, and keep carrying them, and not give up, because he didn't give up on me.

That is our question now. Not how to rebuild the temple of Christendom. How to be the people of God when the temple is ash. I want to push back, gently, on a comfort that pastors reach for at this point, because I've reached for it myself and found it doesn't hold. The comfort is the cyclical theory, the idea that the church has always gone through ups and downs, that there have been dark valleys before and great awakenings after, that decline is just part of a cycle and the upswing is coming, so don't worry, hold on, the pendulum always swings back. And there's a sliver of truth in it, the church has had revivals and recoveries, God has surprised his people before. But I don't think the cyclical theory fits our situation, and leaning on it can keep us from facing what's actually happening. The previous declines the cyclical theory points to mostly happened within Christendom, dips in fervor inside a culture that remained basically Christian, valleys followed by awakenings among people who already knew the story and drifted from it and got revived back to it. What's happening now is different in kind, not just degree. We are not watching a believing culture grow cold and need revival. We are watching a whole civilization stop being Christian at the level of its basic assumptions, and that has happened before in history, but the place it happened, the great churches of North Africa and the Middle East that flourished for centuries and then simply ceased to exist, did not come back. The cyclical theory comforts us by assuming the recovery is guaranteed. It isn't. God may grant a great awakening, and I pray he does. But there's no promise that he will, no law of history that requires the pendulum to swing back, and the churches that assumed their recovery was guaranteed are, some of them, ruins in the desert now.

I say that not to deepen the despair but to push us off a false comfort onto the true one, because the true comfort is better and the false one is a trap. The false comfort says the recovery is guaranteed by the cycle, and when the recovery doesn't come on schedule it collapses into despair, because it was always optimism in disguise, a bet on the trend. The true comfort doesn't depend on the recovery at all. It says that whether or not the Western church recovers, whether or not the awakening comes, whether or not the pendulum swings, the gates of hell will not prevail against the church Jesus is building (Matthew 16:18), somewhere, in some form, possibly not here, possibly not in our civilization, but somewhere, because the promise was to the church and not to any particular cultural expression of it. The North African church died and the church did not die, it lived on elsewhere, because the promise was never to North Africa. If the Western church should die, and I don't think it will but it could, the church would not die, because the promise was never to the West. That's a harder comfort than the cycle, but it's a truer one, and it can hold when the cycle's comfort shatters, because it was never resting on the trend in the first place.

The collapse is the precondition for asking it honestly, which means the collapse, terrible as it feels in the body, may turn out to be the most spiritually clarifying thing to happen to the Western church in a thousand years. We could not have learned this in the cathedral. We can only learn it out here, on the rocks, where the tide has gone out and is not coming back, and the only question left worth asking is whether the God who made the sea is still with us in the drying pond.
chapters.verdict: The water we were swimming in has drained, and we are flopping on the rocks calling it an attack.
reflect: Are you preparing your church for a recovery that isn't coming, or for the country that actually exists?
What did the church's alliance with cultural power cost it in credibility when that power got abused?
Can you name the collapse honestly to your people without either panic or denial?

chapters.title: Grieving the Right Thing
chapters.summary: Before a church can be faithful in exile it has to grieve honestly, and grieving honestly means distinguishing the loss of privilege from the loss of the faith itself, and refusing both the panic that dresses up as courage and the denial that dresses up as hope.
chapters.body:
I've buried a lot of people. It comes with the job, and it's the part of the job I would least give up, strange as that sounds, because there's a clarity at a graveside that you don't get anywhere else. And one thing I've learned standing in those cemeteries in every season Michigan has, in the heat and in the snow with the canvas tent snapping in the wind, is that grief that gets named can be carried, and grief that gets denied turns into something else, something worse, that comes out sideways for years. The widow who can weep at the grave is on her way to healing, slow as it is. The one who squares her shoulders and says she's fine and won't let anyone speak the dead man's name, she's the one I worry about, because the grief didn't go anywhere. It went underground, and underground it does not rest. It rots.

The Western church is the second widow. We have suffered a real loss, and most of us have refused to grieve it honestly, and the ungrieved grief is coming out sideways all over the place. It comes out as rage at the culture. It comes out as conspiracy, the hunt for the enemy who did this to us. It comes out as nostalgia so thick you could cut it, the endless looping back to 1955 as though we could move there. It comes out as panic, and panic dressed up as courage, men pounding pulpits about the war on the church who are really just frightened and won't say so. And it comes out as denial, the cheerful insistence that everything's fine, attendance is just cyclical, the next revival is right around the corner, when the trend lines have been pointing one direction for fifty years. All of it, the rage and the conspiracy and the nostalgia and the panic and the denial, all of it is ungrieved loss looking for a way out that isn't the way out. The way out is to name the thing and weep.

So let's name the thing. What did we actually lose?

We have to be precise, because if you grieve the wrong thing you'll never finish grieving, and you'll defend things that were never worth defending. Here is what we did not lose. We did not lose the gospel. We did not lose the Scriptures, the Spirit, the sacraments, the promises, the presence of Christ, the power of the resurrection, or a single one of the things that make the church the church.
