Every one of those was fully present in the catacombs, fully present in Babylon, fully present in the underground churches of China and Iran where it costs your life to follow Jesus. None of it depends on Christendom. The church had all of it before Constantine and will have all of it after the last cathedral becomes a nightclub. So when a man tells me the church is dying, I want to ask him gently which church he means, because the church Jesus built is not in any danger at all. What's dying is something else.

What we lost was privilege. We lost the home-field advantage. We lost the assumption of agreement, the borrowed authority, the cultural deference, the protected Sunday, the moral monopoly, the sense that the pastor's voice carried automatic weight and the church's blessing meant something socially and the country was, at bottom, on our side. We lost the establishment. And here's where I have to push hard against my own people, because we keep calling the loss of privilege persecution, and it is not, and the confusion is poisoning us.

Persecution is the church in Acts, hauled before councils, beaten, scattered, killed, and rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer for the name (Acts 5:41). Persecution is Bonhoeffer at the gallows. Persecution is the pastor in a country I won't name who I correspond with through the Network, who has been arrested twice and whose church meets in three different houses on a rotation so the authorities can't pin them down, and who wrote to me once that he envies the freedom I complain about. What we have in America is not that. What we have is the loss of being the favored option. We've gone from the host to a guest, from the home team to a visiting one, and being a guest in a house you used to own feels like an injury, I understand that, but it is not persecution, and every time we call it persecution we do three bad things at once.

We insult the actually persecuted, the brothers and sisters for whom this word means torture and prison and death, by stealing their word to describe our hurt feelings about a culture that stopped flattering us. We make ourselves ridiculous to the watching world, which can plainly see we are not being persecuted and concludes, reasonably, that we are liars or fools. And worst of all, we make ourselves into victims, and victims are the one thing the church must never become, because the cross is the opposite of victimhood. The cross is power laid down, not power stolen from us. A persecuted church suffers and blesses. A church that merely lost its privilege and calls it persecution suffers and resents, and resentment is acid. It eats the vessel that holds it.

I have felt the resentment in myself, so I'm not preaching at you from a height. There's a specific feeling, and maybe you know it, when you realize the institution you serve, the one you gave your life to, has become an object of contempt or, worse, of indifference, to people whose grandparents would have respected it without question. There's a hot, defensive thing that rises up in the chest. How dare they. After everything the church gave this country. And that feeling is human and I won't condemn it, but I will tell you where it goes if you feed it. It goes to the place where you start to despise the people you were called to love. It goes to the place where the lost become the enemy. And the moment the lost become the enemy, you have stopped being a pastor and become a culture warrior, and the two cannot occupy the same body, because one washes feet and the other counts heads on the other side of a line.

Now, having said all that about not exaggerating the loss, I have to turn and say the opposite thing, because grief has two failure modes and I've only named one. The first failure is to inflate the loss into persecution and curdle into rage. The second failure is to deny the loss entirely, to wave it off, to refuse to feel it. And the second failure wears the mask of faith, which makes it more dangerous, because it can quote a verse. Everything happens for a reason. God is in control. The next generation will come back, they always do. Revival is coming. And some of those sentences are even true. But spoken too soon, before the grief has been allowed, they're not faith. They're anesthetic. They're a way of not feeling a loss that God actually wants us to feel, because the feeling of it is part of the healing of it.

I want to give you a picture of what ungrieved loss does to a church over time, because I've pastored through it and watched it in others, and it follows a pattern as predictable as the stages of any grief. First there's denial, the years where the decline is happening but nobody will name it, where the leadership keeps talking about next year's growth and quietly stops printing the attendance numbers in the bulletin because the numbers have become embarrassing. Then, when denial can't hold anymore, comes anger, and the anger goes looking for a target, and since the church can't be angry at itself, it gets angry at the culture, at the schools, at the government, at the young people who left, at the vague enemy who must have done this. The anger feels righteous and even energizing for a while, and a church can run on it for years, but it's corrosive, it makes the church mean and small and frightened, and it drives away the very people, especially the young, who might have stayed if the church hadn't turned into an angry old man shaking his fist at a world that had moved on. And then, often, after the anger burns out, comes a deep depression, a settled hopelessness, the church that's just waiting to die, that's stopped trying, that gathers smaller and grayer every year to do the same things in the same way while everyone privately knows the end is coming and no one will say it.

Denial, anger, depression. That's a church grieving badly, grieving without God in it, grieving the way the world grieves, without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). And the thing that's missing, the thing that would let the grief actually move toward healing instead of cycling through those stages forever, is the willingness to do what the world's grief can't do, which is to grieve honestly all the way to the bottom and then turn, not away from the loss but through it, to the God who is still there at the bottom. The widow who heals isn't the one who refused to grieve and isn't the one who grieved forever. It's the one who grieved fully, who wept and raged and despaired and brought all of it to God, and who found, at the bottom of the grief, that God was there, and that there was a life on the far side of the loss. The church has to do the same thing. It has to grieve all the way down, and then discover that God is at the bottom, and that there's a witness to be borne on the far side of the establishment we're mourning.

Let me name something that makes this harder for us than it was for the widow, though. The widow's loss was clean. Her husband died, and it wasn't her fault, and she could grieve a pure loss. Our loss is not clean. Part of why we won't grieve the end of Christendom honestly is that we know, somewhere, that we contributed to it, that some of the church's lost credibility was credibility we threw away ourselves through our hypocrisies and our power-grabbing and our scandals and our coldness. It's easier to grieve a loss that was done to you than a loss you helped cause, because the second kind of grief comes mixed with shame, and shame is the hardest thing to bring into the open. So the church's grief over Christendom has to include repentance, has to include owning the part we played in our own discrediting, and that's a harder, humbler grief than the simple lament of the wronged. We're not only mourning what was taken from us. We're confessing what we wasted. And until we'll confess what we wasted, we'll keep blaming the culture for a wound we partly inflicted on ourselves, and the blaming will keep us stuck in the anger stage forever.

Look at how the Bible handles loss, because the Bible is far more honest than we are. There's a whole book called Lamentations, five chapters of nothing but grief over the fall of Jerusalem, and God put it in the canon. How lonely sits the city that was full of people (Lamentations 1:1). It does not rush to resolution. It sits in the ash and weeps and even accuses God of cruelty, and then, in the dead center of the middle chapter, it turns, not to denial but to a memory. The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning (Lamentations 3:22-23). But notice the order. The hope comes after the grief, not instead of it. You don't get to 3:22 without going through chapters one and two. The lament earns the hope. A church that skips the lament and jumps straight to the hope has hope that's hollow, and people can hear the hollowness, and it's part of why our hopeful preaching rings so false right now. We're announcing resurrection to a body we never let ourselves bury.

There's a kind of grief I haven't named yet, and it's the grief of the older saints in your church, and it deserves its own moment because it's the most poignant and the most easily dismissed. The people in your congregation who are seventy and eighty now gave their whole lives to a church and a country that was Christian in the ways we've described, and they're watching all of it come apart at the end of their lives, watching the world they built and believed in dissolve, watching their grandchildren leave the faith they gave everything for. That's a specific and terrible grief, the grief of an old saint who fears that their life's work is being undone before their eyes, that they're handing off a faith to a generation that doesn't want it, that everything they sacrificed for is slipping away just as they're too old to do anything about it. And the temptation, for a younger pastor impatient with the old ways, is to dismiss that grief as nostalgia, as the natural complaining of old people who can't adjust to change. Don't. That grief is real and it's holy and those saints deserve to have it honored, not dismissed.

What I try to give them, and it's hard, is the truth that their work is not being undone, it's being handed off, which is a different thing. The faith they gave their lives to is not dying; it's changing form, the way it changed form in Babylon, and the things they sacrificed for, the people they discipled, the prayers they prayed, the children they raised, none of that is lost, it's all kept by the God who wastes nothing, and the form of the church may change but the treasure they carried gets passed on. I try to tell them that they ran their leg of the relay faithfully, that the baton is being passed, that they're not failures because the establishment is ending on their watch, any more than the exiles who died in Babylon were failures. They were faithful runners who handed off to the next leg. And I try to let them grieve, fully, the world that's ending, because they have more right to grieve it than anyone, having given the most to it, and the worst thing you can do to a grieving old saint is tell them their grief is just nostalgia and they should cheer up. Honor the grief. Honor the life. And help them see that the faithfulness of their leg of the race is not measured by whether the race is finished in their lifetime, because it never was going to be.

So I want to give you, and your church, permission to grieve. Real permission. Sit by the rivers and weep over what's gone (Psalm 137:1). Weep over the empty rooms in the building that used to be full of children. Weep over the young people who left and aren't coming back. Weep over the respect that's gone, the influence that's gone, the easy assumed agreement that's gone. Don't pretend you don't miss it. You miss it. I miss it. Name it out loud, to God, who is not threatened by your grief and put a whole book of it in his Bible.

But grieve the right thing. Grieve the privilege, not the gospel, because the gospel is fine. And don't let the grief stay grief, because grief that stays grief becomes either rage or despair, and we've covered both of those. Let the grief do its work and then turn, the way Lamentations turns, to the steadfast love that never ceases. The widow who weeps at the grave gets up eventually and walks home and learns to live, and her grief becomes the soil that something new grows in. The one who never weeps stays at the grave for years, digging.

Let me say a word about how a pastor actually leads a congregation through this grief, because it's one thing to say grieve honestly and another to do it from a pulpit in front of frightened people who don't want to be told their church is in decline. The instinct is to protect them from the hard truth, to keep things positive, to not name the decline because naming it might accelerate it, might discourage people, might make them leave. And I understand that instinct, but I've come to think it's a failure of love disguised as kindness, because it leaves people without the truth they need to grieve, and ungrieved loss, as we've said, comes out sideways and poisons everything. The pastor who won't name the decline ends up with a congregation that senses the decline, feels it in their bodies, sees the empty seats, and has no permission to talk about it, so the grief goes underground and turns into the anger and the conspiracy and the despair we've described. Naming the loss honestly, from the pulpit, with tears and without panic, is one of the most pastoral things a leader can do, because it gives the people permission to feel what they're already feeling and to bring it to God instead of burying it.

But there's a way to name it that helps and a way that harms, and the difference is whether you name it inside the larger story or outside it. If you stand up and say the church is declining and the culture is hostile and we're losing, full stop, you've just confirmed their despair and given them nothing to do with it. If you stand up and say the church is declining and the culture is hostile, and here is what that has always meant for the people of God, and here is the God who has met his people in exactly this kind of season before, and here is the assignment that comes with it, then you've named the loss inside the story that makes the loss bearable. You've done what Jeremiah did, told the truth about the seventy years inside the promise of the future and the hope. The naming has to come wrapped in the larger story, or it's just bad news, and people are drowning in bad news. The pastor's job is to tell the truth about the loss and to tell it inside the gospel, so that the grief has somewhere to go besides despair, so that the people can weep and still hope, can bury the establishment and still believe in the resurrection. That's the hardest preaching there is, and it's the preaching the exile requires.

You cannot bury what you will not name, and a church that won't name its grief will keep digging up the corpse, year after year, election after election, trying to make 1955 breathe again. Let it rest. Weep, and then let it rest. There's a city to be loved out here, and you cannot love it with your eyes full of a country that's already gone.
chapters.verdict: You cannot bury what you will not name, and a church that will not name its grief will keep digging up the corpse.
reflect: What exactly have you lost, and have you let yourself feel it instead of immediately strategizing around it?
Where has your grief curdled into resentment and gone looking for someone to blame?
Can you tell your people the truth about the loss without either terrifying them or lying to them?

chapters.title: Babylon Was Always the School
chapters.summary: The exile in Babylon was not God's abandonment of his people but his school for them, where they wrote and remembered and learned to be Israel without the temple, the land, or the king. Jeremiah's letter reframes displacement as vocation.
chapters.body:
When the worst happened, the people assumed God had failed. That's the natural reading of a collapse, and it was the reading of most of Judah in 587 BC, and honestly I understand it better than I used to. The temple was the place God's name dwelt, the one address in all the earth where you could be sure of meeting him. The land was the promise made to Abraham, the soil under the whole covenant. The king was the son of David, through whom God had pledged an everlasting throne. Lose all three at once, the temple burned, the land overrun, the king blinded and chained, and the only sane conclusion seems to be that the covenant is void, that the contract has been breached, that the God who promised is either too weak to keep his word or too cruel to bother.

The false prophets said exactly that, but in reverse and with a smile. They promised a quick return. Two years, said Hananiah, two years and the LORD will break the yoke of Babylon and bring everybody home (Jeremiah 28:11). He even took the wooden yoke off Jeremiah's neck and broke it for a visual, the way a confident man does. The false prophets were the church-growth consultants of their day, selling the recovery everyone desperately wanted to buy, telling the frightened people exactly what the frightened people wanted to hear. Don't worry. This is temporary. We'll be back in the building by spring.

Jeremiah called them liars.

The letter he sent to the exiles in Babylon is the single most important text I know for the moment we're in, and I've come back to it so many times over the years that it reads me now more than I read it. Let me put the heart of it in front of you again, slowly. Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce. Take wives and have sons and daughters; take wives for your sons, and give your daughters in marriage, that they may bear sons and daughters; multiply there, and do not decrease. But seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare (Jeremiah 29:5-7). And then the line that breaks Hananiah's promise clean in half. When seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will visit you (Jeremiah 29:10). Not two years. Seventy. Longer than almost anyone reading the letter would live. They were going to die in Babylon. Their grandchildren might see Jerusalem. Most of them would not.

Read that pastorally and it's devastating and liberating at the same time, and you have to feel both at once or you've misread it.

It's devastating because it forecloses the fantasy of a quick return. There is no strategy that gets the temple back next quarter. There's no candidate, no campaign, no conference, no method that ends the exile on a timeline you can live to see. The people who want the old settlement restored fast, on their watch, are following Hananiah, and Hananiah is lying, and Jeremiah loves the people too much to lie to them the way Hananiah does. I have had to be Jeremiah to pastors who wanted me to be Hananiah, men who came to me wanting to be told that if they just tried the new program or backed the right cause the decline would reverse and the building would fill, and I've had to say, brother, it might not, not in your lifetime, and watch the disappointment land. It's a hard word. But the hard true word is a mercy and the soft false word is a cruelty, even though it doesn't feel that way in the moment.

And it's liberating, because it gives the exiles something to do that is not waiting. This is the part that saves you, if you'll receive it. Jeremiah doesn't tell them to hunker down and endure until the real life resumes back in Jerusalem. He tells them that this, here, now, in Babylon, is the real life. Build. Plant. Marry. Multiply. Have grandchildren. Get good at something. And then the staggering part, the part that should stop a Christendom-shaped church flat. Seek the welfare of Babylon. The Hebrew word is shalom, the deep flourishing, the wholeness, and Jeremiah uses it three times in two verses, and he attaches it to the city that burned the temple. Pray for the shalom of the city that conquered you. Work for the flourishing of the empire that does not worship your God. Because, he says, your shalom is bound up in its shalom. You cannot flourish in a city you're cursing. Your welfare and theirs are tied together now, like it or not.

I want to dwell on that word shalom for a moment, because it carries more than our word welfare suggests, and the depth of it changes the assignment. Shalom is not just the absence of trouble or the presence of prosperity. It's wholeness, the way things are supposed to be, every relationship right, every part flourishing, the deep peace of a world rightly ordered under God. And Jeremiah tells the exiles to seek that, the deep flourishing, for Babylon, for the city of their captors, for the place that burned their temple and dragged them off in chains. That's a staggering command when you let it land. He's not telling them to tolerate Babylon, or to put up with it, or to survive it. He's telling them to actively work for its deepest good, to want Babylon to flourish, to pray for the wholeness of the empire that destroyed them. That's not natural. Nothing in a conquered people wants the conqueror to flourish. The natural prayer of the exile is the prayer at the end of Psalm 137, the prayer for Babylon's destruction, and that prayer is honest and God let it into the Bible. But Jeremiah's command cuts against it, pulls the exile past the natural desire for the enemy's downfall into the unnatural work of seeking the enemy's flourishing.

And here's why it matters for us. The post-Christendom church's natural prayer for the secular culture is the Psalm 137 prayer, the prayer for its downfall, for the collapse of the institutions that pushed us out, and that prayer comes easily and feels righteous. But Jeremiah won't let us pray it as our settled posture. He commands the harder prayer, the shalom prayer, the prayer that the secular city we live in would actually flourish, that our unbelieving neighbors would prosper, that the institutions that have no place for us would nonetheless do well and serve their people well, because our welfare is bound up with theirs and because we're commanded to seek their good. That's a conversion of the heart, not just a change of strategy. It means actually wanting the good of the people who displaced us, actually working for the welfare of a city that would not notice if our church closed tomorrow. Jesus said the same thing in even sharper terms, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matthew 5:44), and Jeremiah's seek-the-welfare is the Old Testament seed of that New Testament flower. The exile is a long school in learning to want the good of the people we'd rather see fail, which is the hardest thing the gospel ever asks and the thing that most clearly marks us as belonging to the God who loved his enemies all the way to a cross.

I want to be careful here, because this is not a command to collaborate with evil, and the next chapter on Daniel is going to draw the lines that keep this from becoming surrender. But it is the flat refusal of two errors that are both deeply seductive to a church in our position, and I see my people falling into one or the other constantly.

The first error is assimilation. You become Babylonian. You lose the distinctive faith, you trim the offense off the gospel, you dissolve into the surrounding culture until there's nothing left of you that's different, nothing the city would even notice if it vanished. This is the church that wants so badly to be relevant and liked that it slowly becomes a chaplaincy to the spirit of the age, blessing whatever the culture already believes, asking nothing, costing nothing, offering a Jesus who is basically a life coach with better lighting. The assimilated church seeks the welfare of the city by becoming indistinguishable from it, and so it has nothing left to offer the city, because you can't give a city the gospel if you've thrown the gospel away to fit in.

The second error is the bunker. You treat the city as Babylon-the-whore, the enemy to be denounced and survived. You pull your children and your money and your presence behind the walls. You curse the city instead of praying for it. You wait for the rapture or the revival or the right election to deliver you, and in the meantime you contribute nothing to the place you live and love no one outside the walls. The bunker church is pure and useless. It keeps the faith intact by keeping it locked up where the faith can't do anyone any good. It seeks its own welfare and not the city's at all, which is exactly what Jeremiah forbids.

Jeremiah won't let his people do either one. He commands a third posture, and it's harder than both errors put together, because it requires holding two things at once that everything in us wants to pull apart. Stay distinct and stay engaged. Keep the faith pure and serve the city anyway. Be unmistakably the people of God and unmistakably a blessing to the place that does not share your God. Hold the line and love the neighbor, in the same body, at the same time. Most of us can do one or the other. The exile asks for both, and it asks for both not as a clever strategy but as the basic shape of faithfulness in a place that isn't home.

I want to sit with the false prophets a little longer, because Hananiah is not a cartoon villain, and if we make him one we'll miss how easily we become him. Hananiah was not a wicked man scheming to deceive. He was, as far as we can tell, sincere. He genuinely believed God would not let the exile stand, because his whole theology was built on God's commitment to Jerusalem and the temple and the Davidic line, and he could not conceive of a God who would let those things fall for seventy years. His error was not malice. It was that he could not imagine God working through the very collapse he was trying to deny. He had a theology that required God to fix this fast, and so he prophesied a fast fix, and he probably believed it, and the believing made him more dangerous, not less, because sincere false hope is more persuasive than cynical lies. The people wanted to believe Hananiah because Hananiah was telling them the comforting thing in the confident voice, and Jeremiah was telling them the devastating thing through tears, and people will follow the confident comfort over the tearful truth almost every time.

I have to watch Hananiah in myself, and so do you, because the pressure to be Hananiah is enormous in a declining church. Your people are frightened. They want hope. They come to you wanting to be told it'll turn around, that the next program or the next pastor or the next generation will bring the recovery, and there is a powerful pull to give them what they want, to be the confident voice promising the fast fix, because it's what they're aching to hear and because, honestly, it's what you ache to believe yourself. And the temptation is strong precisely because it's not a temptation to lie, exactly. It's a temptation to hope wrongly, to attach your hope to the recovery of the establishment instead of to the promise of God, to prophesy return in two years because you cannot bear to tell your people seventy. The faithful pastor has to be Jeremiah, has to love his people enough to tell them the hard true thing instead of the soft false thing, and that's a lonely place to stand, because the Hananiahs will always be more popular, right up until their two years pass and the exile is still there and the people they comforted are left without any framework for the suffering they were promised wouldn't come.

And notice what Jeremiah does after he delivers the hard word. He doesn't gloat. He doesn't say I told you so. The same prophet who shattered the comfortable lie about the timeline turns around and gives the people the most tender promise in the whole letter, just after the seventy years. I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope (Jeremiah 29:11). We've turned that verse into a graduation card, ripped it clean out of its context, but look at where it actually sits. It sits right after the announcement that the exile will last seventy years and most of them will die in Babylon. The future and the hope are not a promise that the suffering will end soon. They're a promise that God has not abandoned them in the suffering, that the exile is not random or meaningless or final, that there's a plan running through it even though the plan includes seventy years they won't live to see the end of. That's the only hope worth offering an exile. Not it'll be over soon, which is a lie. But God has not lost the thread, your suffering is inside his purpose, there is a future on the far side even if you don't live to see it. Jeremiah tells the truth about the seventy years and the truth about the future and the hope in the same breath, and that's the model. Don't soften the seventy years to make room for the hope. Let the hope be big enough to hold the seventy years.

But here is what I most want you to see about Babylon, the thing that turns the whole story. Look at what the people of God became there, because they could not have become it anywhere else. Babylon was the school. With the temple gone, they could no longer locate God in a building, so they learned, slowly and against everything they'd assumed, that the LORD was not confined to Jerusalem, that he was God in Babylon too, present to his people in a foreign land where his name was not honored and his day was not kept. That's an enormous theological leap and they only made it because they were forced to. With the sacrificial system gone, no altar, no priest performing the daily offerings, they leaned hard into the word, and the synagogue was born, a gathering around the reading and study of Scripture that needed no temple and no priesthood and could happen anywhere ten men could meet. The synagogue carried the faith for the next twenty-five hundred years and shaped the very form of the Christian congregation; when you gather your people around an open Bible on a Sunday, you are doing something that was invented in exile. With the king gone, they learned that the LORD himself was their king, and the longing for David's son sharpened in the dark into the messianic hope that Jesus would one day fulfill. And the Scriptures themselves, much of the Old Testament as we have it, were collected and shaped and edited in and after the exile by people who suddenly understood that if they didn't write it down and guard it, it would be lost.

Stop and feel the weight of that. The faith we hold was forged in displacement. Israel went into Babylon a temple-and-land religion, tied to a building and a country, and came out a people of the book, portable, able to be the people of God anywhere, under any empire, with no political privilege at all. They came out portable. And portability is exactly what a post-Christendom church needs, because portability is the one thing Christendom never taught us. We have been a temple-and-land faith, fused to our buildings and our budgets and the favor of the powers, and when the building empties and the budget shrinks and the favor evaporates we panic, because we never learned to carry the faith without the props. Babylon is going to teach us. It's going to teach us to be a people of the book again, gathered around the word, present to God without the cultural scaffolding, capable of bearing witness under an empire that does not love us. We could not learn this while we held the temple. We can only learn it here, with the temple in ashes behind us.

I keep using the word school, and I want to press on what kind of school it was, because it wasn't a school you'd choose and it wasn't a school that felt like learning while you were in it. It felt like loss. It felt like punishment. It felt, day to day, like God had turned his back. The exiles did not wake up in Babylon thinking, what an excellent formative experience this is, how grateful I am for this curriculum. They wept. They raged. They wrote Psalm 137 with its terrible ending. The school did not announce itself as a school. It announced itself as a catastrophe, and only later, looking back, could anyone see that the catastrophe had been a classroom, that the very things that felt like abandonment had been the lessons. And that's almost always how God's deepest schooling works. You don't recognize it as formation while it's happening. You recognize it as suffering. The recognition that it was formation comes later, sometimes much later, sometimes only in the next generation, when the grandchildren who inherited the portable faith look back and understand what the exile cost and what it made.

This matters enormously for how we pastor through our own exile, because it means we cannot expect our people to experience the collapse as a gift while they're in it. They're going to experience it as loss, as grief, as catastrophe, and we shouldn't shame them for that or rush them past it, because that's the honest first response and the exiles had it too. What we can do, what Jeremiah did, is give them a frame that lets them hold the catastrophe as something other than meaningless, that lets them suspect, even through the tears, that God might be doing something in this that they can't yet see, that the classroom might be disguised as a disaster. We can't make it feel like a gift. We can help them refuse to call it meaningless. We can stand in the rubble with them and say, I know it feels like he's gone, and I'm telling you he's not, he's here, he was here before we arrived, and someday, maybe not in our lifetime, this will turn out to have been the place we learned the things we could never have learned in the temple. That's not denial. The exiles really did learn those things. It's just learning to read the suffering with the eyes of faith while you're still inside it, before the lesson is finished, which is the hardest kind of faith there is.

God did not lose his people in Babylon. He taught them there. And the curriculum was not how to get their power back. The curriculum was how to be his people without it, which turned out to be the only thing that ever lasted anyway, the only Israel that survived being the portable one.

I think often about the seventy years. About the man who got that letter, sat down on the dirt floor of his new Babylonian house, did the math, and understood that he would not see the return. That his task was to plant a garden whose fruit his grandchildren would eat, to be faithful in a season he would not see finished. That's a hard word for a culture like ours that wants results inside a fiscal year, that wants the harvest in the same season as the planting. The exile asks us to plant trees in whose shade we will never sit. The recovery of the Western church, if it ever comes, will almost certainly not come on our watch, and a faithfulness that requires seeing the harvest is not yet faithfulness. It's just a more spiritual version of wanting the census back.

I want to draw out one more implication of the seventy years, because it changes how we think about success and failure in ministry in a way I'm still absorbing. If the exile is going to last longer than any individual's working life, then no individual is going to see the whole thing. Which means the right unit of measure is not the individual ministry but the generations, the relay, the handoff. The man who got Jeremiah's letter was not going to finish anything. His job was to receive the faith, keep it, deepen it, and hand it to children who would hand it to children who might, three generations later, see the return. He was a runner in a relay, and the relay was longer than his leg of it, and the temptation, the deep temptation, was to measure his life by whether he personally crossed the finish line, when his actual job was just to run his leg well and pass the baton without dropping it.

That reframes the whole question of a faithful ministry in exile. I am not going to finish this. You are not going to finish this. We are running a leg of a relay that started before us and will continue after us, and faithfulness is not crossing the finish line, which we won't, it's running our leg well and handing the baton cleanly to the next runner. And there's a freedom in that, once you accept it, because it takes the impossible weight off your shoulders, the weight of having to personally reverse the decline and save the Western church in your lifetime, which you cannot do and were never asked to do. You were asked to run your leg. To receive the faith faithfully, to keep it and deepen it in your season, and to hand it on to people who'll carry it past where you can see. The exiles who built houses and planted gardens and raised children in Babylon were running their leg, and they ran it well, and they handed the baton to the generation that saw the return, and the fact that they died in Babylon does not mean they failed. It means they ran their leg and passed the baton, which is all any of us is asked to do, and the One who organized the relay will see it through to the finish line we won't live to cross.

Build the houses. Plant the gardens. Seek the welfare of the city, and pray for it, and mean it. Settle in for seventy years. The school is in session, and the lesson is the oldest one we know, and the Teacher is the One who went into exile with us and was there before we arrived.
chapters.verdict: God did not lose his people in Babylon. He taught them there.
reflect: What is your church being taught now that it could never have learned while it held cultural power?
Are you seeking the welfare of the city that doesn't share your faith, or only the welfare of your own institution?
Where are you praying for return when God is calling you to settle in and serve?

chapters.title: Daniel and the Discipline of the Line
chapters.summary: Daniel and his friends served Babylon faithfully and rose within it, yet drew firm lines where worship was at stake. Their example teaches the difference between the engagement Jeremiah commands and the assimilation that would erase the church.
chapters.body:
Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon. Daniel shows us a man who did exactly that, and then shows us the wall he hit, the place where seeking the city's welfare stopped and faithfulness to God required him to refuse and not move. If the last chapter was about engagement, this one is about its limit, because an engagement with no limit is not engagement. It's surrender wearing engagement's clothes, and a lot of what passes for relevance in the church right now is surrender that has learned to dress well.

Look at how far in Daniel went, because we usually rush past it to get to the lions. Daniel and his three friends were taken as young men, teenagers probably, into the Babylonian system, and they were not sent to the margins. They were sent to the center. Selected for their intelligence and their bearing, enrolled in the king's own training program, taught the language and the literature of Babylon, given Babylonian names, groomed for imperial service at the highest level (Daniel 1:3-5). And notice what they did not do. They did not refuse the education. Think about that. They learned the literature of Babylon, which would have included the myths, the astrology, the whole pagan intellectual apparatus. They did not refuse the new names, even though the names honored Babylonian gods. They did not refuse the service. Daniel rose to become one of the most powerful administrators in the empire, serving a pagan king, then a second pagan king, then a third, with such excellence and such evident integrity that he was trusted above all others and his enemies could find nothing to accuse him of except his religion (Daniel 6:4-5). He sought the welfare of the city to the point of running large parts of it. This is the engagement Jeremiah commanded, lived out at the very top. A man can serve Babylon faithfully, competently, even gladly, work inside its institutions, master its learning, and remain wholly and entirely the LORD's.

I need my people to hear that, because the bunker instinct says the only faithful response to a pagan culture is to flee it, to keep your hands clean, to refuse to participate. Daniel says no. Daniel went all the way into the king's court. He did not keep his hands clean in the sense of avoiding the city's work. He kept his soul clean while doing the city's work, which is much harder.

And yet, from the very first chapter, there is a line. The young men resolve not to defile themselves with the king's food (Daniel 1:8). And it seems small, almost fussy. A dietary matter. A request for vegetables and water instead of the rich provisions from the royal table. You could be forgiven for thinking it's the wrong hill, that surely a man who'll accept a pagan name and a pagan education shouldn't strain at the menu. But this small refusal establishes the pattern that governs the entire book, and the pattern is the whole point. There is a place where the empire's provision becomes the empire's claim, where to accept what Babylon offers is to accept Babylon's definition of who you are and whose you are, and at that place Daniel quietly, respectfully, immovably declines. He doesn't make a scene. He doesn't denounce the king or stage a protest. He goes to the official privately, asks for an alternative, and proposes a test, ten days on vegetables and water, and let's see who looks healthier. The line gets drawn early, in private, over something small, so that when the great test comes it has already been settled in the soul.

That's the pastoral genius of the whole thing, and it's a lesson we have almost completely lost. The line has to be located before the furnace, not in front of it. By the time the music plays and the golden image is set up and the whole assembly is told to fall down and worship or be thrown into the fire, it is far too late to start deciding what you believe. Daniel's three friends, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, could stand before Nebuchadnezzar and refuse to bow because the matter had been settled in them long before the orchestra struck up. Listen to what they say, because it's one of the most important sentences in the Bible for a church in exile. O Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you in this matter. If this be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up (Daniel 3:16-18).

But if not. Stop on those three words. Even if God does not rescue us, we will not bow. The faithfulness did not depend on the rescue. The line held whether or not heaven moved. That's the thing I most want to drive into your bones, because most of our courage is conditional, it depends on God coming through in the way and on the timeline we want, and a courage that depends on the rescue is not yet courage. It's a wager. The three friends had a faith that had already let go of the outcome, and a faith that has let go of the outcome cannot be coerced by any furnace, because there's nothing left to threaten. You cannot bend a man who has already decided he'll burn before he bows. And they could decide that, in the moment, under that pressure, because they'd been deciding it for years, starting with a plate of vegetables.

Here's where this presses hard on a church in exile, and I'm going to say it about my own tribe and not someone else's. Exile creates an enormous pressure to assimilate, and assimilation almost never announces itself as apostasy. Nobody stands up and says, I have decided to abandon the faith of my fathers to fit in with Babylon. It never looks like that. It comes dressed as relevance, as winsomeness, as meeting the culture where it is, as not wanting to be the kind of Christian that gives Christianity a bad name. And much of that instinct is good and right. Daniel was winsome. Daniel was excellent. Daniel was the opposite of the obnoxious culture warrior who can't hold a job in Babylon because he won't stop picking fights. But there's a point where the desire to be acceptable to Babylon quietly becomes the willingness to worship what Babylon worships, and a church that has not located that line in advance will cross it without ever deciding to. It will simply drift, one reasonable accommodation at a time, each one defensible on its own, until one day there's nothing left that Babylon would ever need to persecute, because there's nothing left in the church that contradicts Babylon at all. That's not a furnace. That's a slow fade, and the slow fade kills more churches than the furnace ever did.

And the bunker fails the opposite way, just as completely. The sealed enclave draws the line everywhere. It defiles itself on nothing because it touches nothing. It serves the city's welfare not at all because it has fled the city entirely. The bunker would have had Daniel refuse the whole Babylonian enterprise, refuse the education as pagan, refuse the court as compromise, refuse to dirty his hands in the administration of an idolatrous empire, and Daniel would have been pure and useless. He'd have saved his own soul and abandoned the city Jeremiah told him to seek. Instead he did the harder thing, the thing that requires more nerve than either error. He went all the way into the center, served with total excellence, earned the trust of kings, and still did not bow. Engagement to the hilt. Worship to no one but God. Both at once.

Let me push on the question of where the line actually goes, because it's easy to say draw the line in advance and much harder to know which line, and getting this wrong in either direction does real damage. There's a passage later in Daniel that I find clarifying. When Daniel learns that the king has signed a law making prayer to anyone but the king illegal for thirty days, what does he do? He goes home, and he opens his windows toward Jerusalem, and he gets down on his knees and prays three times a day, as he had done previously (Daniel 6:10). Notice the as he had done previously. Daniel doesn't ramp up his defiance for the cameras. He doesn't stage a public protest or organize a resistance movement or pick a dramatic fight. He just keeps doing the thing he was already doing, openly, without hiding it and without flaunting it, because the thing he was already doing was right and a king's law could not make it wrong. The line for Daniel was not drawn at every place where Babylon offended him. It was drawn at the place where Babylon required him to stop worshiping God or to worship something else, and at exactly that place he did not bend, and everywhere short of that place he served Babylon with all his heart.

That as he had done previously is the whole discipline in three words. The faithful exile doesn't pick new fights when the pressure comes. He just keeps doing the right thing he was already doing, refusing to be either provoked into rebellion or pressured into compliance. He doesn't go looking for furnaces, and he doesn't run from the one that finds him. There's a kind of Christian who seems almost eager for the furnace, who's disappointed when the persecution doesn't come, who picks fights so he can feel like a martyr, and that's not Daniel. And there's another kind who'll do anything to avoid the furnace, who keeps finding reasons why this particular hill isn't worth dying on, who rationalizes one compromise after another, and that's not Daniel either. Daniel just keeps praying toward Jerusalem with the windows open, neither hiding nor provoking, and lets the chips fall, and when the chips fall into a den of lions, he goes into the lions the same way the three friends went into the fire, with the matter already settled.

So how do you know where your line is? I think you find it by asking one question about each potential hill, and the question is, is Babylon asking me to disobey God, or is Babylon merely asking me to be uncomfortable, to lose status, to be inconvenienced, to be disliked? Because we confuse those constantly. We treat every loss of comfort as a line-in-the-sand worship issue, and we treat some genuine worship issues as mere preferences we can let slide. The discipline is sorting them honestly in advance. Losing your good standing because you're a Christian is not a line you have to defend against, it's a cost you accept; you don't fight to keep your reputation, you let it go like Daniel let go of his safety. But being required to actually deny Christ, to affirm what's false, to call evil good, to bow to the image, that's the line, and you don't move on that one whatever it costs. Most of us have it backwards. We fight hard to keep our comfort and our standing, dying on hills of mere inconvenience, and then when a genuine worship issue comes we've spent all our nerve and we fold. Daniel held the opposite posture. He let his comfort and standing and safety go without a fight, again and again, and held the worship line like iron.

A number of years ago a writer named Rod Dreher put out a book called The Benedict Option that got argued about in every pastor's group I'm part of, and I think it's worth bringing in here because it gets the diagnosis right and risks getting this balance wrong, and the risk is exactly Daniel's lesson. Dreher is correct, plainly correct, that the church can no longer assume the surrounding culture will form its people, that we need thick communities and deliberate practices that can transmit the faith when the culture is actively dissolving it. He's right that a church which does nothing intentional to form its children will lose its children, because the culture is forming them twelve hours a day and the church is getting ninety minutes a week if it's lucky. On all that he's right, and the church that ignores him will pay for ignoring him with its own grandchildren. But the danger, which Dreher himself works to qualify and which his more anxious readers blow right past, is that the strategic withdrawal hardens into the bunker, that the formation becomes flight, that the thick community becomes a sealed one with the drawbridge up, that the church saves its life and loses the city. Daniel is the corrective. Daniel was as deeply formed in the faith as any monk in any monastery, and he ran the empire. The thick formation was for the sake of the faithful presence in Babylon, not as a substitute for it. Form your people deeply, yes, more deeply than you've ever bothered to, and then send them into the king's court to serve, with the line already drawn in their bones so it'll hold when the music plays.

I'll tell on myself here, because I find I'm much better at preaching one half of this than living the whole of it. It's easy to draw lines from a pulpit and easy to be winsome in a coffee shop, and the actual work is doing both, in the same body, in the same week, often with the same person. I have watched myself blur a line just to keep a relationship comfortable, told myself I was being gracious when really I was being a coward, letting something pass that I should have named because naming it would have cost me a friendship I wanted to keep. And I have watched myself draw a line in a place God never asked me to defend, dying on a hill of mere preference, of culture or politics or taste, just so I could feel like I was being faithful and bold, when really I was being rigid about something that didn't matter to dodge the harder work of being soft and present with a real person. The discipline of the line is harder than either of those failures, because it requires knowing, actually knowing in advance, which hills are worship and which are merely preference. And most of the hills we die on are preference. The few that are genuinely worship, the places where Babylon is actually asking us to bow, we too often surrender, because by the time we get there we've spent all our nerve fighting over the music and the carpet and the politics.

There's a detail in the furnace story I skipped, and it's too good to leave out, because it complicates our triumphalism in exactly the right way. After Nebuchadnezzar sees the fourth man in the fire and calls the three out, unburned, not even smelling of smoke, he's so impressed that he issues a decree, and the decree threatens to tear limb from limb anyone who speaks against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego (Daniel 3:29). And you might read that as a happy ending, the pagan king converted, the true God vindicated, religious freedom established by royal command. But look closer. The king hasn't been converted. He's just decided that this God is powerful and shouldn't be crossed, which is a pagan's conclusion, not a believer's, and he expresses his new respect by threatening to dismember anyone who disrespects this God, which is the same coercive logic he used to throw the three into the furnace in the first place. He's learned nothing about the nature of the God he's now defending. He's just changed which god he'll use violence to enforce. The furnace did not convert Babylon. It just impressed Babylon, temporarily, and an impressed empire is still an empire, still running on coercion, still one bad day away from the next golden image.

I find that detail clarifying because it kills a fantasy I'm prone to, the fantasy that if we're just faithful enough, if we just stand in the furnace bravely enough, the watching empire will be so impressed that it'll convert, that our faithfulness will win the culture back. The three friends were as faithful as anyone has ever been, God showed up in the fire as dramatically as he ever has, and the result was a pagan king who was impressed for an afternoon and back to his old self by the next chapter, where he's building monuments to his own greatness and getting humbled all over again. Faithfulness in exile does not reliably convert the empire. Sometimes it impresses the empire, briefly. Sometimes it enrages the empire. Sometimes it's simply ignored by the empire. The faithfulness is not a strategy for winning Babylon over, and if we do it in order to win Babylon over we'll quit when it doesn't work, which it usually won't. We do it because it's right, because we will not bow, because the God we serve is worth not bowing to whether or not anyone is impressed. The outcome is his business. Ours is the not bowing. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego did not stand in that fire to convert Nebuchadnezzar. They stood in it because they would not worship a false god, and what Nebuchadnezzar did with it afterward was between Nebuchadnezzar and God.

So do what the three friends did. Find the line now, in private, over something small, while it's calm and no one's watching and the cost is low. Decide now what you will not bow to, so that when the furnace is hot and the whole assembly is on its face and your job and your reputation and maybe more are on the table, the decision is already made and your body just does what your soul settled years ago. Let me bring this all the way down to where my readers actually live, because most of us are not going to face a literal golden image and a literal furnace, and the danger is that we'll keep the lesson safely in ancient Babylon. Where's your furnace? It might be the workplace where saying the wrong true thing, gently and respectfully, could cost you the promotion or the job. It might be the family gathering where holding your convictions means being the difficult one, the one everyone wishes would just go along. It might be the professional association, the licensing board, the school, the institution that increasingly requires you to affirm things your conscience can't affirm, not violently, just as the price of belonging in good standing. These are real furnaces, mild compared to fire, real enough to make you sweat. And the discipline is the same as Daniel's. Decide now, in the calm, over the small things, where your line is, so that when you're standing in front of the institution and everyone's looking and the cost is real, the decision is already made and you're just executing what your soul settled long ago. The people who fold in those moments mostly fold because they never decided in advance, never drew the line over the small thing, and so they had to decide under maximum pressure with everyone watching, which is exactly when human beings are worst at deciding.

And here is what I most want you to take from Daniel into your particular furnace. He drew the line at worship, not at discomfort, and he held it without making himself obnoxious about everything else. So locate your actual line, the place where you'd be required to deny Christ or affirm a lie or call evil good, and hold that one like iron. But don't multiply furnaces. Don't turn every workplace annoyance and every cultural disagreement into a worship issue, because if everything's a hill to die on, you'll die on the wrong hills and have nothing left for the real one, and you'll be the obnoxious Christian who can't hold a job in Babylon because he picks fights over things that were never worth fighting over. Daniel served Babylon with such excellence that his enemies could find no fault in him except his religion. Be that. Be so excellent, so trustworthy, so genuinely good at serving your city and your workplace and your family, that the only thing anyone could ever hold against you is your faith, and then, on that one thing, on the actual worship line, do not move. That's the posture. Excellent everywhere, immovable at the core, the line drawn in advance over something small so it'll hold when the furnace finds you, as it will.

They served the empire fully, right up to the edge of worship, and then they did not move an inch. That's the posture. Engaged to the hilt, immovable at the core, the line settled in advance over a plate of vegetables so that it would hold over a fiery furnace. The exile does not ask us to flee Babylon. It asks us to know what we will not bow to, and to know it now, before the king ever asks.
chapters.verdict: They served the empire fully right up to the edge of worship, and then they did not move an inch.
reflect: Where is the line in your ministry between faithful engagement and idolatrous assimilation, and have you actually located it before the test comes?
Are you teaching your people to serve the culture excellently while refusing its ultimate claims?
What furnace are you quietly avoiding by blurring a line you should be defending?

chapters.title: Three Words for the City
chapters.summary: Faithful presence in exile means refusing three tempting postures toward the surrounding culture, the postures of conquest, condemnation, and conformity, and learning instead the harder posture of a people who bless the city they cannot control.
chapters.body:
I want to slow down on something Jeremiah and Daniel both assume but never spell out, because I think it's where most of our churches actually live, in the daily question of how to hold ourselves toward the people around us who don't believe what we believe. Seek the welfare of the city, Jeremiah said. Fine. But the city is full of people who think we're wrong, some who think we're dangerous, some who used to be us and left angry. How exactly do you carry yourself toward a city like that, day to day, in the grocery store and the school pickup line and the township meeting? There are three wrong answers that come naturally, and each one is a way of refusing the hard middle that the exile actually requires.

The first wrong answer is conquest. This is the posture that still believes, somewhere underneath, that the job is to take the country back. To win. To get the establishment restored, the favor returned, the culture re-Christianized from the top down through political power and cultural force. The conquest posture reads the collapse as a battle we're losing and concludes that we need to fight harder, organize better, vote smarter, and seize the levers of power before the other side does. And I understand the appeal, because there's a half-truth in it. Christians should be involved in public life. We should vote, run for school board, care about laws, speak to the common good. I'm not preaching withdrawal from the public square; the next chapters will argue hard against that. But the conquest posture turns the city into a territory to be captured rather than neighbors to be loved, and the moment you do that, you've made the people around you into the enemy, and you cannot love an enemy and seek to conquer him in the same motion. Jeremiah did not tell the exiles to take Babylon. He told them to bless it. Those are different verbs, and the difference is everything. You cannot bless a city you are trying to conquer, because conquest needs the city to lose and blessing needs it to flourish, and you cannot want both at once.

There's a deeper problem with conquest, and it's theological. The conquest posture assumes that the kingdom of God advances by the same means as the kingdoms of this world, through power, coercion, the seizing of high ground. But Jesus refused exactly that. When they came to make him king by force, he withdrew (John 6:15). When Peter drew a sword in the garden to defend him, he told him to put it away and healed the man Peter had wounded (John 18:10-11, Luke 22:51). When Pilate asked if he was a king, he said his kingdom was not from this world, and that if it were, his servants would fight (John 18:36). The whole logic of conquest is the logic Jesus laid down at the cross. We keep wanting to pick the sword back up because the sword feels like it works, and sometimes in the short run it does, but a church that advances by the sword has stopped advancing the kingdom of the crucified and started building something else that it has labeled with his name.

The second wrong answer is condemnation, and this is the bunker again but pointed outward, the church as a voice of perpetual denunciation. This is the posture that sees the city as Babylon-the-whore, ripe for judgment, and takes up the role of the prophet of doom, naming the sins of the culture loudly and often, mostly to an audience of the already-convinced. The condemnation posture feels righteous, and it has biblical-sounding fuel, because the prophets did denounce sin, loudly. But look closer at the prophets. They wept while they denounced. Jeremiah is called the weeping prophet for a reason; he hated delivering the judgment he delivered, and his eyes were a fountain of tears for the people he had to rebuke (Jeremiah 9:1). Our condemnation, too often, is dry-eyed. It's relished. There's a satisfaction in it, a self-righteous warmth in cataloging the sins of people we've already decided are the enemy, and that warmth is the tell. When denouncing the culture feels good, you've stopped being a prophet and started being a Pharisee. The prophet's denunciation comes out of love for the city and grief over its sin. The Pharisee's comes out of contempt for the sinner and satisfaction in his own difference. Same words, opposite hearts, and the watching world can tell which is which even when we can't.

And condemnation, like conquest, fails the city it claims to care about. A church known mainly for what it's against, a church whose public voice is a long list of denunciations, is a church no lost person will ever walk toward when their life falls apart. And their lives are going to fall apart, all of them, eventually, because that's what lives do. The question is whether, when the marriage collapses or the diagnosis comes or the kid overdoses, the lost neighbor thinks of the church as a possible refuge or as the people who've been yelling at them. If all they've ever heard from us is condemnation, they will not come to us in their grief, and we will have closed the one door the gospel most needs open.

The third wrong answer is conformity, and I've already named it as assimilation, but I want to come at it from a slightly different angle here, because it's the one my own kind of church, the kind that wants to be winsome and welcoming and not weird, is most tempted by. Conformity is the posture that seeks the welfare of the city by becoming the city, by sanding off every edge that might offend, until the church is just the city at prayer, holding the city's values and blessing the city's choices and offering a religious flavor to a life that's otherwise identical to everyone else's. The conformist church is very nice. It's very welcoming. It would never condemn anyone. And it has nothing to offer, because it has nothing the city doesn't already have. It seeks the city's welfare by agreeing with everything the city already believes, which means it can't actually do the city any good, because the one thing the city most needs, the gospel that confronts and heals and transforms, is the one thing the conformist church has thrown away to be liked.

I want to add a fourth temptation that's really a hybrid of the others and maybe the most common one in practice, which is oscillation, the church that swings back and forth between the three errors depending on the week and the news cycle. Monday it's in conquest mode, fired up about the latest cultural battle, rallying the troops. Wednesday it slides into condemnation, denouncing the decay from the pulpit. By Sunday it's drifted into conformity, soft-pedaling the hard truths so as not to lose anyone. And then a news story hits and it's back to conquest. The oscillating church never settles into the hard center because settling there is exhausting and lonely, so it keeps reaching for whichever escape hatch the week makes most attractive, and the result is a church with no coherent posture at all, that confuses its own people, that's angry one week and accommodating the next, that can't be trusted because it doesn't know what it is. I've pastored a church through oscillating seasons, where I myself swung between the postures depending on my mood and the headlines, and the people felt it, the inconsistency, and it cost me their trust, because a shepherd who keeps changing direction is a shepherd the sheep can't follow. The cure for oscillation is the same as the cure for the other three, the deliberate, settled, costly commitment to the hard center, held steady regardless of the week, so that your people always know what you are, distinct and engaged, full of truth and full of grace, the same on the angry weeks and the accommodating ones.

Here's the trap all three share, and seeing the trap is most of the way out of it. All three, conquest and condemnation and conformity, are ways of relieving the unbearable tension of the exile. The exile asks us to do something that feels impossible, to be fully distinct and fully engaged at the same time, to keep the whole offensive truth of the gospel and to love the people who reject it, to neither rule the city nor flee it nor dissolve into it but to live in it as a blessing it cannot account for. That's hard. It's so hard that we keep reaching for one of the three escape hatches. Conquest relieves the tension by trying to make the city ours, so we don't have to be distinct from it because we'd be ruling it. Condemnation relieves the tension by writing the city off, so we don't have to engage it because we've damned it. Conformity relieves the tension by joining the city, so we don't have to be distinct because we've become identical. Each one drops one half of the assignment to make the other half bearable. And the exile won't allow any of them. It makes us hold both halves, distinct and engaged, full of truth and full of love, in the same body, forever, with no relief.

I want to address the political question head-on, because it's where the three postures fight hardest in a pastor's actual congregation, and where I've watched churches tear themselves apart. Somebody's going to read all this and hear me saying stay out of politics, retreat, don't engage the public square, and that is not what I'm saying, so let me be clear. Christians are citizens, and citizenship in a country like ours comes with real responsibilities, and to abandon the public square entirely would be its own failure to seek the welfare of the city. We should vote. We should care about laws, especially laws that protect the weak. We should be involved in our communities, our schools, our towns. Jeremiah's command to seek the city's welfare is, among other things, a command to be a good citizen, to contribute to the common good, to not be the people who take everything from the city and give nothing back. So I'm not preaching withdrawal from public life. The bunker is one of the errors, remember.

What I'm preaching against is the posture, the spirit, the way we hold our political engagement. The conquest posture turns politics into the main event, into the place where the kingdom advances or retreats, into a battle for control where the other side is the enemy. And when politics becomes the main event for a church, three things happen, all of them poisonous. The church starts to find its identity in a political tribe rather than in Christ, so that to be a member in good standing you have to hold the right political positions, and the gospel quietly gets demoted to a junior partner of the political program. The church becomes unable to reach anyone on the other side of the political line, because it's marked itself as their enemy, and you cannot evangelize people you've defined as the opposition. And the church puts its hope, functionally, in political victory, so that elections become spiritual events, and the people swing between elation and despair depending on who won, which is just optimism and despair wearing red and blue jerseys, and neither one is the hope of the gospel.

I've had to discipline my own heart hard on this, because the pull is real and it runs both directions. I've felt the satisfaction of the political win, the sense that our side advanced, and I've felt the gut-punch of the loss, the sense that the country is slipping away. And I've had to keep preaching to myself that the kingdom of God was not on the ballot, that it did not advance when my side won and did not retreat when my side lost, that Jesus is Lord regardless of who holds the office, that the early church flipped the Roman world upside down without a single Christian in the government and with an emperor who wanted them dead. The church that has its hope in politics will be a church of anxiety and rage, lurching from election to election, treating the neighbors as enemies, and that church cannot bless the city Jeremiah told it to bless, because it's too busy trying to win the city or fearing the city or both. Engage, yes. Vote, yes. Care, yes. But hold it all loosely, as a citizen of a city that's not your final home, and keep the kingdom off the ballot, and keep loving the neighbor who voted the other way, because the neighbor was never the enemy and your hope was never in the outcome.

So what does the right posture actually look like, on a Tuesday, in a real town? Let me try to make it concrete, because I get tired of books that diagnose beautifully and never tell you what to do on Tuesday. It looks like a church that is unmistakably itself, that preaches the whole gospel without trimming it, that holds its convictions about God and sin and salvation and the body without apology, and that is also, in the same week, the first to show up when the unbelieving family down the street loses a child. It looks like a congregation that would never water down what it believes about marriage and would also, without hesitation, sit in the hospital with the gay neighbor whose mother is dying, and bring the casseroles, and mow the lawn, and mean it, expecting nothing. It looks like a people who vote their convictions and then, the day after the election, regardless of how it went, go right back to loving the neighbors who voted the other way, because the neighbors were never the enemy and the kingdom was never on the ballot. It looks like a church that the lost in town cannot quite figure out, because it's clearly not trying to conquer them, clearly not condemning them, and clearly not just agreeing with them, but is doing this stranger thing, this blessing them while disagreeing with them, this loving them without needing them to change first.

I want to name the cost of the third way, because I keep making it sound noble and it mostly just feels exhausting and lonely while you're doing it. The trouble with holding the center, distinct and engaged, truth and love at once, is that it satisfies no one and gets you attacked from both sides. The people who want conquest will think you're a coward for not fighting hard enough, for loving the enemy, for not treating the culture war as the main event; they'll call you compromised, soft, unwilling to take a stand. And the people who want conformity will think you're a bigot for not letting go of the convictions, for still believing the hard things, for not just affirming what the culture affirms; they'll call you harsh, behind the times, unloving. You'll get it from both directions, and there will be days you'd give anything to just pick a side and be done with the tension, to be fully a culture warrior and get the cheers from the right, or fully an affirming progressive and get the cheers from the left, because either of those would be easier and would come with a team. The third way comes with no team. It's lonely precisely because it refuses the tribes, and the tribes are where the belonging is.

But this is exactly where the network from later in this book becomes survival rather than luxury, and where Jesus himself becomes the model and the company. Because Jesus walked the third way and got attacked from both sides for it, called a friend of sinners by the religious and a threat by the powerful, too holy for the prostitutes' crowd and too scandalous for the Pharisees', belonging fully to neither tribe because he was bringing a kingdom that judged them both. He held truth and grace together so completely that John says he was full of grace and truth (John 1:14), both, full of both, not a compromise between them but the fullness of each at once, and it got him crucified by an unlikely coalition of everyone he wouldn't fully join. So when you hold the third way and take fire from both sides and feel the loneliness of belonging to no tribe, you're in the best possible company, walking where the Lord walked, and the loneliness is not a sign you've gotten it wrong. It might be a sign you've gotten it right, because the third way always was lonely, always did get attacked from both sides, always did refuse the tribes in favor of a kingdom that judged them all. Find your few who are walking it with you, and walk it, and let the tribes say what they will.

That church is rare, and I've fallen short of leading one more times than I can count. I've let our church drift toward conformity when I wanted to be liked, and I've let it drift toward condemnation when I was tired and angry and the culture had hurt people I loved. The drift is constant, and the holding of the center takes a kind of attention that wears you out. But when I've seen it, when I've seen a church genuinely hold the center, distinct and engaged, full of truth and full of mercy, I've seen the watching world do the thing the early church made the pagans do. I've seen them get confused, in the good way. I've seen a hard man go quiet and say, I don't understand why you people are being kind to me. And that confusion, that inability to file the church under any of the categories the world knows, is the opening the gospel walks through.

Let me put one more concrete picture down, because I keep promising Tuesdays and I want to deliver one. There's a man in our town, not a believer, never has been, who lost his wife a few years back, and in the months after, it was people from our church who showed up, not to evangelize him, just to be there, to bring food and shovel his driveway through that first awful winter and sit with him on the porch when he couldn't stand to be inside. None of them ever gave him a tract. None of them made it a project. They just loved him because he was hurting and he was their neighbor, and they kept it up long after the casseroles other people brought had stopped. And about a year into it he showed up at church one Sunday, in the back, uncomfortable, and afterward he told me, almost angry about it, that he didn't understand why those people had cared, that nobody had ever cared for him like that, and that he'd come to find out what kind of people do that. He's still not a believer, as of this writing. But he's in the room now. Something cracked open in him because a handful of ordinary Christians loved him past the point the world thought reasonable, with no agenda, for a long time, and he couldn't explain it, and the not-being-able-to-explain-it is what brought him through the door.

That's the third way, on a Tuesday. Nobody conquered him, nobody condemned him, nobody pretended to agree with him about everything to make him comfortable. They just loved him, distinctly Christian love, the kind that shows up and stays and asks nothing, and the love was so out of step with everything he'd come to expect from the world that it made him curious about its source. That's the whole strategy, if you can even call it a strategy, and it's slower and humbler than the alternatives and it can't be scaled and it can't be measured and it works, sometimes, in the way the gospel has always worked, by getting under someone's defenses through a door they didn't know they had. I can't promise it'll always work. Plenty of people received that same kind of love from our church and never came near the door, and that's fine, because we didn't love them in order to get them through the door, we loved them because that's what we are now. But when it works, this is how. Not the megaphone. The casserole. Not the campaign. The shoveled driveway. Not the argument. The neighbor who stayed.

You cannot bless a city you are trying to conquer, and you cannot save a city you are trying to escape. There's a third way, harder than all three wrong ways combined, and it's the only one Jeremiah ever offered. Stay. Be different. Bless anyway. Love the city that does not love you back, and trust the One who loved a world that nailed him to a tree.
chapters.verdict: You cannot bless a city you are trying to conquer, and you cannot save a city you are trying to escape.
reflect: Which of the three postures, conquest, condemnation, or conformity, is your church most tempted by right now?
When was the last time your church did something purely for the good of neighbors who will never join it?
Do the non-Christians in your town experience your church as a threat, an irritant, or a gift?

chapters.title: The Pastor Without Borrowed Power
chapters.summary: Pastoral leadership in Christendom rested on borrowed cultural authority; in exile that authority is gone, and the pastor has to learn to lead by the cross-shaped power the New Testament actually describes. Losing borrowed power is not losing ministry. It is recovering it.
chapters.body:
