This is the chapter I least want to write, because it's about me, and about every pastor I serve in the Network, and about a wound the collapse has pressed on directly. Christendom gave the pastor borrowed power. Exile takes it away. And the taking-away exposes how much of our identity was built on the borrowed power instead of on the gospel, which is to say it exposes us, and it is not a comfortable thing to be exposed.

Think about what the pastor inherited from the long establishment, all of it free, none of it earned. He inherited a presumption of authority that came with the office and had nothing to do with his character. The title, the building, the standing in the community, the seat on the platform at the civic events, the assumption that when the pastor spoke he was worth hearing. The culture handed him a hearing it granted to almost no one else. He could assume the moral high ground because the culture had assigned it to his office, not to his life. He could expect the wayward member to feel the pull of the church's disapproval, because the church's approval still mattered socially and getting crosswise with the church could cost you in the wider community. He had borrowed power, a whole set of cultural mechanisms that made people listen and defer and comply even when their hearts weren't in it. Christendom did a lot of the pastor's work for him. It applied social pressure where his own words couldn't reach. It lent him an authority the gospel never promised, an authority enforced by the surrounding culture's residual fear of God and church.

Now take all of that away, and ask what's left. In exile, the pastor stands in front of a room, or sometimes an emptying one, with nothing but the gospel and the Word and his own credibility, and none of it is backed by the culture anymore. No one has to listen. The teenager in the back row has a thousand louder, funnier, more interesting voices in his pocket, and he knows it, and so do you. The wider community does not care what the pastor thinks about anything; his opinion is one opinion among eight billion, and not a trending one. The wayward member feels no social cost for leaving, because leaving costs nothing now; nobody at the office will think less of him, nobody at the club, nobody at all. The borrowed power is gone. And the pastor discovers, often in something close to horror, how much of his sense of himself was propped on the borrowed power. Strip it away, and there's a man standing there who needed to be listened to, who needed to be deferred to, who measured his own significance by an authority the culture has now quietly withdrawn. The collapse is a mirror, and the pastor is the one in it, and a lot of us do not like what we see.

I'll go first. There's a specific moment I keep having, and maybe you have it too. I'm preaching, and I can feel the room not with me, not hostile, just not there, the attention diffuse, the phones glowing in laps, and I hear my own voice start to push, to strain, to reach for a weight it used to have automatically and now has to manufacture. And the strain is the sound of a man who needed the borrowed power more than he knew. Because in the old world the weight was just there. The room granted it before I opened my mouth. Now I have to earn it sentence by sentence, and when I can't, I push, and the pushing is ugly, and I can hear it, and afterward in the car I have to ask the Lord the hard question. Do I want these people to follow Christ, or do I want them to defer to me? Christendom let me confuse those two things for twenty years, because deference to me and devotion to Christ looked identical when the culture enforced both. Exile pulls them apart, and forces the question, and I don't always like my answer.

But here's the turn, and it's the whole reason I can write this chapter without despair. This is brutal, and it is grace, both at once. Because the borrowed power we're losing was never the power Jesus gave us in the first place. Go read the New Testament's actual descriptions of spiritual authority, and you'll find something that contradicts the entire machinery of Christendom's borrowed power, top to bottom.

Listen to Paul, who had every reason to lean on his credentials and refused to. When I came to you, brothers, I did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with lofty speech or wisdom. I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified. And I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling, and my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God (1 Corinthians 2:1-5). Read that as a job description for the exilic pastor. Paul deliberately refused the borrowed power available to him, the rhetorical power, the credentials, the impressive bearing, because he understood that if the Corinthians' faith rested on his impressiveness it would be resting on the wrong foundation, and the wrong foundation would not hold. He wanted their faith resting on the power of God, and to get it there he had to get himself, and his pull, out of the way.

Listen to him again. We have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us (2 Corinthians 4:7). The cracked, ordinary, breakable clay pot is the whole point. If the vessel were gold, you'd credit the vessel. God uses clay so that when the power shows up, everyone knows it didn't come from the pot. And when Paul begged the Lord three times to take away his thorn, the answer he got is the sentence that ought to be carved over every post-Christendom pastor's desk. My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). Not despite weakness. In it. Through it. Perfected by it. The authority of the apostle was cross-shaped. It looked like weakness because it was weakness, deliberately, on principle, because borrowed power would have put the people's faith in the wrong place.

And Jesus said it plainly, to men who wanted exactly what Christendom would one day hand the church. You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant (Mark 10:42-43). The whole apparatus of borrowed power, the lording, the social pressure, the borrowed clout, the borrowed compulsion, is precisely what Jesus forbade, and precisely what Christendom quietly restored and called normal. We've been leading like Gentile rulers for sixteen centuries, with the culture's permission, and we mistook it for spiritual authority. Exile is taking away the very thing Jesus told us not to use. We ought to grieve it the way a man grieves the loss of a crutch he was never supposed to need, with some real sadness, sure, and also with the slow realization that maybe now he'll finally learn to walk.

So what's the authority that remains, the power Jesus actually gave, the power no collapse can touch? It's the authority of the Word truly preached, which does not need the culture's enforcement to pierce a heart, because the Spirit does the piercing, and the Spirit was never on the culture's payroll. It's the authority of a life that matches the message, the credibility of a shepherd who actually smells like the sheep, who's wept with the dying and sat through the long night with the doubting and not flinched and not left. Eugene Peterson spent his whole ministry insisting that the pastor's real work was not running an organization or wielding influence but the slow, unglamorous, uncoercible labor of attending to actual souls, what the old writers called the cure of souls, the long obedience in the same direction, the refusal to become a religious executive. I read Peterson when I was younger and thought he was describing a quaint, outdated, small-church ministry that the rest of us had moved past. I understand now that he was describing the only ministry that was ever going to survive the collapse, because it was the only kind that never depended on the borrowed power in the first place. Presence. Patience. Prayer. The Word. Those, no empire can take, because no empire ever gave them.

I think the loss of borrowed power exposes a particular wound in pastors, and I want to name it because I carry it and most of the men I serve carry it too. A lot of us went into ministry, if we're honest underneath the calling language, partly because we needed to matter. We needed to be needed, to be looked up to, to have a significance that the world would recognize, and ministry offered that, especially in Christendom, where the office came with built-in significance. The collar made you somebody. And for a man with a hole in him, a man who, say, grew up without a father telling him he mattered, the borrowed significance of the pastoral office can become a way of medicating a wound that was never healed. I'll speak for myself. I grew up without a father, and I have spent a good portion of my life trying to be significant enough that the absence wouldn't ache, and the pastorate gave me a significance I could point to, a way of being important that felt holy. And the exile, by stripping away the borrowed significance of the office, has pressed directly on that wound, has forced me to ask whether I can be a nobody and still be okay, whether my significance can rest in being a son of God rather than in being a respected man, and that question goes a lot deeper than ministry strategy. It goes to whether I ever really believed the gospel I preach, the gospel that says I'm accepted not because I'm significant but because Christ is, that my standing before God has nothing to do with my standing before the culture.

This is why the loss of borrowed power, brutal as it is, is also a strange kind of healing, because it forces the wound into the open where the gospel can actually get at it. As long as the borrowed significance held, I could leave the wound buried, could medicate it with the respect of the community and never have to bring it to Christ. The exile took away the medication, and now the wound throbs, and the throbbing is awful, but it's also the first time in years I've actually had to bring it to God instead of numbing it with significance. The collapse of Christendom is, for a wounded pastor, an intervention. It's God taking away the thing we were using to avoid him, the way you'd take a bottle away from a man you love, knowing the withdrawal will be terrible and necessary. I don't enjoy the withdrawal. But I'm starting to see it as mercy, the severe kind, the kind that takes away your crutch because it loves you too much to let you keep limping.

There's an objection here I want to take seriously, because I don't want to romanticize weakness in a way the New Testament doesn't. Someone will say, fine, but pastors do have real authority, the Bible says to obey your leaders and submit to them (Hebrews 13:17), elders are to be given honor (1 Timothy 5:17), so aren't you overcorrecting, throwing out genuine spiritual authority along with the borrowed cultural kind? And that's fair, so let me distinguish. There is a real authority given to the shepherd, but read carefully what kind it is. Peter, writing to elders, tells them to shepherd the flock, not domineering over those in their charge, but being examples to the flock (1 Peter 5:2-3). The authority is the authority of the example, of the shepherd who goes first, who leads by being out front in obedience and sacrifice, not the authority of the boss who issues commands and expects compliance because of his position. The borrowed power of Christendom was positional, it worked by borrowed clout and social pressure, it could compel without persuading. The genuine authority of the shepherd is moral and exemplary, it works by going first, by a credibility earned in blood and tears, by a life the people can follow because they can see it's true. I'm not throwing out the second. I'm saying the first was never ours and we're better off without it. The shepherd who can no longer compel can still lead, but only by example, only by going first into the very weakness and obedience he's calling his people to, which is, not coincidentally, exactly how Jesus led.

And there's a strange freedom in the loss, which I've only begun to taste and want more of. When you can no longer assume anyone has to listen to you, you stop performing for the people who never had to, and you start actually loving the few who choose to be there. When the building empties of the merely cultural Christians who came because it was expected, who were never converted and never claimed to be, the ones who remain are the ones who actually want Christ, and a small body that wants Christ is worth infinitely more than a large one that wants respectability. When the borrowed power goes, the temptation to manipulate goes with it, because manipulation needs borrowed power to work, and the pastor without it cannot coerce, cannot pressure, cannot trade on social fear, cannot run the old plays. He can only do what Paul did. Preach Christ crucified, in weakness, and trust the Spirit to do what the culture used to do for us. And it turns out, this is the thing I keep being surprised by, the Spirit is much better at it than the culture ever was. The culture produced full buildings of unconverted people. The Spirit produces small rooms of people who would die for Jesus. I know which I'd rather pastor, even if my flesh keeps voting for the full building.

I think the deepest test of whether a pastor has made his peace with the loss of borrowed power is what he does with church discipline and with conflict, because those are the moments where the old borrowed power was most useful and is now most plainly gone. In Christendom, when a member was living in open sin or causing division, the pastor had clout. The social cost of being put out of the church, or even just being on the wrong side of the pastor, was real, and it kept people in line even when their hearts weren't in it. Now that clout is gone. You can confront a man in sin and he can simply leave, drive ten minutes to the next church or to no church, and pay no social price at all, and you have no power to compel him to stay and face it. And this terrifies pastors, because it feels like the loss of the ability to maintain any standard at all, and some respond by abandoning the standards, by never confronting anything, because what's the point when they'll just leave. But others respond by getting harsh, by trying to manufacture through intensity the compulsion the culture used to supply, by being heavy-handed in a way that's really just panic at the loss of borrowed power.

Both responses miss what the loss of borrowed power actually exposes, which is that real discipline was never supposed to work by coercion in the first place. Read Matthew 18, where Jesus lays out how to handle a brother in sin, go to him privately, then with two or three, then before the church (Matthew 18:15-17). There's not an ounce of coercion in it. It's all relationship, all appeal, all the patient work of trying to win a brother, and if he won't be won, you let him go, sadly, as one outside, but you don't compel him, you were never able to compel him, the whole process assumes he can walk away and is trying to win his heart rather than force his compliance. Christendom let us short-circuit that, let us skip the patient relational appeal and just apply social pressure, and it worked, sort of, the way coercion always sort of works, by producing outward conformity and inward resentment. The loss of borrowed power forces us back to Jesus's actual method, which was always relational and never coercive, which never had the power to compel and never wanted it, which aimed at the heart and accepted that the heart cannot be forced. Discipline without coercion is harder and slower and produces fewer outward results, and it's the only kind Jesus ever authorized. The borrowed power we're losing was a shortcut around the patient relational work, and the shortcut was never holy.

This is the indictment, and I want to be sure I'm standing inside it and not lobbing it over a wall at someone else. We built ministries on borrowed authority and called it a calling. We measured ourselves by clout and named the clout anointing. I did this. The loan is being called in, all over the Western church, and the calling-in is painful, and it is also the kindest thing God could be doing to us, because he is taking back a power we were never supposed to have so that we'll finally reach for the power he actually gave.

There's a scene I keep returning to, and it's the foot washing, because it's Jesus showing the disciples what leadership in his kingdom actually looks like at the exact moment they expected him to show his power. It's the last night. He knows who he is, John tells us, knows that the Father has given all things into his hands, knows that he has come from God and is going to God (John 13:3), which is to say he is at the height of his authority, the most powerful being in the room by an infinite margin, and what does he do with all that authority? He gets up from the table, takes off his outer garment, wraps a towel around his waist like a household slave, and washes the dirt off the feet of the men who are about to abandon him, including the feet of the one who's about to betray him. The most powerful being in the universe, knowing the full extent of his power, expresses it by kneeling on the floor with a basin, doing the job of the lowest slave in the house. And then he says, do you understand what I have done to you? I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you (John 13:12-15). This is the example. This is the leadership. Not the throne, the towel. Not the lording, the kneeling. Not the throne's pull, the basin.

And I have to ask myself, honestly, whether I would have washed Judas's feet. Whether I, knowing what he was about to do, would have knelt and cleaned the dirt off the feet of the man who was selling me for thirty pieces of silver. And I know the answer, and the answer is that I would have wanted the upper hand, would have wanted to confront him, expose him, use what power I had to stop him or shame him, would have done almost anything except kneel and serve him. The foot washing is the death of borrowed power. It's leadership that has so completely renounced the use of power-over-people that it can kneel and serve even the one who's destroying it. That's the leadership Jesus gave us and Christendom buried under sixteen centuries of thrones and titles and borrowed power. The exile is digging it back up, handing us back the towel and the basin we set aside when the empire handed us the crown. It feels like a demotion. It's actually a restoration. We're being given back the only kind of authority Jesus ever modeled, the authority of the one who kneels, and if we'll receive it instead of grieving the crown, we might finally lead the way he led.

The borrowed power we are losing was never the power Jesus gave us. He gave us a towel and a basin (John 13:4-5), a Word and a cross, and a promise that his strength is made perfect in our weakness. We've spent long enough trying to lead like kings. Maybe out here in Babylon, with the crutch gone and the crowd thinned and nobody required to listen, we'll finally learn to lead like him.
chapters.verdict: The borrowed power we are losing was never the power Jesus gave us.
reflect: How much of your authority as a leader has rested on cultural standing rather than on the cross and the Word?
What would your leadership look like if you could no longer assume anyone had to listen to you?
Where is the loss of borrowed power exposing a self that needed the power more than the gospel did?

chapters.title: The Hidden Life of the Exiled Pastor
chapters.summary: When the borrowed power is gone and the visible results are gone, what holds a pastor up is the interior life almost nobody sees, the life of prayer and hiddenness and the long friendship with God that the old success never required.
chapters.body:
I almost didn't write this chapter, because it's the most exposing one in the book, and a man doesn't like to admit in print that his relationship with God has spent years on life support. But I left it in, and put it near the middle where it belongs, because I've become convinced that the hidden life is the hinge the whole exile turns on for a pastor. Everything else in this book, the leadership without borrowed power, the long defeat, the network, the formation, the suffering, all of it depends on a pastor who has something inside him to draw from, and the something inside is built in secret or it isn't built at all. You can fake almost everything else in ministry. You can fake competence, fake warmth, fake confidence, fake a sermon, fake your way through a hospital visit when you're empty. The one thing you cannot fake, and the one thing the exile most requires, is a real, living friendship with God, because that's the only thing that produces the endurance the long exile demands, and it can't be borrowed or performed or manufactured under pressure. It has to be there, built up over years in the quiet, before the pressure comes. So I put my own failure on the page, because I'd rather you learn from my emptiness than repeat it.

There's a question I've started asking the men in the Network, and it makes them uncomfortable, and that's exactly why I keep asking it. If God removed every visible reward from your ministry tomorrow, the attendance, the affirmation, the sense of momentum, the people telling you that the sermon helped, everything you can see and measure, would there be enough left underneath to keep you in it? Would the secret life with God be enough? And the long pause that usually follows that question is the most honest thing in the conversation, because most of us don't know, and the exile is going to find out for us whether we want it to or not.

Here's what I've come to believe after watching a lot of pastors thrive and a lot of pastors crater. In Christendom you could run a ministry on a thin interior life, because the visible rewards kept refilling the tank. The full room fed you. The respect fed you. The growth fed you. The sense that you mattered to the community fed you. A man could go years on almost no prayer, no real communion with God, no hidden life at all, and stay upright, because the external supports held him up like scaffolding around a building with no internal structure. The scaffolding did the work the soul was supposed to do. And it worked, right up until the scaffolding came down.

The scaffolding is coming down now. The external rewards are drying up, and what's being exposed, building by building, pastor by pastor, is whether there was ever any internal structure underneath, whether there was a real life with God holding the man up or only the scaffolding of cultural reward. And for a lot of good, sincere, hardworking men, the terrifying discovery of the exile is that the scaffolding was all there was. They were sustained by the results, not by God, and when the results stopped, they had nothing to fall back on, because they'd never built the thing the scaffolding was supposed to be temporary support for. They prayed in public and not in private. They knew about God and didn't know God. They'd traded communion for productivity so gradually they never noticed the trade.

I'm describing myself in seasons, so don't hear distance in this. There have been years where I could not honestly have told you the last time I prayed for any reason other than to prepare to lead someone else in prayer. Where my entire relationship with God had become professional, a relationship I maintained because it was my job to maintain it, the way a dentist maintains an interest in teeth. I read the Bible to find sermons in it. I prayed to open meetings. I talked about God all day and went weeks without talking to him, just the two of us, with nothing to produce. And I got away with it, for a long time, because the work was going fine, the church was healthy, the externals were holding, and a man can hide a hollow interior life behind a successful exterior one indefinitely, until something happens that the externals can't fix.

For me it wasn't the collapse of the culture. It was smaller and more personal, the way these things usually are. It was a stretch where the work was going fine and I was dying inside anyway, where I had everything the old metrics said I should want and felt like a fraud holding all of it, and I realized that if the church grew to ten thousand it would not fix the thing that was wrong, because the thing that was wrong was that I had a public relationship with God and no private one, and you cannot live on a public relationship with God any more than you can live on a public marriage. The exile is doing to the whole Western church, slowly, what that season did to me suddenly. It's stripping away the externals to reveal whether there's anything underneath.

So let me say the unglamorous thing as plainly as I can. The exiled pastor will be sustained by his hidden life with God or he will not be sustained at all. There is no third option out here. In Christendom there was a third option, the scaffolding, but the scaffolding is gone. What remains is the oldest thing, the thing the externals always tempted us to skip. The long, slow, mostly invisible friendship with God, built in the hours nobody sees, the early mornings, the prayer that produces nothing you can point to, the Scripture read for no reason except that you're hungry for it, the silence you keep before God when there's nothing to ask for and nothing to report and you just sit there because he's there.

Jesus modeled this and we managed not to notice for sixteen centuries because we didn't need it. Look at how often the Gospels stop the action to tell you he withdrew. Rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed (Mark 1:35). The day before had been a triumph, a whole town at the door, every sick person in Capernaum healed, the kind of ministry day we'd build a conference around. And the next morning, before any of it could feed him, he got up in the dark and went where no one could find him and prayed, and when the disciples tracked him down to tell him everyone was looking for him, that the momentum was building, that they should ride the wave, he said it was time to leave and go somewhere else (Mark 1:36-38). He would not be governed by the externals even when the externals were good. He was sustained by the Father in the dark place, and the public ministry flowed out of the hidden one, never the reverse. We reversed it. We built ministries that ran on the public reward and squeezed the hidden life into the margins, and now the public reward is gone and we're learning, the hard way, that Jesus had it right and we had it backwards.

Henri Nouwen, who left a prestigious academic post to live with profoundly disabled adults who had no idea he was famous and could not have cared less, wrote that the great temptation of the minister is to be relevant, to be spectacular, to be powerful, and that the antidote to all three is the hidden life of prayer, the willingness to be with God in a place where you are nobody, where nothing you do is impressive, where the only audience is the One who sees in secret. He learned that among people who couldn't read his books or attend his lectures or affirm his gifts, who only knew whether he showed up and was kind. That's the school the exile is enrolling all of us in. Ministry before an audience of One, in a place where the relevance and the spectacle and the power have all been taken away, where the only thing left to do is the thing we should have been doing all along, which is to love God and be loved by him in the hidden place.

There's a temptation, when a pastor's interior life is dry, to fix it the way we fix everything else, with a program. We'll buy a new devotional, sign up for a reading plan, download an app that pings us to pray, attend a retreat, read a book on spiritual disciplines, and there's nothing wrong with any of those things, but I've noticed they often function as one more way of avoiding the actual thing. Because the actual thing isn't a technique. It's a relationship, and relationships don't get fixed by programs. If my marriage were dying, my wife would not be helped by me announcing a new marriage-improvement system with daily metrics. She'd want me, present, attentive, honest, choosing her. God is the same. The dryness in a pastor's soul is almost never solved by a better method. It's solved by coming to him, actually coming, as a person and not a professional, and being with God the way you'd be with someone you love, which is mostly just being there, without agenda, over time, letting the relationship be real instead of managed.

I think this is why so much of the Bible's language for knowing God is the language of marriage and friendship rather than the language of management. Abraham was called the friend of God (James 2:23). Moses spoke with God face to face, as a man speaks to his friend (Exodus 33:11). The whole prophetic tradition uses marriage as the central image of the covenant, God as the husband, his people as the bride, with all the intimacy and the jealousy and the heartbreak that implies. And Jesus, on the last night, told his disciples, no longer do I call you servants, but I have called you friends (John 15:15). Friends. Not employees, not subordinates, not staff. Friends. And a pastor can spend his whole ministry relating to God as an employer rather than as a friend, doing the work, meeting the expectations, maintaining the professional relationship, and never once experiencing the friendship that's actually on offer, the staggering, almost unbelievable thing that the God of the universe wants to be known by us, not just served by us. The hidden life is where the friendship happens, or doesn't. It's the only place it can happen, because friendship requires unhurried, unproductive, unwitnessed time, the very thing the visible ministry never has room for.

Augustine wrote a whole book that's really just one long prayer, the Confessions, addressed directly to God, telling God his own life story as though God didn't already know it, and the reason he did that, I think, is that he understood the difference between knowing about God and talking to God. The Confessions opens with that line everyone quotes, you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. But the line that gets me is later, when Augustine, looking back on all his years of religion and philosophy and seeking, writes that God was within him the whole time and he was outside, that he'd been looking for God out there in the things God had made while God was waiting inside, closer to Augustine than Augustine was to himself. Late have I loved you, he writes, beauty so old and so new, late have I loved you. That's the cry of a man who finally found the friendship after years of mistaking the religion for the relationship, and it's the cry I hear from pastors in the Network when the exile finally drives them off the scaffolding and back to the well. Late. Late have I loved you. I had you confused with the work for thirty years, and now the work has been taken from me, and underneath it, where you'd been waiting the whole time, here you are.

I want to be practical, because I get suspicious of spiritual writing that floats. What does the hidden life actually require of a working pastor with a full week and a phone full of needs? It requires, first, that you guard a time and a place for being with God that produces nothing, that has no agenda, that is not sermon prep in disguise. If every minute you spend with God is harvested for use, you don't have a relationship with God, you have a supplier. Find the time that's just for him. Defend it like your life depends on it, because in exile it does. Second, it requires that you let yourself be small before God, that you stop performing for him the way you've learned to perform for everyone else, that you bring him the fear and the doubt and the envy and the lust and the exhaustion instead of the curated version of yourself you bring to the congregation. God is not impressed by your competence and not fooled by your performance, and the hidden life is the one place you get to stop maintaining both. Third, it requires silence, which is the hardest, because silence is where we meet ourselves and we don't like the company. The phone has made silence almost extinct, and the pastor who cannot be silent before God will not survive the exile, because the noise will eventually drown out the only voice that can hold him up.

There's a cost to this, and the cost is that the hidden life will make you, by the world's measures and even by the church's measures, less productive for a while. Time spent in prayer that produces nothing is time not spent on the work that produces something, and in a results-starved season the pull to abandon the unproductive thing for the productive one is enormous. I feel it constantly. I sit down to pray and within ninety seconds my mind is on the email I need to send, the call I need to return, the problem I need to solve, and the prayer feels like a luxury I can't afford when the church needs me. But that's exactly the lie the scaffolding tells. It tells you that the visible work is the real work and the hidden life is the optional extra, when the truth is the reverse, the hidden life is the real work and the visible ministry is supposed to be its overflow. A pastor who has it backwards will pour out and pour out until there's nothing left, because he's drawing from a well he never fills, and then one day the bucket comes up dry and he doesn't understand why, and the not-understanding is itself the symptom.

Let me say a word about the desert, because the hidden life is going to feel, for long stretches, like a desert, and pastors quit the hidden life when it gets dry because we assume the dryness means we're doing it wrong. We're not. The dryness is part of it. The great teachers of prayer across the centuries all describe seasons of dryness, of darkness, of God's apparent absence, when the prayer produces no feeling and no sense of his presence and you sit there in what feels like an empty room talking to a wall, and they tell you, with one voice, to keep coming anyway, because the dryness is not the absence of God, it's the weaning of the soul off of the feelings of God onto God himself. As long as prayer feels good, you can't fully tell whether you're seeking God or seeking the good feeling. The dryness strips the feeling away so you can find out, and if you keep praying in the dryness, when there's nothing in it for you, no comfort, no sense of presence, nothing but the bare choosing of God for his own sake, that's when the relationship gets real, because that's when it stops being about what you get and starts being about him.

I wish someone had told me that early, because I quit the hidden life a dozen times over the years precisely when it got dry, assuming the dryness was a sign of failure or of God's displeasure or of my own hypocrisy, when it was actually an invitation deeper in. The pastor who only prays when it feels good is a pastor who will pray less and less as the exile wears on, because the exile is dry and the feelings are scarce. The pastor who learns to pray in the dryness, to show up to the empty-feeling room and stay, choosing God when there's nothing in it but God, is the pastor who'll still be praying in year forty when the feelings have long since stopped being reliable, because his prayer was never resting on the feelings. The desert is not a detour from the hidden life. The desert is the hidden life's deepest classroom, the place where the soul learns to love God and not God's gifts, to want the Giver and not the feeling of being given to. Don't quit when it gets dry. The dryness is where it gets real.

I've come up dry. I've stood in front of my people with nothing real to give them, going through the motions, preaching from notes about a God I hadn't spoken to all week, and the awful thing is that most weeks nobody could tell, because the externals were intact and the machine ran fine without me. That's the danger of competence. It lets you fake the thing the longest, right up until you can't, and then the collapse is total because there was nothing underneath. The exile is mercy precisely because it's removing the externals that let us fake it, forcing us back to the well we should never have stopped drinking from.

There's a paradox here that I've had to make peace with, and it took me years. The hidden life produces the public ministry, but the moment you start cultivating the hidden life in order to produce a better public ministry, you've ruined it, because you've turned the hidden life into one more productive activity, one more input to the visible output, and the whole point of the hidden life is that it's not for anything, it's just for God. If I pray in order to preach better, my prayer has become sermon prep, and God knows it, and the friendship can't happen because I've turned the friend back into a supplier. The hidden life only works if it's genuinely useless, genuinely for its own sake, genuinely just being with God because he's God and I love him and that's enough. And then, paradoxically, out of that uselessness, the public ministry gets fed, the way a well you're not constantly draining stays full enough to draw from. But you can't fake the uselessness. You can't pretend to seek God for his own sake while actually seeking him for the sermon. He's not fooled, and the well stays dry, because you never actually went to him, you went to the sermon and called it him.

I think this is the hardest thing for a working pastor to grasp, because everything in our training and our temperament says our time should be productive, that an hour spent should yield something, and an hour of prayer that yields nothing measurable feels like waste, feels irresponsible, feels like time stolen from the people who need us. And the only way I've found past that is to believe, really believe, that being with God is not a means to an end but the end itself, that the friendship with God is not the fuel for the ministry but the actual point of the whole human life, the thing we were made for, the thing the ministry is supposed to serve rather than the other way around. We were not made to do ministry. We were made to know God, and ministry is one thing that flows from knowing him, and a pastor who has those backwards, who lives to do ministry and fits God in around the edges, has inverted his own existence. The exile, by stripping the rewards out of the ministry, is forcing the inversion back to right side up, forcing us to discover whether we actually want God or only wanted what knowing him could produce. It's a brutal question and a clarifying one, and most of us have never had to face it because the productive ministry let us avoid it. Out here, we can't avoid it anymore.

A ministry the culture can no longer reward will only be sustained by a God the culture cannot see. That's not a burden. In the end it's the gift hidden inside the whole hard providence, because the God the culture cannot see was always the only One worth being sustained by, and the externals, even when they were good, were always a thinner thing than they felt. Out here, in the dark place, early, with nothing to produce and no one watching, the exiled pastor finally meets the only audience that was ever going to be enough. And the strange testimony of everyone who's been driven there is that he's enough. He really is. We just couldn't find it out while the scaffolding held.
chapters.verdict: A ministry the culture can no longer reward will only be sustained by a God the culture cannot see.
reflect: If no one but God ever saw your ministry, would there be enough there to keep you going?
What in your interior life with God has atrophied because the visible work crowded it out?
Are you praying, or are you only working and calling it ministry?

chapters.title: A Church You Cannot Explain Without God
chapters.summary: In Christendom the church could be explained by sociology and self-interest; in exile its witness has to be a common life so distinct that it requires the resurrection to account for it. The church's first apologetic is not its argument but its body.
chapters.body:
If the pastor's authority in exile is cross-shaped instead of cultural, then the church's witness in exile has to be communal instead of positional, because the church no longer has a position in society to witness from. The question quietly shifts from what does the church say to what is the church, and that shift is the single most important reorientation a post-Christendom congregation can make. In Babylon, the people of God are read before they're heard. The body is the first argument, and if the body isn't making the argument, the words won't either.

Hauerwas has been pounding this one anvil for forty years, and most of us couldn't hear him in the old world because we didn't need to. He says the church does not have a social ethic; the church is a social ethic. Its primary task is not to make the surrounding society more just by lobbying it, though justice matters; its primary task is to be itself, to be a community whose common life is so shaped by the gospel that it constitutes a visible, embodied alternative to the way the world organizes itself. The church's job is to be the kind of community the world could not produce on its own and cannot account for once it sees it. Not a pressure group with a position. A people with a peculiar life. And the peculiar life is the witness, prior to anything the people say.

This is what we lost in Christendom and what the exile gives us a chance to recover, which is one more reason to receive the exile as gift rather than only as loss. When everyone in the society was nominally Christian, the church could not be a contrast to the society, because the church was the society at prayer. There was no edge. No visible difference between the church's common life and the culture's, because the two had fused into one thing. So the church became a chaplaincy. It blessed the existing arrangements, sacralized the status quo, provided religious services to a population that already shared its values whether or not it shared its Lord. And a chaplaincy can be entirely explained without reference to God. Its hospitality is just good manners. Its charity is just civic virtue, the same impulse that funds the food bank and the Rotary scholarship. Its gatherings are just a club for pleasant people who enjoy a particular style of music and value the same things their neighbors value. The watching world looks at a chaplaincy church and sees nothing it couldn't produce on its own, nothing that requires God to explain, and so it does the entirely rational thing. It ignores it. A church the world can fully explain is a church the world can safely ignore, and most of our churches are eminently explainable.

So what would it actually mean to be a church you cannot explain without God? We don't have to guess, because we have the original exiles to look at, and the early church witnessed without a shred of the cultural power we keep grieving. They had no political clout and no social prestige and no protected day and no respected office. What they had was a common life so strange that it forced the question out of the mouths of the people watching.

They held their possessions loosely and met each other's needs, so that, Luke says, there was not a needy person among them (Acts 4:34). Set that against the world it happened in. The Roman Empire ran on patronage and the hoarding of wealth and the rigid stratification of who owed what to whom. A community where the people with means simply sold what they had and laid it at the apostles' feet so that nobody among them went hungry, that was not normal generosity dialed up a notch. It was inexplicable. It didn't compute. It required a different account of what money is for and who your real family is, and the only account that made sense of it was that these people actually believed a dead man had risen and was coming back and that compared to that, their stuff didn't much matter.

They welcomed the people the empire threw away. In the Roman world, an unwanted infant, often a girl, often a sickly child, was simply exposed, left outside the city or on a hillside to die or be taken by slavers. It was legal, common, unremarkable. And the Christians went out and gathered those babies and raised them as their own. When plague swept through a city and everyone who could afford to fled, leaving the sick to die alone, the Christians stayed and nursed them, and a lot of the Christians died doing it, caught the disease from the people they wouldn't abandon. They ate together across lines the empire treated as unbreakable, slave and free at one table, Jew and Gentile, rich and poor, in a world where the table was where the social order was most rigidly enforced (Galatians 3:28). They forgave the people who killed them. They refused to retaliate, refused to expose their children, refused the easy out of just burning the pinch of incense to Caesar that would have spared their lives, and they loved the empire's poor while the empire ignored them. The pagan world looked at all this and could not explain it, and the not-being-able-to-explain-it was the witness. See how they love one another, the outsiders said, with something between contempt and wonder. Even an enemy of the church, an emperor who hated it, complained that the Christians cared not only for their own poor but for everyone's, and shamed the old religion by it. The body was the apologetic. Nobody got argued into that church. They got loved into it, and then they wanted to know what could possibly make people live like that.

Let me make this uncomfortably concrete, because it's easy to admire the early church from a safe distance and never let it indict the present one. Run the test on your own congregation. Walk through everything your church did last month, and ask of each thing, could a thoughtful unbeliever explain this without reference to the resurrection? The Sunday gatherings, the music, the programs, the budget, the building, the staff, the way decisions get made, the way conflict gets handled, the way money gets spent, the way people are welcomed and the way people are let go. Be ruthless about it. And I think most of us, if we're honest, will find that the overwhelming majority of what our churches do is entirely explainable. The music is explainable as a preference for a certain emotional experience. The programs are explainable as services that meet felt needs and keep families coming. The budget is explainable as the budget of any nonprofit, with a building to maintain and staff to pay and programs to fund. The welcome is explainable as good customer service. The conflict, when it comes, gets handled exactly the way conflict gets handled in any organization, with politics and power and hurt feelings and people leaving angry, nothing there that requires Jesus to have risen.

And then ask the harder question. What, specifically, did your church do last month that an unbeliever could not explain without the resurrection? Where was the forgiveness too costly to make sense, the generosity too reckless, the welcome too wide, the love that crossed a line the world wouldn't cross, the joy that held up under a suffering that should have crushed it? And if you struggle to find much, if the inexplicable column is thin and the explicable column is thick, that's not a reason for despair, it's a reason for repentance and redirection, because it means you've been building an explainable church and praying for an inexplicable harvest, and the two don't go together, and the diagnosis is the beginning of the cure.

Here's where I have to handle an objection, because a sharp reader will raise it. Aren't you setting an impossible standard? The early church's radical sharing and care for the dying, isn't that a high-water mark we can't reasonably expect of ordinary believers with mortgages and jobs and limited bandwidth? Aren't you just laying a guilt trip on tired people? And I feel the force of that, so let me be careful. I'm not saying every Christian has to sell everything and nurse plague victims to the death. I'm saying the church's common life, taken as a whole, ought to contain things the world cannot account for, and that the bar for those things is not heroism but ordinary love practiced past the point the world considers reasonable. It doesn't take a martyr. It takes a congregation where, when a young mother's husband leaves her, the church doesn't just pray for her on Sunday but shows up Tuesday with groceries and Thursday to fix her car and stays for two years until she's on her feet, expecting nothing, because that's what family does and she's family now. The world can explain a casserole. The world cannot explain two years of casseroles for someone who can never repay you and isn't even, yet, one of you. That's not heroism. It's just love that doesn't quit when the world's love would have quit, and a church full of that kind of love is a church the world cannot explain, and you don't need a single martyr to build it. You need ordinary people loving past the ordinary limit, which is hard, but it's not impossible, and it's the actual assignment.

Lesslie Newbigin saw this with a missionary's clear eyes, and he saw it precisely because he'd been gone. He spent decades as a missionary in India and came back to a Britain that had secularized while he was away, came back as a foreigner to his own homeland, and he could see what those of us who never left couldn't. He argued that the only real hermeneutic of the gospel, the only thing that could make the good news believable again to a culture that had stopped finding it plausible, was a congregation of men and women who actually believed it and lived it. Not a better argument. Not a slicker presentation. A community. He called the local congregation the hermeneutic of the gospel, the lens through which a watching world could finally read what the words alone could no longer make credible. Because in a culture whose plausibility structures rule out the resurrection before you ever open your mouth, the argument lands only after the body has made the argument seem possibly true. The existence of people whose life together can't be accounted for unless Jesus rose, that's what cracks the immanent frame open enough for the words to get in. First the strange community, then the believable claim. We've been trying to do it in the other order for fifty years, leading with the argument to people whose whole world says the argument is impossible, and wondering why the argument bounces off.

I have to confess that the church I've often led was eminently explainable. A reasonable sociologist could have accounted for nearly everything we did without once invoking the resurrection. The music chosen to attract a target demographic. The programs designed to retain young families. The hospitality that never cost us anything we'd actually miss, the coffee and the handshake and the welcome that asked nothing of us. The giving that never threatened our own comfort, the tithe off the top that left the lifestyle untouched. We were a well-run religious organization providing valued services to people who already shared our values, and there is not one thing on that list that requires God to explain it. We were a chaplaincy. We were explainable. And being explainable, we were ignorable, and then we stood around wondering why the world ignored us. We did this. I did this. I built an explainable church and prayed for an inexplicable harvest, and the two don't go together.

I keep thinking about that complaint from the ancient world, the one even the church's enemies made, that the Christians cared for everyone's poor and not only their own. Set that next to how a church is usually evaluated today, even by us, and feel the distance. We evaluate churches by what they offer their members, the quality of the experience, the programs for the family, the music, the preaching, the facilities, the services rendered to the people inside. The early church was known, by its enemies, for what it gave to the people outside, the ones who weren't members, weren't going to join, couldn't repay, the poor and the sick and the abandoned of a city that wasn't even Christian. The witness was not the excellence of what they offered insiders. It was the recklessness of what they spent on outsiders, the love that overflowed the boundaries of the community onto people who had no claim on it. And I think that's a piece of the inexplicability we've most lost, because a chaplaincy church spends its resources on its own members, which the world can completely explain, that's just a club serving its dues-paying members, and a church that cannot be explained spends itself on the people who will never join, the city's poor and not only its own, which the world cannot explain, because no club spends itself on non-members.

So here's a question to put to your church's budget and calendar, harder than the explainability test, more specific. What does your church spend on people who are not its members and never will be? What goes out the door to the city, to the poor who won't come, to the neighbors who'll never join, with no expectation of return, no membership drive attached, no strings? Because that number, the number a church spends on outsiders with no hope of return, is a pretty good measure of how inexplicable it is, of how much it resembles the church that scandalized the empire by caring for everyone's poor. Most of our budgets go almost entirely to ourselves, to our staff and our building and our programs for our people, with a small slice for missions and a smaller one for local mercy, and that allocation is the allocation of a club, fully explainable, safely ignorable. The church that wants to be inexplicable has to spend itself outward, recklessly, on the city that isn't going to thank it or join it, the way Jesus spent himself on a world that nailed him up, because that kind of spending, love poured out on people who can't repay it, is the one thing the world has never been able to explain and never been able to ignore.

The exile is asking for a different church, and not a more effective version of the chaplaincy. It's asking for a community whose common life requires the resurrection to make sense, where the forgiveness is too costly to be explained by therapy, where the welcome is too wide to be explained by good manners, where the generosity is too reckless to be explained by civic virtue, where the joy is too durable under real suffering to be explained by temperament or privilege. That kind of church does not need borrowed cultural power to witness, which is good, because the borrowed power is gone. Its plain existence is the witness. And the watching world, which has heard every Christian argument and learned to tune them all out before the second sentence, has not yet seen many of these churches, and would not know what to do with one if it walked past it on a Tuesday.

I want to say one more thing about why this is so hard, because I don't want to leave the impression that it's a matter of trying harder, that we just need to crank up the love and the church will become inexplicable. The reason it's hard is that the inexplicable church cannot be programmed. You can program a service, schedule a program, organize an outreach, budget a ministry. You cannot program two years of casseroles for an ungrateful neighbor. You cannot schedule the moment a man forgives the brother who wronged him from the heart. You cannot organize the kind of love that gets up at three in the morning to sit with the dying. Those things are not programs. They're fruit, and fruit grows on trees, and trees grow slowly from roots, and the roots are the formation we talked about and the hidden life of the people and the actual presence of the Spirit producing his actual fruit in actual hearts over actual years. Which means the inexplicable church is not something a pastor can build by being a better organizer. It's something the Spirit grows as a congregation gets formed, over a long time, into the likeness of Christ. The pastor's job is to tend the conditions, to preach the Word and keep the table and gather the people and pray, and then to wait, like the farmer, for fruit he cannot manufacture. We are so addicted to building what we can control that the call to grow what we cannot control feels like passivity, but it isn't passivity, it's the harder thing, the patient tending of conditions for a fruit that only God can produce.

And here's the encouragement in that, because I don't want to leave you only with the weight of it. If the inexplicable church is the Spirit's fruit and not the pastor's product, then a small, poor, unimpressive church in a forgotten town has exactly the same access to it as the largest, best-resourced church in the country, because the Spirit is not impressed by resources and does not produce his fruit in proportion to budget. The most inexplicable church in your county might be the tiny congregation of forty people that the conference circuit would never look at twice, where the love runs so deep and the forgiveness so costly and the welcome so wide that the watching town cannot account for it. Christendom measured churches by the things money can buy. The exile measures them by the fruit only the Spirit can grow, and on that measure the playing field is suddenly, gloriously level, and the small faithful church is not the junior partner of the big impressive one, it might be the realer thing, the more inexplicable thing, the church Babylon actually can't ignore even though the conference circuit already did.

A church the world can fully explain is a church the world can safely ignore. The only church Babylon cannot ignore is the one it cannot explain. Build that, slowly, with the actual people God actually gave you, and the seventy years will not be wasted, whatever the census says.
chapters.verdict: A church the world can fully explain is a church the world can safely ignore.
reflect: Could an outside observer explain everything your church does without ever mentioning God?
What practices of your common life would only make sense if the resurrection were true?
Where has your church become a religious version of the surrounding culture instead of a contrast to it?

chapters.title: The Table, the Word, and the Long Work of Formation
chapters.summary: A church that cannot be explained without God doesn't happen by accident; it gets formed, slowly, by the ordinary means the church has always had, the Word preached, the table kept, the people gathered, in a culture that is forming everyone all day long whether the church competes or not.
chapters.body:
The kind of church I described in the last chapter, the one you can't explain without God, doesn't happen because a pastor preaches a sermon about it. It gets formed, and formation is slow, and formation is the thing Christendom let us neglect because the culture did our forming for us. That's the piece I most want pastors to grasp, because it changes what we spend our energy on. In the old world, the surrounding culture formed people into something roughly compatible with the faith, and the church mostly added a religious layer on top of a person the culture had already shaped. The home was Christian-ish. The school assumed the basics. The neighbors went to church too. The whole environment was a slow-acting catechism, and the church coasted on it. We could spend our energy on programs and production and assume the deep formation was happening offstage, because it was.

It isn't anymore. The culture is still forming people every waking hour, but it's forming them into something the faith has to actively contradict. Think honestly about how much formation your people are absorbing Monday through Saturday and from where. The phone, first, hours of it, an algorithm that knows their fears and feeds their appetites and trains them, with every swipe, to want more, to compare, to consume, to never be satisfied, to treat their own desires as the final authority on everything. The screens that tell them, ten thousand times before they're grown, that the meaning of life is the satisfaction of the self and the good life is the one you can photograph. The work that catechizes them into believing their worth is their output. The whole machinery of late-modern life, which is not neutral, which is teaching a gospel of its own all day every day, the gospel that you are your own, that you owe nothing to anyone you didn't choose, that freedom is the absence of constraint, that the body is a tool of the will, that death is a problem we'll eventually solve and meanwhile shouldn't think about. That's the catechism your people are sitting under forty, sixty, eighty hours a week.

And against all of that, the church gets ninety minutes on a Sunday, if the family makes it, which increasingly they don't, because the kid has travel soccer and the catechism of travel soccer is also relentless and also forms them and the church scheduled itself into the one slot the culture was willing to spare. So let me say the thing plainly. Ninety minutes a week will not hold the line against eighty hours of counter-formation unless those ninety minutes form something the eighty hours cannot. And mostly, in the late-Christendom church, they didn't, because we filled those ninety minutes with the same thing the culture was already giving people, entertainment, a show, an emotional experience engineered with the same techniques the entertainment industry uses, a religious version of what they could get anywhere. We competed with the culture on the culture's terms, and you cannot out-entertain the entertainment economy. It has better budgets and no Sabbath and no scruples.

Daniel and his friends did not survive Babylon on ninety minutes a week of Babylonian entertainment with a Hebrew flavor. They survived because they'd been formed, deeply, before they ever arrived, in something thick enough to hold when the pressure came. And the church has always had the means of that kind of formation, the ordinary means, the ones we let drift to the edges while we chased the production values. The Word preached. The table kept. The people gathered around both, week after week, year after year, in a rhythm the culture cannot offer because the culture has no Sabbath and no body and no bread.

Start with the Word, because it's where I live as a preacher and where I've most repented. For a long stretch I preached to move people, to give them something useful for the week, a takeaway, a felt need met, a problem solved, and there's a place for that, but I had let the deeper thing slide. I had stopped preaching to form people, over years, into a whole different account of reality, into people who think with the mind of Christ because they've been soaked in the Scriptures long enough that the Scriptures have rearranged their imaginations. That's slow work and it doesn't fill a room next Sunday, which is exactly why Christendom let us skip it. Expository preaching that walks people through whole books over months and years, that doesn't flinch from the hard texts, that builds a biblical imagination brick by brick, that's not a stylistic preference, it's a formation strategy for exile. People who only know a few inspirational verses cannot withstand a hostile week. People who have the whole counsel of God in their bones, who can think biblically because they've been taught to, who have an alternative story deep enough to live inside when the culture's story presses on them, those people can stand in the furnace, because they were formed before the music played.

Then the table, which I think we have catastrophically underestimated, especially in my own low-church tradition where we tucked the Lord's Supper into a quarterly add-on at the end of a service, an afterthought, a few crackers and some grape juice while the band played something quiet. The table is formation. It's an embodied catechism that does something words alone can't do. Every time the church gathers at the table, it rehearses the gospel in the body, takes it in, enacts the thing it believes. It says, with bread and cup, that we are one body though we are many, in a culture that's atomizing people into ten thousand lonely individuals each curating a personal brand. It says that we live by a death, that our life comes from outside us, from a body broken and blood poured out, in a culture that says you make your own meaning and owe your life to no one. It says we are waiting, that this is not all there is, that we eat this meal until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26), in a culture that says this world is all you get so grab what you can. The table preaches all of that without a single word, straight into the body, and it does it weekly, repetitively, the way real formation always works, by repetition, by habit, by the slow grooving of a different way of being into people who came in shaped by Babylon. We treated it as a memorial tacked on the end. It's a weekly counter-catechism, and a church in exile cannot afford to keep it at the edges.

James K. A. Smith helped me see this, and I'll name him because his books genuinely changed how I think about a Sunday. His argument, boiled down, is that human beings are not primarily thinking things who occasionally feel, and not even primarily believing things; we're loving things, desiring things, and our loves are shaped less by what we're taught to think than by what we're trained to want, and we're trained to want by repeated, embodied practices, by liturgies, in the broad sense, the habits that aim our hearts. The mall is a liturgy. The phone is a liturgy. The stadium is a liturgy. They form our loves by repetition, by ritual, by enacting a vision of the good life over and over until we want it without deciding to. And the church, Smith says, has its own liturgy, its own set of formative practices, and in the late-Christendom church we either neglected them or stripped them down or replaced them with practices borrowed straight from the mall and the stadium, and so we formed people who could recite Christian beliefs while their hearts had been trained by Babylon's liturgies to want Babylon's life. The disconnect between what our people believe and how our people actually live, which torments every honest pastor, is largely a formation problem. We taught them right doctrine and let the culture train their loves, and the loves won, because loves always win.

I want to add prayer to this, because we treat corporate prayer as filler, the thing we do to transition between the real elements of the service, and I think that's a catastrophe for formation. When a church prays together, out loud, regularly, it's being formed in something the culture cannot give and actively works against. It's being formed in dependence, in the bone-deep posture that says we cannot do this ourselves, we need God, in a culture that catechizes us hour by hour into self-sufficiency, into the belief that we are our own and can manage our own lives and need no one. Every time the church gets on its knees together, it's enacting a counter-truth, that we are not our own, that we are needy, that there is a God who hears, and the enacting forms the people even when they're barely paying attention, the way repeated practice always forms us beneath the level of conscious thought. A praying church is being trained, week by week, out of the autonomy the culture trains into it. A church that's abandoned real corporate prayer for slick transitions has handed that formation back to the culture.

And Sabbath. I almost left it out, which tells you how thoroughly even I've absorbed the culture's contempt for it. The Sabbath is one of the most counter-formational practices the church has, and we've nearly lost it. The culture forms us to believe that our worth is our productivity, that to stop working is to lose value, that rest must be earned and is faintly shameful, that we must be always available, always producing, always on. And against all of that, the Sabbath says stop, the world will keep turning without you, your worth is not your output, you are a creature and not the Creator and the universe does not depend on your labor, so put it down and rest in the God who holds it all while you sleep. To keep a Sabbath in a culture like ours is an act of defiance, a weekly declaration that you do not belong to the machine, and it forms people, slowly, into people who can rest, who are not enslaved to their own usefulness, who know they are loved for who they are and not for what they produce. The exhausted, anxious, always-on people in our pews are being formed by a culture with no Sabbath, and the church that recovers the Sabbath is handing them a practice that could, over years, reform their relationship to time and work and worth at the deepest level. We treated it as a legalism to escape. It's a gift to recover.

So the work of the exilic church, underneath everything else, is the recovery of formation. Real catechesis, the deliberate teaching of the faith to adults and children alike, not assuming anymore that they picked it up somewhere, because they didn't. The recovery of the church's own formative practices, the Word and the table and prayer and confession and Sabbath, held at the center and not pushed to the margins by production. The building of homes that are themselves little churches, where the formation continues all week, because no church can form people in ninety minutes that their homes are de-forming the other hundred and sixty-seven hours. The patient, unglamorous, unmeasurable work of making disciples instead of attracting crowds, which produces nothing you can put on a dashboard for years and then, slowly, produces the only thing that lasts, people who actually belong to Jesus deeply enough to keep belonging to him when it costs.

I want to address the family directly here, because the church cannot do this alone and the late-Christendom church tried to, outsourcing formation to the professionals and the programs while the home opted out. In a believing culture the home could be passive about formation and the kids would still absorb the faith from the surrounding air. In our culture the home has to be the primary place of formation or it won't happen, because ninety minutes of church a week cannot compete with a hundred and sixty-seven hours of life, and most of those hours are at home or shaped by home. So the recovery of formation means the recovery of the home as a place where the faith is taught and lived and practiced, where there's prayer at the table and Scripture in the evening and honest talk about God in the car, where the parents are the primary disciplers and the church supports them rather than replacing them. The early church and the church through most of history understood this. The home was a little church, the father a kind of pastor to his own household, the daily rhythms of the family shot through with the faith. We professionalized all of that, handed it to the children's ministry and the youth program, and told parents their job was to drop the kids off, and we are now reaping the children of that arrangement, raised by programs that got them a couple hours a week and a culture that got them all the rest.

This is going to require something hard of the church, which is to stop competing with the family for the family's time and start equipping the family to do the formation the church can never do for it. We built churches that demanded so much of a family's week, so many programs and events and commitments, that we actually crowded out the home formation we most needed the family to be doing. We became one more activity stealing the evenings, and then we wondered why the formation wasn't taking. A church serious about formation in exile might do less, not more, might pull back on the programs that fragment a family's week and instead pour its energy into equipping parents to disciple their own children, into teaching fathers and mothers to lead family worship, into building the home as the primary site of formation and the church as the gathering that supports and supplements it. That's a hard turn for a church culture built on busyness, on the full calendar as evidence of health. But the full calendar was a Christendom measure too, and it may be one more thing the exile asks us to lay down, so that families have the evenings back to do the formation that actually forms.

This is a hard sell in a results-starved season, because formation is the opposite of fast. You will form people for a decade and not be able to prove it worked until a furnace comes and they don't bow, and by then you may not be the pastor anymore, or even alive. Formation is planting trees in whose shade you will not sit. But it's the only thing that produces a church you can't explain without God, and a church you can explain is a church the world ignores, and so we're back where the last chapter left us, except now we know the mechanism. The inexplicable church gets built by the ordinary means, the Word and the table and the gathered people, applied with patience over years, while the culture catechizes against us every hour.

I should be honest that this turn toward formation is going to cost a church members, at least at first, and a pastor needs to count that cost before he makes the turn. A church built on attraction, on giving people a compelling experience that meets their felt needs, has a congregation that came for the experience, and when you shift the center from experience to formation, from entertainment to discipleship, some of the people who came for the experience will leave, because you've stopped giving them what they came for. The music gets less like a concert. The teaching gets harder, longer, more demanding. The church starts asking things of people instead of just serving them. And the consumers, the ones who were shopping for the best religious experience in town, will shop elsewhere, and your numbers will dip, and the census will look worse before it looks better, if it ever looks better by the old measures at all.

This is where a pastor finds out whether he actually believes what this book is arguing, because the easy thing, the Christendom thing, is to chase the consumers, to keep the experience compelling enough to retain them, to measure success by whether they stay. And the faithful thing, the exile thing, is to let them go, sadly, and to pour your energy into forming the ones who actually want to follow Jesus, even if there are fewer of them, even if the building feels emptier, even if the census judges you a failure. Jesus let people walk away. When his teaching got hard, when he said things the crowd couldn't stomach, John tells us that many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him, and Jesus didn't chase them, didn't soften the message to keep them, but turned to the twelve and asked, do you want to go away as well? (John 6:66-67). He was willing to be left with twelve. He prioritized the depth of the few over the size of the crowd, formed the twelve so deeply that they turned the world upside down, and let the crowd that wanted the bread and not the cross go find its bread elsewhere. The exilic church has to be willing to do the same, to choose depth over breadth, twelve over five thousand, because twelve formed deeply changed history and five thousand who wanted bread changed nothing.

The culture is catechizing your people every waking hour, and ninety minutes on Sunday will not hold the line unless those ninety minutes form something the rest of the week cannot. So make those ninety minutes count for formation and not just for attendance. Preach the whole Word. Keep the table at the center. Gather the people and teach them the faith as though they've never heard it, because half of them haven't. And then send them out formed deeply enough to carry the faith into a week designed to dissolve it. It's slow. It's the only thing that works. It was always the only thing that worked; Christendom just let us forget by doing the forming for us. Now the forming is ours again, and the exile, hard as it is, has handed us back our actual job.
chapters.verdict: The culture is catechizing your people every waking hour, and ninety minutes on Sunday will not hold the line unless those ninety minutes form something the rest of the week cannot.
reflect: What is actually forming your people Monday through Saturday, and have you reckoned honestly with how much of it there is?
Are the gathered means of grace at the center of your church, or have they been pushed to the edges by programs and production?
What would it take to form your people deeply enough that they could carry the faith into a hostile week?

chapters.title: Raising Children in Babylon
chapters.summary: The hardest cost of the exile for most Christian parents and pastors is the fear of losing their children to a culture that catechizes them harder than the church does, and the answer is neither the bunker nor the gamble of hoping it works out, but the deliberate, costly formation of children who can hold the faith in a world that won't reinforce it.
chapters.body:
Let me get personal in a way the rest of this book has mostly avoided, because this is the chapter where the exile stops being a theory about the culture and becomes the thing that keeps Christian parents awake at two in the morning. I have five sons. And I cannot write a book about the church in exile without writing the chapter that every parent in my church and every pastor in the Network actually wants the answer to, which is not how do we survive the collapse of Christendom in general but how do I not lose my kids. Because that's the fear underneath the fear. The numbers about the nones aren't abstract to a parent. They're a face at the dinner table. They're the very real possibility that the child you carried to the front for dedication will, at twenty-two, want nothing to do with any of it, and you won't fully understand why, and you'll lie awake wondering what you did wrong.

I won't pretend I've got this solved, because I don't, and any pastor who tells you he's cracked the code of guaranteeing his children's faith is selling something, probably a parenting curriculum. There are no guarantees. Faith is a gift of God and not a product of technique, and there are faithful parents whose children walk away and unfaithful parents whose children come to Christ, and the sovereignty of God in salvation means I cannot manufacture my sons' belief no matter how perfectly I parent, which is both terrifying and, when I can receive it, the only thing that lets me sleep. But the absence of a guarantee is not the absence of a calling.
