I'm still commanded to teach these things diligently to my children, to talk of them when I sit in my house and when I walk by the way and when I lie down and when I rise (Deuteronomy 6:7), and the how of that command in a post-Christian age is worth thinking hard about, because the strategies that worked in Christendom will not work now.

Here's the brutal arithmetic every Christian parent has to face. In Christendom, the culture helped you raise your kids in the faith. The school reinforced it, or at least didn't actively undermine it. The neighbors' values matched yours. The wider environment was a tailwind. So a parent could be fairly passive about formation and still end up with children who held a basic faith, because the whole world was nudging them the same direction the home was. Those days are over. Now the wider environment is a headwind, a strong and constant one, and it's blowing your children somewhere you don't want them to go. Count the hours honestly, the way I had to count them about my own boys and didn't like the total. The screen gets them for hours a day, and the screen is not neutral; it's a catechist with a curriculum, and the curriculum is the gospel of the self, repeated endlessly, more compelling than anything I say at dinner because it comes with motion and music and the faces of people they admire. The school, even a decent one, mostly assumes a frame in which God is irrelevant. Their friends are being formed by the same forces. And against all of that, the question is what the home and the church are putting in, hour for hour, and for most Christian families the honest answer is, not nearly enough to compete.

Your children are being raised by someone every day, every single day, whether you're intentional about it or not. There's no neutral. There's no childhood that just happens. They are being formed, every hour, by something, and if it isn't you and the church, then it's the empire, and the empire is extraordinarily good at it, far better than we are, with more money and more talent and more access and no scruples about what it's doing to their souls. The passive parenting that worked in Christendom, the drop-them-at-Sunday-school-and-hope model, is now a way of choosing, by default, to let Babylon disciple your children, because Babylon will gladly fill every hour you don't claim. I had to face that about my own home. I'd been assuming a tailwind that wasn't there, assuming the culture was helping when the culture was working against me the whole time, and I was being out-discipled in my own house and didn't realize it because I was measuring my effort against a Christendom standard that no longer applied.

So what do you do? There are two wrong answers and they're the same two wrong answers we keep running into, because the exile only ever offers the same handful of escape hatches and the same one hard road.

The first wrong answer is the bunker. Lock them down. Pull them out of everything. Control every input, screen every friend, flee every contaminating influence, build the walls high and keep them inside until they're grown. And I understand the impulse all the way to the bone; when you love a child and you can see the danger, the instinct to wall it out is overwhelming, and there's even some wisdom in it, because some limits on the inputs are simple sanity and a parent who lets the algorithm raise their twelve-year-old unsupervised is not being faithful, they're being negligent. Wise limits, yes. But the bunker as a total strategy fails, and it fails predictably, in two ways. It fails because you cannot actually seal the walls; the world gets in, it always gets in, and a child raised to fear the world rather than to engage it from a settled faith is a child who, the first time the walls fail, has no idea how to stand, because he was protected instead of prepared. And it fails because the bunker often raises children who experience the faith mainly as a set of restrictions, a list of the things they couldn't do that everyone else could, and who associate Christianity with the cage and freedom with the door, and the day they get the chance, they bolt. I've watched it happen to good families. The tightest homes sometimes produce the angriest leavers, because the faith was presented as a wall and not as a treasure, and you cannot make a child love a wall.

The second wrong answer is the gamble, which is just passivity with a hopeful face. It's the parent who senses the headwind, feels overwhelmed by it, and quietly gives up on competing, telling themselves the kids will find their own way, that faith can't be forced, that they don't want to push too hard and make the kids resent it, and so they do very little and hope it works out. And it almost never works out, because you do not win a contest of formation by not competing in it. The culture is not going to be passive. The algorithm is not going to ease up because you decided not to push. The gamble is just the bunker's opposite error, the abandonment of formation instead of the over-control of it, and it loses children just as surely, only more quietly, with less drama and the same empty pew at the end.

The hard road, the only road, is the road Daniel's parents must have walked, though Scripture doesn't show us, because Daniel didn't get his settled faith in Babylon out of nowhere. Somebody formed him before Babylon got him. The hard road is deliberate, costly, deep formation aimed not at protecting children from the world but at preparing them for it. Preparing, not protecting, and the difference is the whole chapter. Protection tries to keep the furnace away from the child. Preparation accepts that the furnace is coming, that you cannot keep it away, that your child will face Babylon whether you like it or not, and asks the only useful question, which is what does this child need to have in them so that when the furnace comes they don't bow.

What they need is a faith that's theirs and not just yours, deep enough to cost them something and still be worth it. And that gets handed down not mainly through rules but through a few things that are hard and slow and unglamorous, the same things this whole book keeps coming back to, applied to the people you love most. It gets handed down through a home where the faith is plainly real to the parents, not performed but lived, where the children see their father and mother actually pray, actually repent, actually treasure Christ, actually forgive each other when they've blown it, because children believe what they see modeled long before they believe what they're told, and a faith that's only talked about and not lived in the home gets correctly read by children as a thing the adults don't really mean. It gets handed down through the deliberate teaching of the faith, real catechesis, sitting with your children and teaching them what Christians believe and why, not assuming they'll absorb it, because they won't, the culture is teaching them its catechism with great deliberation and we cannot answer deliberate formation with accidental formation. It gets handed down through the church, through embedding children in a community of believers who aren't their parents, other adults who know them and love them and model the faith, because the day will come, and it comes for every child, when the parents' faith isn't enough and the child needs to have seen that other people, people they respect, also believe this and also live it. And it gets handed down through honesty, through refusing to give children a brittle, defensive, fearful faith that can't survive a hard question, and instead letting them ask the hard questions out loud, at the dinner table, while you're still there to walk through them, so that the doubts get processed inside the relationship and inside the church instead of alone at college with no one who loves them in the room.

There's a piece of this I have to add, because growing up without a father taught it to me at a cost I'd rather not have paid, and it's the single most important thing I know about handing faith to children. The picture a child forms of God is built, for better or worse, partly out of the father he had or didn't have. I'm not saying that's all of it, and I'm not saying a fatherless child can't know God, because I'm living proof that he can. But I'm saying the raw material a child uses to imagine God includes the father standing in front of him, and a child whose father is absent or harsh or unreliable will have to fight, sometimes for the rest of his life, against a picture of God built out of that absence or that harshness. I fought it. When I came to faith and started calling God Father, the word came loaded with everything I'd learned about fathers, which was that they leave, that they're unreliable, that you don't lean your weight on them because they're not there to catch you. It took me years to let the true Father heal the wound the absent father left, years to be able to call God Father and mean trustworthy rather than gone.

So here's what that means for raising children in Babylon, and it's heavier than any technique. The most powerful catechism your children will ever receive is your own life, and especially, if you're a father, your own fathering. They are learning what God is like by watching what you are like, before they can read, before they can reason, in the preverbal place where the deepest pictures get set. A father who is present, who is reliable, who disciplines without cruelty and loves without condition, who admits when he's wrong and asks forgiveness, who keeps his promises, is handing his children a true picture of God built into the structure of their imagination, a picture that will hold them long before they can articulate a doctrine. And a father who is absent, or harsh, or who says one thing and lives another, is handing them a lie about God that all the right teaching in the world will struggle to overcome. This is terrifying, and it should be, because it means the formation of my children's faith is not mainly a matter of what I teach them but of who I am with them, and who I am with them is exposed every single day, in the car, at the table, when I'm tired, when they've pushed me too far. I cannot hand them a God I'm not living. They'll believe my life over my words every time.

I'll tell on myself one more time, because I've made every mistake in this chapter. I've been the bunker dad, white-knuckling the controls, trying to keep the world out, and watched it make one of my sons more curious about the very thing I was walling off, because forbidden fruit is forbidden fruit. And I've been the gamble dad, too busy with the church to disciple my own children, pouring out for other people's families while assuming my own would somehow be fine, which is its own particular pastoral sin, the man who saves the town and loses his own house. The exile has forced me to face both, to stop assuming a tailwind that left decades ago, and to do the slower, harder, more relational work of actually forming my sons rather than either caging them or coasting. It costs more than the old way. It costs time I want to spend on the ministry, attention I want to spend on the crisis, evenings I want to spend resting. But they are being formed by someone every one of those evenings, and I would rather it be me and the church and the Lord than the empire that wants them and does not love them.

I want to speak to the parent reading this whose child has already left, because I've been writing as though the children are all still young and formable, and for many of you that ship has sailed and the grief is present-tense. Your son doesn't believe anymore. Your daughter walked away. You did the formation, or you didn't, and either way here you are, and the chapter on raising children in Babylon feels like salt in a wound because your child is grown and gone and you can't go back and do it differently. I'm not going to give you a formula, because there isn't one, and anyone who tells you that if you'd just done X your child would have stayed is lying to you and adding cruelty to your grief. Children are not products of parenting. They are free souls before a sovereign God, and faithful parents lose children and unfaithful parents keep them, because the final factor is not the technique but the grace of God working in a heart no parent can reach. So first, lay down the false guilt. You are not God. You could not save your child, you were never able to save your child, salvation was always God's to give and not yours to manufacture, and the fact that your child has walked away is not the verdict on your parenting that the shame keeps telling you it is.

And second, do not give up praying, because the story isn't over while you're both still breathing, and even after. I came back to God from a contempt as hard as anything your child feels, and there were people praying for me, some I never knew about, and I cannot tell you it was their prayers that brought me back because I don't have the books of heaven open in front of me, but I cannot tell you it wasn't, either. Augustine's mother Monica prayed for that brilliant dissolute son for years while he ran the other direction as fast as he could, and she wept over him, and a bishop told her, famously, that it was not possible that a son of so many tears should perish, and he didn't, he became the greatest theologian of the early church, but Monica prayed for decades before she saw it and there were years it must have looked completely hopeless. The God who pursued me and pursued Augustine is pursuing your child right now, in ways you cannot see, down roads you'll never know about, with a patience that outlasts your lifetime if it has to. Keep praying. Keep loving. Keep the door open and the porch light on. And entrust the child you could not save to the only One who could, who loves that child more than you do, who went into the far country after prodigals and is in the far country still, looking down the road, ready to run.

Your children are being raised by someone every day, and if it isn't you and the church, it's the empire, and the empire is very good at it. You cannot keep them from Babylon. You were never going to be able to keep them from Babylon. But you can, by grace, with no guarantees, send them into it the way Daniel went into it, formed deeply enough that the faith is theirs, with the line already drawn in their bones, prepared rather than merely protected, able to stand in the king's court without bowing to the king's gods. One more thing, because I think it's the thing parents most need permission for and least give themselves. The single most powerful gift you can give your children's faith is your own joy in God. Not your rules, not your doctrine, not your vigilance, though those matter. Your joy. Children can tell, with a radar that never switches off, whether the faith you're handing them is a burden you carry grimly or a treasure you actually delight in. If they grow up watching you obey God resentfully, attend church dutifully, follow the rules joylessly, treating the whole thing as a heavy obligation, they will conclude, reasonably, that the faith is a cage, and they will leave the cage the first chance they get. But if they grow up watching you actually delight in God, actually love the Scriptures, actually find your deepest joy in Christ, actually treat Sunday as the best day and prayer as a privilege and the faith as the most precious thing you have, they will want to know what you have, because joy is contagious and attractive in a way that duty never is. You cannot fake this for them; they'll see through fake joy faster than through anything. But if it's real, if you genuinely delight in God, that delight will preach to your children every day in a register that no lecture can reach.

So the deepest formation question for a Christian parent is not how do I get my children to believe, it's do I myself actually delight in God, because my children will catch my real relationship with God far more than my stated one. And this sends me back, again, to the hidden life, because the joy in God that my children need to see in me is not something I can manufacture for their benefit. It can only overflow from a real friendship with God that exists for its own sake. The pastor who's running on empty, who has the public faith and not the private one, cannot give his children the joy they need to see, because he doesn't have it himself. So the formation of my children turns out to depend, in the end, on the same hidden life everything else in this book depends on, my own actual, joyful, delighting friendship with God, lived where my children can see it, overflowing onto them not as a strategy but as the natural runoff of a man who genuinely loves the God he's trying to hand them. Hand them your joy. It's the most evangelistic thing you'll ever do, and you can only hand them a joy you actually have.

That's the work. It's slow and it's costly and it might not work, and you do it anyway, because they're worth it, and because the God who gave them to you loves them more than you do and went into exile to get them.
chapters.verdict: Your children are being raised by someone every day, and if it isn't you and the church, it's the empire, and the empire is very good at it.
reflect: Who is actually discipling your children, hour for hour, and have you looked the numbers in the face?
Are you trying to protect your children from Babylon or prepare them for it, and do you know the difference?
What faith are you handing your children, a thin inheritance or a thing deep enough to cost them something and still be worth it?

chapters.title: The Long Defeat and the Longer Hope
chapters.summary: Faithfulness in exile means learning to work for outcomes you will not live to see, refusing both the despair that says nothing matters and the triumphalism that demands victory on our timeline. Hope is not optimism. It is fidelity to a promise about the end.
chapters.body:
The hardest discipline of exile is the discipline of time, and I keep circling back to it because it's the one I personally have the least handle on. Jeremiah's seventy years are not incidental to the lesson. They are the lesson. The exiles who got the letter had to make peace with the fact that they would die in Babylon, that the return would belong to grandchildren they might never meet, that faithfulness in their generation meant planting gardens whose fruit they would not taste. And a culture like ours, formed to expect results inside the fiscal year, the quarterly report, the church-growth dashboard, the conference success story told from a stage, finds this nearly unbearable. We want the win, and we want it on our watch, and the exile tells us we may get neither, and something in us would rather rage or quit than accept that.

This is where I've watched good pastors break, and they break by falling off one of two cliffs, and the cliffs are on opposite sides of the same narrow road.

The first cliff is despair. The numbers don't turn around. The culture doesn't relent. The church keeps shrinking, the children keep leaving, the funerals outpace the baptisms, and the pastor slowly concludes that nothing he does matters, that the cause is lost, that he's presiding over a managed decline whose only mercy will be his eventual retirement, if he can hang on that long. The despair is completely understandable, and I've tasted it, the Sunday you look out at the thinning room and the math just does itself in your head and you think, what is the point of any of this. And the despair is a lie, but it's a sophisticated lie, because it's built on a true observation. The trend really is down. The despair just draws the wrong conclusion from the true fact, the conclusion that because the visible trend is bad, the work is worthless, and that conclusion does not follow, though it feels like it does at four o'clock on a gray afternoon in February.

The second cliff is triumphalism, which is the refusal to accept the exile at all. It's the insistence that with the right strategy or the right candidate or the right cultural offensive we can take the country back, restore the settlement, get the census back on our watch. The triumphalism is energizing, which is part of why it sells, and it's also a lie, the same lie Hananiah told, return in two years, don't settle in, this is temporary, victory is at hand. Both cliffs, and this is the thing to see, share a single hidden assumption. They both assume that faithfulness has to be validated by visible victory in our lifetime. The despairing man assumes it and concludes there's no victory coming so the work is pointless. The triumphalist assumes it and concludes the victory must be coming so let's go seize it. Pull out that shared assumption, the assumption that our faithfulness needs to be vindicated by results we can see, and both cliffs simply vanish, because the whole structure that held them up is gone.

Tolkien gave us a phrase that has held me steady through more dark seasons than I can count, and I keep it close. He wrote, in a letter, about fighting the long defeat. He did not mean despair; he was the opposite of a despairing man, a man of deep and stubborn hope. He meant that the Christian works for the good while knowing that history, this side of the end, does not trend toward our triumph, that we will lose many battles, that the darkness will press hard and often win the day, that we are not promised a winning streak inside time, and that we labor anyway, faithfully, because the outcome of the war does not depend on the outcome of the day. The long defeat is fought in hope, not because we expect to win the next battle, but because we know who wins the last one. The seed of the woman crushes the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15). The Lamb who was slain is worthy to receive the kingdom and the power (Revelation 5:12). The dwelling place of God is finally with man, and he wipes away every tear, and death itself is no more, and the former things have passed away (Revelation 21:3-4). The end is not in doubt. The timeline of the middle is simply not ours to control, and our peace was never supposed to depend on controlling it.

This is the difference between hope and optimism, and getting it wrong has wrecked a lot of preaching in this season. Optimism is a prediction about outcomes. Things will get better, the numbers will turn, the culture will swing back, the pendulum always swings. Optimism is a bet on the visible trend, and in a season of genuine collapse it's simply false, which is exactly why optimistic preaching rings so hollow to people watching their own churches empty. They're not stupid. They can see the trend, and when you stand up and predict an upturn the evidence doesn't support, you sound like Hananiah, and they stop trusting you. Hope is something else entirely. Hope is not a prediction about the trend; it's fidelity to a promise about the end. The Christian hope does not require that things improve on our watch. It requires that the tomb was empty, that the King is coming, that our labor in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58), and therefore that no act of faithfulness, no garden planted, no soul attended through a long night, no truth told at cost, no child catechized at the dinner table, no enemy forgiven, is ever finally lost, even when it never bears one ounce of visible fruit in our sight. Hope can stand in a shrinking church in a hostile culture in the middle of a long defeat and keep planting, because its confidence is anchored not in the trend line but in the resurrection, and the resurrection already happened, in the past, where the trend can't touch it.

I keep a parable close that helps me hold this, and it's the parable of the growing seed, the short strange one only Mark records. The kingdom of God, Jesus says, is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear (Mark 4:26-28). He knows not how. The farmer's job is to scatter the seed and then to live his life, to sleep and rise, and the growth happens by a power that is not his, in a way he doesn't understand and can't control and mostly can't even see. He doesn't make the seed grow by watching it anxiously or by pulling it up to check the roots. He scatters, and he sleeps, and he trusts the ground to do what the ground does by a power he didn't put there. That parable is a rebuke to the whole anxious results-driven machinery I was trained in, where the pastor is supposed to engineer the growth and measure the growth and take credit for the growth and despair over its absence. Jesus says, no, you scatter, and you sleep, and the growth is God's, and it happens underground where you can't see it, and your job is faithfulness in the scattering, not control over the harvest. The exile is forcing us back into that parable, back into a posture where we scatter and sleep and trust, because the visible control we thought we had turned out to be an illusion Christendom let us maintain.

There's a hard grace in he knows not how. It means the absence of visible growth is not the absence of growth. Underground, in the dark, in soil you can't see into, the seed may be doing exactly what God designed it to do, and your inability to see it proves nothing, because the farmer never could see it. The pastor in a shrinking church who scatters the word faithfully and sees no visible result is not necessarily failing. He may be in the long underground season before the blade appears, the season that looks like nothing and is actually everything, the season where the real work happens precisely where no one can watch it. Some of the most fruitful ministries in history looked, in their own time, like failures, and the fruit came up years or generations after the sower was in the ground himself. William Carey labored in India for seven years before his first convert. Adoniram Judson labored in Burma for years and buried much of his family in that soil before the church he planted began to grow, and it grew into hundreds of thousands long after he was dead. They scattered, and they slept, and they died, and the earth produced by itself, and they knew not how. So can we, if we'll let go of needing to watch the seed.

Brueggemann taught me that hope is itself a prophetic act, maybe the prophetic act, in a culture organized around despair on one side and denial on the other. The empire, whether it's Babylon or the immanent frame, wants the people of God either crushed or co-opted, either hopeless or comfortable, because a people who genuinely hope are a people the empire cannot finally control. To hope, in the prophetic sense, is to refuse to accept that the present arrangement is permanent, to insist against all the visible evidence that God will keep his promise, to grieve honestly everything that's dying and yet to announce a future that the empire cannot deliver and cannot prevent. And this hope is not naive, which is the crucial thing, because we tend to think hope and realism are opposites. The prophet's hope has fully absorbed the collapse, has wept at the grave, has refused to pretend the loss isn't real. That's why it can hope without lying. The prophet weeps and hopes at the same time, in the same breath, and the weeping is exactly what keeps the hope honest, and the hope is exactly what keeps the weeping from becoming despair. You need both, held together, and Christendom let us lose the muscle that holds them together because it gave us neither real grief nor real hope, just a comfortable management of a status quo that felt permanent.

I keep a verse near my desk for the despairing days, and it's an odd one to find comforting, but it does the job. It's the end of the great resurrection chapter, where Paul has spent the whole thing arguing that the dead are raised, that death is swallowed up in victory, that the sting is gone, and then he lands the entire towering argument on a single practical command. Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). Notice where the resurrection leads. Not to a prediction that your work will succeed. Not to a guarantee of visible fruit. It leads to be steadfast, keep working, and here's the anchor, your labor is not in vain. Not your labor will produce results you can see. Your labor is not in vain. There's a difference, and the difference is the whole consolation. In a world where the dead are raised, no faithful work is ever wasted, even the work that produces nothing visible, even the sermon no one seemed to hear, even the prayer over the child who walked away, even the decades in a shrinking church, because the resurrection means that the final accounting is not done by the census but by the God who raises the dead and forgets nothing and wastes nothing.

That word, vain, is the word the despairing pastor most needs answered, because despair is precisely the conviction that the labor is in vain, that it amounts to nothing, that he's pouring his life into a hole. And Paul, having proven the resurrection, says the opposite, says it flatly, your labor is not in vain, and he doesn't qualify it, doesn't say your successful labor or your fruitful labor, just your labor, all of it, the visibly fruitful and the apparently fruitless alike, because in a resurrection world the value of the labor doesn't depend on what you can see it produce. The seed that fell and seemed to die is not in vain. The garden planted for grandchildren you'll never meet is not in vain. The faithfulness no one noticed and the trend never reflected is not in vain. The resurrection guarantees it, not by promising you'll see the harvest, but by promising that the One who raises the dead has it all recorded and will bring it all to its end. That's not optimism. Optimism would say the trend will turn. This says something better, that whether or not the trend ever turns, your labor is kept, held, treasured, not in vain, by a God who raises the dead and is coming to make all things new.

So what does all of this ask of a pastor's ordinary Tuesday? It asks for a recalibration of how we measure a faithful day, and I find I have to do this recalibration over and over because the old measures keep creeping back in. In Christendom we measured by results we could see, the growth, the buildings, the conversions we could count and report. In exile we measure by obedience we can offer. The questions change. Not, was the room full, but, did I preach the Word truly today, whether or not anyone was visibly moved. Not, is the church growing, but, did I love the few God actually put in front of me. Did I plant the seed. Did I attend to the dying woman in the nursing home who will never give a dollar or bring a friend. Did I tell the truth I was afraid to tell. Did I forgive the man who hurt me. Did I catechize my children. Regardless of whether I will live to see one thing come of any of it. The exile pastor plants trees in whose shade he will never sit, and he learns, slowly, against everything in him, to be at peace with that, because his peace was never supposed to rest on seeing the harvest. It was supposed to rest on the One who promised the harvest, and the promise doesn't expire when the pastor does.

I'm going to be honest in the way this book keeps forcing me to be, because I won't pretend to a peace I don't fully have. I am not at peace with it yet. Not all the way. I want to see the harvest. I want the win on my watch. I want to know, before I die, that the church I've given my life to will flourish in this country again, that my sons will worship in full rooms, that the decline I've watched for thirty years will reverse and I'll get to see it reverse. And there is a real and serious chance that I will die without that assurance, with the trend lines still pointing down, with the church I love smaller than when I started, and the flesh in me hates that, fights it, wants the validation of the visible result like a man wants water. The exile is killing that wanting in me slowly, which is exactly what it's for, and the dying of it is not comfortable, but I think it's holy, because what it's killing is an idol, the idol of the visible result, the idol that made me need to see the harvest in order to feel that my obedience counted. We were never promised the win on our watch. We were promised the King at the end of all watches, and he is enough, and I am still learning, at my age, after all these years, to let him be enough.

Let me put one more frame on this, because I find pastors need a working definition of success they can actually live with, something to replace the census they're letting go of. Here's mine, hard-won and still being tested. Success, for a pastor in exile, is faithfulness over a lifetime, measured not by the size of the harvest but by the consistency of the sowing. Did I keep turning up? Did I keep preaching the Word when the room was thin and nobody seemed moved? Did I keep loving the people God gave me, the difficult ones and the leaving ones, year after year? Did I keep my hands in the soil, planting seed I'd never see grow, for a lifetime, without quitting? That's success. Not a number. A direction held over decades, a faithfulness that didn't break under the long absence of visible result. The world calls that mediocre, because the world measures by the harvest, and a man who sows for forty years and reaps little looks like a failure on the world's books. But on the only books that matter, the man who sowed faithfully for forty years is a roaring success, because he did the one thing he was actually asked to do, which was to be faithful, and the harvest was never his job, it was God's.

And I take comfort, real comfort, from the prophets, because most of them were failures by every visible measure and faithful by the only one that counts. Isaiah was told, at his commissioning, that his preaching would harden hearts rather than soften them, that he'd preach until the cities lay waste and the land was utterly desolate, that his whole ministry would look like failure (Isaiah 6:9-12). Jeremiah preached for forty years and watched his nation ignore him and collapse exactly as he'd warned, and got thrown in a cistern for his trouble, and never saw a single revival come of all his faithfulness. Ezekiel preached to a people God told him in advance would not listen. By the census, every one of them failed. By the only measure that matters, they were the most faithful men of their generations, and we're still reading their words twenty-five hundred years later while the names of the popular court prophets who told the comfortable lies are forgotten. The exile pastor stands in that line, the line of men who sowed faithfully into hard ground and were judged failures in their time and vindicated by God in the end. It's not a comfortable line to stand in. It's the line the faithful have always stood in, and there's no shame in it, only the long company of the prophets and the patient vindication of God.

So we fight the long defeat in the longer hope. We grieve what's dying without despairing of it, and we labor for what's coming without demanding to see it arrive. We plant the gardens of Babylon and we entrust the harvest to the only One who was ever going to bring it in. The seventy years are long, and most of us will die well inside them, with the work unfinished and the trend unreversed. The King is coming anyway. That has always been enough for the church in its truest seasons, and we are only now, in our weakness, being forced to find out whether we actually believed it or were just saying it because the buildings were full.
chapters.verdict: We were never promised the win on our watch. We were promised the King at the end of all watches.
reflect: Are you measuring faithfulness by results you can see, or by obedience you can offer?
Where has the absence of visible victory tempted you toward either despair or denial?
What are you planting that you don't expect to harvest, and are you at peace with that?

chapters.title: When the Furnace Is Real
chapters.summary: Most of what the Western church calls suffering isn't, but real suffering is coming, the loss of jobs and standing and relationships for taking the hard positions, and the exile asks us to learn the difference between the persecution complex and the actual cost, and to be ready to pay the actual cost without flinching and without self-pity.
chapters.body:
I need to handle this carefully, because I spent a whole chapter telling you that what we're experiencing isn't persecution, and now I want to tell you that real suffering for the faith is coming and you'd better be ready for it, and those two things have to be held together without contradiction. So let me draw the line clearly. What we have suffered so far, in the American church, is mostly the loss of comfort and status, and that is not persecution. But the loss of comfort and status is the doorway, and on the other side of the doorway is something that will, in places, become a genuine cost, and a church that confused the doorway for the room will be unprepared for the room.

Here's what I mean. The thinning of our cultural privilege has so far cost us things that sting but don't bleed. Respect. Deference. The assumption of agreement. The easy social standing of the churchgoer. The pastor's automatic credibility. Losing those things hurts, in the way that losing any privilege hurts, but let's be honest about the scale of it. The early church was fed to animals in arenas while crowds cheered. Bonhoeffer was hanged. The brother I correspond with overseas has been arrested twice and may be again. Set our losses next to that, and our losses look like what they are, the wounded pride of a formerly dominant group adjusting to no longer being dominant. We have wept over insults and trembled at the thought of inconvenience, and we have not yet been asked, most of us, to suffer anything that would have made the early church even look up from their work.

I want to say that bluntly because the persecution complex is doing real damage and it needs to be named as the spiritual problem it is. When a church marinates in the language of persecution while suffering almost nothing, it produces people who are simultaneously fragile and aggressive, who feel attacked at the smallest slight and respond with disproportionate fury, who interpret every cultural disagreement as an assault on the faith and every loss of advantage as martyrdom. That kind of church is exhausting to the watching world and embarrassing to the gospel, because the watching world can see plainly that these people are not being persecuted, they're being thwarted, and the constant cry of persecution from people who are manifestly comfortable reads as exactly the self-pity it is. The persecution complex also makes a church spiritually soft in the precise place it needs to be hard, because a people who treat inconvenience as martyrdom have spent their courage on nothing and will have none left when a real test comes. You cannot cry wolf about insults for thirty years and then expect anyone, including yourself, to take you seriously when the wolf actually shows up.

But the wolf is going to show up, in measure, in places, and that's the other half I have to say. The exile is not going to stay at the level of lost status. As the culture's frame closes further, there will be, in some sectors and some regions and some professions, genuine costs for holding the historic Christian faith with any public clarity. Not lions, almost certainly, not here, not soon. But real costs. The job you don't get or the job you lose. The professional license threatened, the business pressured, the contract pulled, because you would not affirm what your conscience cannot affirm. The relationships that fracture, the family member who stops speaking to you, the friend who decides your beliefs make you a bad person and walks away. The reputation that takes a real and permanent hit, the social death of being known as one of those Christians. These are not nothing. These are not lions, but they are not nothing, and for the person living through them they can be brutal, isolating, frightening, the loss of a livelihood and a community and a name. A church that cried persecution over insults will be no help to the man actually losing his job over his convictions, because it spent all its language and all its credibility on the small thing and has nothing left for the real one.

So the work of the exilic church is to learn the difference, and to prepare its people for the real cost without inflating the fake one. This is delicate pastoral work and I'm still learning to do it. On the one hand, you have to keep your people from the persecution complex, keep teaching them that lost privilege is not martyrdom, keep them from the fragility and the aggression and the self-pity, keep them able to lose status gracefully, even cheerfully, the way Jesus told us to rejoice when we're reviled (Matthew 5:11-12), with actual joy and not a clenched jaw. And on the other hand, you have to prepare them for the day when the cost stops being mere status and becomes a job, a relationship, a name, so that when that day comes they're not blindsided, they've counted it, they've already decided, like the three friends, that they'll pay it if they have to, because the matter was settled before the furnace got hot.

I want to handle a hard version of the objection, because it presses on something real. Someone says, all this talk about being ready to suffer, about not crying persecution, sounds like it could become a way of telling Christians to just take it, to never resist injustice, to be doormats, and isn't there a place for the church to fight, to push back, to defend the vulnerable, to refuse to go quietly when something genuinely evil is being done? And yes, there is, and I don't want my critique of the persecution complex to become a counsel of passivity, because those are different things. There's a difference between suffering for the faith and refusing to resist evil being done to others. Daniel resisted, in his way, by not bowing. The apostles resisted, by saying we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29) and continuing to preach when ordered to stop. The church has, at its best, resisted real evil, has hidden Jews from the Nazis, has run the underground railroad, has stood against tyrants. Resisting evil, especially evil done to the weak, is not the same as crying persecution over your own lost comfort, and a church can be ready to suffer for the faith and also willing to stand against injustice, and the two are not in tension.

The distinction I'm drawing is about what we're willing to suffer for and how we suffer it. The persecution complex suffers for its own status and suffers it with self-pity and rage. Faithful suffering suffers for Christ and for the vulnerable and suffers it with the strange joy of the persecuted church, blessing rather than cursing, returning good for evil, refusing to become like the thing it opposes. When the church resists evil, it has to resist it as the church, in the manner of the cross, without becoming cruel, without dehumanizing the opponent, without adopting the very tactics of coercion and contempt that it's standing against. The danger in the conquest posture from earlier is exactly that it resists evil by becoming evil's mirror image, fighting fire with fire until you can't tell the firefighters from the arsonists. Faithful resistance looks like the martyrs and the underground railroad and Bonhoeffer, people who stood against real evil at real cost while remaining recognizably people of the cross. It does not look like a comfortable church screaming persecution while it tries to grab back the power it lost. Resist evil, yes, especially evil to the weak. Suffer for Christ, yes, gladly, when the cost comes. But do both as the church, in the manner of the Lamb, and never confuse defending your own privilege with either one.

How do you prepare people to suffer well? Not, mainly, by talking about suffering, though you do have to talk about it honestly, refusing the false gospel that promises following Jesus will make your life easier, because it won't, he said it wouldn't, he said in the world you will have tribulation (John 16:33) and take up your cross (Luke 9:23) and a servant is not greater than his master, if they persecuted me they will persecute you (John 15:20). A church fed a steady diet of your-best-life-now is a church being actively disarmed for the exile, taught to expect comfort right up until the comfort is removed and then to conclude that God has failed them, when God promised them the opposite of comfort all along and we just preached around it. So first, tell them the truth. The Christian life includes suffering, not as an accident but as a feature, because we follow a crucified Lord and the servant is not above the master.

But the deeper preparation isn't information, it's formation, which brings us back to everything this book has been saying. People suffer well when they've been formed into a faith deep enough and a hope strong enough that the thing being threatened isn't their ultimate thing. The three friends could face the furnace because the worst Babylon could do, kill them, didn't touch what they most loved, which was God himself, and you cannot threaten a man with the loss of his life if his life is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3) and the loss of his earthly life is gain (Philippians 1:21). The martyrs across the centuries didn't suffer well because they were braver than us by temperament. They suffered well because they'd been formed to value something more than the thing being taken from them, and you can't manufacture that valuing in the moment of the test. It has to be built in advance, the same way the line gets drawn in advance, through the slow formation of a people whose treasure is genuinely in heaven, so that when the earthly treasures are threatened, the threat, while real and painful, is not ultimate, because the ultimate thing is out of the empire's reach.

Let me make it concrete with the kind of moment that's already happening. A woman in a church I know lost a professional opportunity she'd worked years for because she wouldn't say something her conscience wouldn't let her say. Not dramatic. No headlines. She just quietly didn't get the thing, and everyone understood why, and it cost her real money and real standing and a door that won't reopen. And here's what I watched. She didn't cry persecution. She didn't make herself a martyr or go looking for a microphone. She grieved it honestly, because it was a real loss and she's not made of stone, and then she went back to work somewhere else and kept loving the very people whose disapproval had cost her, and she told me, almost embarrassed, that she'd half expected to feel abandoned by God and instead felt strangely close to him, closer than the easy years. That's the furnace done right. Real cost, paid without self-pity, that turned out to be a place of God's nearness rather than his absence. That's what we're trying to form people into. Not the loud complainers who suffer nothing and cry constantly, and not the naive who think faith exempts them from cost, but people who can pay a real price quietly and find God in the fire.

I want to say something about the global picture, because the American church's persecution complex looks especially ridiculous and especially sad when you set it next to what's actually happening to the church in other places, and the contrast is instructive in both directions. Right now, while we're aggrieved about insults, there are believers being imprisoned, tortured, and killed for the name of Jesus in numbers that are hard to take in, in regions where conversion can cost you your family, your freedom, or your life. I correspond with some of these brothers through the Network, and the thing that undoes me every time is not their suffering, terrible as it is, but their joy. They are not bitter. They are not consumed with self-pity. They count it an honor to suffer for the name, the way the apostles did, leaving the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name (Acts 5:41). And they are puzzled by us, gently, charitably puzzled, that a church as free and wealthy and safe as ours could be as anxious and joyless and aggrieved as we are. One of them wrote to me, and I've never forgotten it, that he prays for the American church not because we're persecuted but because we're comfortable, and comfort, he said, has killed more Christians than persecution ever has. He was not being clever. He meant it. He's watched comfort do to the Western church what the prison could not do to his.

That cuts two ways, and I want to hold both. On one side, it's a rebuke to our self-pity, a reminder that we don't know the first thing about real suffering for the faith and should be ashamed of how loudly we complain about so little. On the other side, it's a promise about what the furnace, when it does come, will actually be, because the persecuted church's joy is not in spite of the suffering, it's somehow through it, in the nearness of Christ that the suffering opens up. The persecuted church is not a warning that following Jesus leads to misery. It's a witness that following Jesus all the way into the fire leads to a joy the comfortable church has never tasted, a joy that has been purified of everything the world can take, because everything the world can take has already been taken and the joy is still there, which proves it was never resting on the things the world can take. That's the strange testimony. The places where it costs the most to follow Jesus are not the places with the least joy. They are often the places with the most, and the comfortable Western church, busy protecting its comfort, has cut itself off from the very fire where that joy gets forged.

Because that's the promise hidden in the furnace, and it's the only thing that makes any of this bearable. When the three friends went into the fire, the king looked in and saw not three men but four, and the fourth was like a son of the gods (Daniel 3:25), and the only thing the fire burned was the ropes that bound them. The furnace is where the fourth figure shows up. The presence of God is promised most explicitly not to the comfortable but to the suffering, I will be with you, when you walk through fire you shall not be burned (Isaiah 43:2), and the testimony of the persecuted church across two thousand years is monotonously consistent on this point. The ones who suffer most for Jesus report knowing him best. The fire is terrible and the fourth man is real, and you do not get the fourth man in the comfortable room. You only get him in the fire.

I'll close this chapter by telling on myself one final way, because I have not been tested the way some of my brothers have, and I don't know how I'd do, and that uncertainty is itself important to confess. It's easy to write bravely about the furnace from a comfortable study in a free country where the worst I've faced is criticism. I don't know if I'd stand. I'd like to think I would, but Peter thought he would too, and Peter denied him three times before the rooster crowed (Matthew 26:34-35, 74-75). So I don't write this as a man who's passed the test. I write it as a man trying to be ready, trying to draw the line in advance, trying to value the right things so deeply that if the day comes I won't bow, and trying not to fool myself with brave words while my treasure is still quietly buried in the comforts I'd hate to lose. The honest prayer of the exilic pastor is not Lord, I am ready. It's Lord, make me ready, because I'm not sure I am, and keep me from crying persecution over nothing so that I'll have some courage left for something.

There's a strange mercy in the order of all this, and I want to name it before I close the chapter. The mild costs come first. Before the real furnace, there's the loss of status, the inconvenience, the awkwardness, the social discomfort, and I think those mild costs are a kind of training, a chance to practice paying a price before the price gets steep. A church that learns to lose its privilege gracefully, that learns to be the minority without self-pity, that learns to accept the small costs of being out of step with the culture without crying persecution, is a church being prepared, in the gym of the small costs, for the day the costs get larger. And a church that can't even lose its privilege without rage and self-pity is a church that will certainly collapse when the real cost comes, because it never learned to pay the small price and so has no muscle for the large one. So the mild costs we're experiencing now are not just the appetizer of suffering. They're the training for it, the chance to build the muscle of faithful loss while the stakes are still low, so that the muscle's there when the stakes go high. Use the small costs that way. Let them train you. Practice losing your status without bitterness now, so that you'll be able to lose more than status without bitterness later.

And keep the eyes on the fourth man, because that's what makes the whole thing possible. The reason the persecuted church across the world and across the centuries can suffer with joy is not that they're tougher than us. It's that they've seen the fourth man, met him in the fire, found that the thing they were most afraid of turned out to be the place he was most present. We're afraid of the furnace because we've never been in it, and from the outside it looks like nothing but pain, like abandonment, like the place God isn't. But the testimony of everyone who's been in it is the opposite. The furnace is where he is. The fire burns the ropes and leaves the man, and the man walks in the fire with one who is like a son of the gods. We don't have to manufacture courage for a furnace we haven't faced. We have to keep our eyes on the One who promised to be in it with us, so that if the day comes, we walk in not trusting our own nerve, which would fail, but trusting his presence, which won't, because he has never once let a faithful sufferer go into the fire alone, and he is not going to start with you.

We have wept over insults and trembled at the thought of inconvenience, and we have not yet been asked to suffer anything that would have made the early church look up. May God forgive us our self-pity, and may he prepare us, before the furnace, for the cost that's actually coming, and may we find, when we walk in, that the fourth man was there the whole time, waiting in the fire we were so afraid of.
chapters.verdict: We have wept over insults and trembled at the thought of inconvenience, and we have not yet been asked to suffer anything that would have made the early church look up.
reflect: What has following Jesus actually cost you, and is it more than embarrassment?
Are you preparing your people to suffer well, or only to complain loudly?
What would you lose if you held the line where the line actually needs holding, and have you counted that cost yet?

chapters.title: The Network in the Wilderness
chapters.summary: Isolated pastors do not survive exile; the conditions crushing the solitary leader can only be borne in a connected body of leaders who hold each other up. The exile makes the network of pastors not a strategy but a survival.
chapters.body:
There's a temptation, when you read a book like this, to receive it as a personal challenge, to go back to your own church and your own pulpit and try to be a faithful exile all by yourself, to read it as a call to gird up and try harder. I want to name that instinct and call it what it is, because it's the instinct that will kill you, and I've watched it kill men I loved. The lone pastor is not heroic in exile. He is the first casualty. The conditions this whole book describes, the lost borrowed power, the long defeat, the hostile plausibility structures, the hidden interior life under constant assault, the daily grind of preaching to a culture that doesn't have to listen, these are not conditions a solitary human being can bear for seventy years. They will grind a man to powder, and the wreckage of burned-out, disillusioned, fallen, and simply vanished pastors that litters the late-Christendom church is the evidence, a generation of good men who tried to carry alone a weight that was never meant to be carried alone.

Let me describe how it actually ends for the men who fall, because the abstraction of burnout hides how concrete and how preventable it usually is. It rarely ends in a single dramatic blowup. It ends in a slow erosion that nobody catches because nobody's close enough to catch it. The prayer life goes first, quietly, no one notices. Then the joy goes, and the man starts going through the motions, and from the outside he still looks fine because he's competent and competence hides a lot. Then the resentment builds, toward the people, toward the board, toward the spouse, toward God, and he tells no one because there's no one safe to tell. Then comes the secret comfort, whatever it is, the drinking or the screen or the wrong relationship or the just-checked-out numbness, the thing he reaches for because the well is dry and he has to get water somewhere. And then one day it surfaces, the affair or the breakdown or the resignation letter or the worse thing, and everyone is shocked, and the shock is the tell, because the shock means nobody was close enough to see it coming, and nobody was close enough because the man was isolated, performing sufficiency, holding everyone and held by no one, exactly as Christendom trained him to be. The fall looks sudden. It was never sudden. It was a slow erosion in the dark that a few close friends would have caught a year earlier if there had been a few close friends. That's the whole case for the network in one sad paragraph.

I founded the Pastors Connection Network because I watched this happen, and because I felt it happening to me, and I want to be honest about both halves of that. The men I serve are not weak men. They're faithful, capable, often gifted, frequently more gifted than I am, and they are dying alone in their studies under a weight that Christendom never prepared them for and never told them was coming. They were trained to lead with an authority the culture has since withdrawn, and nobody updated the training. They measure themselves by results that aren't coming and were taught no other way to measure. They preach into rooms that thin out a little more every year, and they do it, most of them, in near-total isolation, because the Christendom model made the pastor a solo professional, the religious chief executive of a standalone franchise, quietly competing with the church down the road for the same shrinking pool of families, too proud or too busy or too frightened to admit to anyone, least of all a fellow pastor who might be a rival, how hard it has all become. That isolation was survivable when the culture carried the pastor, when the externals held him up. It is not survivable now that the externals are gone, and the men who try to survive it alone are falling at a rate that should alarm us far more than the attendance numbers do.

The exile itself testifies against the solitary model, if we'd read it carefully. Notice that the people of God in Babylon were never sent into exile as individuals. They were sent as a people, deported in groups, settled together by the rivers and the canals of Babylon, and their survival depended absolutely on staying a people, gathering, remembering together, holding the faith corporately when no single family could have held it alone in a sea of Babylonian religion. The synagogue, that great exilic invention, was not a building for solitary devotion. It was a gathering. A community of mutual holding around the Word, where the faith got carried by the body when any individual would have dropped it. And Daniel, the man we keep coming back to, did not stand before the king alone. He had three friends. And the three friends stood before the furnace together, and the resolve of each one was strengthened by the resolve of the other two (Daniel 1:6, 3:16-18). When the great test came, no one of them faced it in isolation. They faced it as a body, and the body held when a solitary man, even a strong one, might have bent under the music and the heat and the crowd all bowing around him. It is much harder to be the only one standing. It is much easer to stand when you look to your left and your right and your friends are standing too.

Scripture knows this in its bones, and says it plainly enough that I don't know how we missed it. Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10). Woe to him who is alone when he falls. That's not a sentimental verse about the niceness of friendship to cross-stitch on a pillow. It's a sober, almost clinical warning about the lethal vulnerability of isolation, and it reads like a case study of the modern pastorate, men falling with no one positioned to catch them, falling in slow motion over months while everyone assumes someone else is checking on them and no one is. The whole architecture of the New Testament church is the architecture of mutual burden-bearing. Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ (Galatians 6:2). The members of the body cannot say to one another, I have no need of you (1 Corinthians 12:21). And yet the Christendom pastor was trained to need no one, to project a competence and a self-sufficiency that was always partly a lie and is now a fatal one, because the man performing sufficiency cannot be helped, since to be helped he'd have to admit he needs help, and the performance forbids the admission.

So the network is not a strategy I'm promoting from a stage. It's a survival I'm insisting on, the way a doctor insists on a treatment, because I've signed too many of the figurative death certificates. In exile, the connection of pastors to one another, real connection, not the conference-handshake-and-business-card kind, becomes a load-bearing wall, and when it's missing the structure comes down. The network is the place where a man can finally tell the truth about how hard it is without it ending up in somebody's sermon illustration the next week, without it becoming gossip, without it threatening his job. It's the place where the resolve of one strengthens the resolve of another, where the line one man has drawn helps the next man find the courage to draw his, where the long defeat gets fought shoulder to shoulder instead of in a thousand separate isolated trenches where each man thinks he's the only one losing. It's where the false prophets of triumphalism and the demons of despair both get answered, because a body can hold a truth that an individual simply cannot carry alone at three in the morning. The pastor who is held by other pastors can stand in the furnace, because he is not standing in it by himself, and the difference between held and alone is, very often, the difference between the man who lasts and the man who doesn't.

I want to say something to the wives, and to the men about their wives, because there's a particular failure I've watched destroy pastors and their marriages, and it grows directly out of the isolation. A lonely pastor, with no other men to carry his burdens, will often make his wife his only confidant, his sole support, the one person who knows the truth about how hard it is. And that sounds healthy, sounds like intimacy, but it isn't, not when it's the only support he has, because it puts a weight on her that no spouse was built to carry alone. She becomes his pastor, his counselor, his entire support system, the only one holding up a man who's holding up a church, and it crushes her, slowly, and it distorts the marriage, because she stops being able to be his wife, the one he delights in, and becomes his crisis-management team, perpetually absorbing the overflow of a ministry that's drowning him. A man needs his wife. He does not need his wife to be the only other person who knows he's struggling, because that's not a marriage, that's a hostage situation, and it's one of the reasons pastors' marriages buckle under the exile. The network, the three friends, the other men who can carry the load, they don't replace the wife, they protect her, by giving the man somewhere else to take the weight so that he can come home and be a husband instead of a patient.

And there's a danger that runs the other way too, which is the pastor who has no real friends and so makes the congregation his friends, blurring the line between shepherd and sheep in a way that always ends badly. A pastor needs friends who are not his church members, who don't depend on him spiritually, who aren't in the relationship of being led by him, because he cannot fully unburden himself to the people he's responsible to lead, and if he tries, he either has to lead from a false strength that's killing him or he overshares with people who needed him to be steady and now can't trust his steadiness. The lonely pastor with no peers will reach for intimacy where he shouldn't, with his wife as his only support or with congregants as substitute friends or, God help us, in the affairs and addictions that are the predictable fruit of a man starving for connection and finding it nowhere safe. The network of peers, of other pastors who aren't his members and aren't his wife, is the thing that lets the marriage be a marriage and the church be a church, by giving the man the peer relationships that every human being needs and that his role denies him everywhere else. This is not a luxury. It's the thing that keeps the other relationships from being crushed under weight they were never meant to bear.

And there's a strategic dimension I'll name plainly because it's true and it matters. A network of connected, faithful pastors is the single most potent thing the post-Christendom church has, and not because it generates programs or campaigns or movements, but for the unglamorous reason that it ends isolation, and ending isolation keeps faithful men in the field who would otherwise have fallen out of it. Do the math on that. Every pastor who is held instead of broken is a garden that keeps getting planted, year after year, a witness that keeps standing in some small town that would otherwise have gone dark when its pastor quit or fell or simply disappeared into despair. The connection multiplies the faithfulness across the wilderness, not by amplifying any one voice into a platform, but by keeping a thousand small fires from going out. The synagogue kept Israel alive in Babylon by keeping it together, by refusing to let the exiles scatter into isolated households that would have been assimilated within a generation. The network keeps the exilic pastorate alive by exactly the same means, by refusing to let the shepherds scatter into isolated studies where they die one at a time, unnoticed, each one assuming his struggle is unique and his failure is his alone.

I should say plainly what kind of connection I mean, because the church is drowning in fake connection and starving for the real kind, and they're easy to confuse. The conferences are not it, mostly, though they have their place. You can attend conferences for thirty years, shake a thousand hands, collect a thousand cards, follow a hundred pastors online, be connected in the technical sense to more ministers than any generation before you, and be utterly, lethally alone, because none of those connections is a place where you can tell the truth. Real connection is not breadth, it's depth, and depth requires a few specific things that the conference circuit and the online network actively prevent. It requires people who know you over time, who've seen you across seasons, who know your wife's name and your kids' struggles and the church fight you went through two years ago. It requires safety, the absolute confidence that what you say will not travel, will not become gossip, will not be used against you, will not end up as a cautionary tale told from somebody else's stage. And it requires mutuality, the willingness to be known and not just to know, to confess and not just to counsel, because a man who only ever helps others and never lets himself be helped is not actually in relationship, he's running a charity with himself as the sole benefactor, and that's its own kind of isolation, the loneliness of the helper who can't be helped.

What I've found is that this kind of connection almost never happens by accident and almost never happens at scale. It happens small, with a handful, deliberately, over years. Daniel had three. Not three hundred, not a movement, three. Jesus had twelve, and inside the twelve a three, Peter and James and John, the ones he took up the mountain and into the garden, the inner ring. Even the Lord did not try to be deeply known by everyone. He had his three. And I think part of what's killing pastors is that we've been sold the idea that connection means a large network, a platform, a following, when the connection that actually saves a man's soul and ministry is small and slow and specific, a few men who know everything and stay anyway. If you take one practical thing from this whole book, let it be this. Find your three. Not your audience, not your network, not your followers. Three men who will know the worst of you and not flinch and not leave and not tell. If you don't have them, you are in more danger than you know, however strong you feel right now, because the furnace is coming and no one walks into it alone and walks out.

This costs something, and the cost is pride, which is precisely why most pastors won't pay it until they're nearly destroyed, until the marriage is in crisis or the depression is clinical or the secret sin has metastasized or they're standing in the kitchen at midnight wondering whether anyone would notice if they just stopped. To be genuinely connected to other pastors, you have to let them see you without the borrowed power, without the platform, without the curated competence you show the congregation. You have to let another man see the fear, the doubt, the marriage under strain, the church that's shrinking on your watch, the sermon you preached last Sunday that you didn't believe while you were preaching it, the website you can't stop visiting, the bottle in the drawer, the resentment toward the people you're supposed to love. Christendom trained us to perform sufficiency, and the performance is the very thing that's killing us, because a man performing sufficiency cannot be held, and a man who cannot be held cannot survive the exile. The humility to be known, actually known, by at least a few other men who will not flinch and will not gossip and will not leave, is not optional in Babylon. It's the literal price of staying alive in it.

I've paid that price unevenly, and I'll confess the irony, because it's instructive. I built a network for other men partly because I could not, for years, admit how much I needed one myself. It's a great deal easier to be the one who connects others than the one who confesses he's drowning, easier to organize the help than to ask for it, easier to be the strong one in everyone else's story than to need to be carried in your own. I founded a thing to rescue isolated pastors while remaining, in the ways that mattered most, an isolated pastor, holding everyone and held by no one, which is its own slow death just dressed up in usefulness. The exile has been teaching me, slowly and very much against my pride, that the man who founded the network needs the network as much as anyone in it, maybe more, because the helpers are often the loneliest people in the room. There came a point, and I won't detail it, where I had to stop being only the one who held and let myself be held, had to call a brother and say the true thing instead of the strong thing, and it was one of the hardest phone calls of my life and one of the few that actually saved me. We do this together or we do not do it at all. There is no faithful solitary in Babylon. There never was. The hero who carries it alone is not a hero. He's a casualty who hasn't fallen yet.

I want to address the obstacle that keeps most pastors from this, because it's not that they don't believe they need it, it's that they don't believe it's safe, and they're not entirely wrong. The reason pastors don't open up to other pastors is that we've been burned, or we've seen someone burned, by the confidence that became gossip, the vulnerability that became ammunition, the struggle shared in trust that showed up later in a denominational meeting or a sermon illustration or a conversation that got back to the elders. The world of ministry can be brutally competitive and shockingly unsafe, full of men who will use your weakness against you if it advances their position, and a pastor who's been betrayed once will not open up again, and so he seals himself off and dies slowly in the name of self-protection. So when I say find your three, I'm not naive about the risk. I'm saying you have to find the right three, the safe three, and that takes discernment and time and usually some trial and error, and it's worth every bit of the effort because the alternative is dying alone.

How do you find the safe ones? You test small before you trust big. You share something modestly vulnerable and watch what happens to it, whether it stays where you put it or whether it travels. You look for men who are themselves vulnerable, who open up to you in return, because the man who only ever receives your confessions and never offers his own is not a peer, he's a confessor with the upper hand, and that's not safe. You look for men outside your immediate competitive sphere, often, men who aren't up for the same positions or pastoring the church across the street, because the competition poisons the safety. And you go slow, building trust over years, the way trust is actually built, in small deposits that prove out over time. It's a lot of work to find your three, and the work is part of why most pastors never do it, because we're busy and tired and the search itself requires the vulnerability we're afraid of. But it's the most important relational work an exilic pastor will do, more important than any networking, because it's the difference between surviving and not, and there's no shortcut to it and no substitute for it, and the men who skip it because it's hard are the men who fall.

The lone pastor is not heroic in exile. He is the first casualty. Find your three friends before the furnace, not after, because the music is already playing and the heat is already rising, and no one, not you, not me, not the strongest and most gifted man you know, stands in that fire alone and comes out alive. Daniel had his three. Find yours. And if, like me, you're the one everyone else leans on, the helper, the founder, the strong one, hear this especially. You need them too. Stop holding everyone and let yourself be held. Make the phone call. It might be the thing that keeps your fire from going out.
chapters.verdict: The lone pastor is not heroic in exile. He is the first casualty.
reflect: Who actually holds you up when the borrowed power is gone and the results aren't coming?
Have you built genuine connection with other pastors, or only a network of contacts?
What would it cost your pride to admit you cannot survive this exile alone?

chapters.title: The Song in the Strange Land
chapters.summary: The book ends not with a strategy but with a charge, to sing the Lord's song in Babylon, to be faithful in a season we did not choose and will not see completed, trusting the exile to the God who has always met his people there.
chapters.body:
By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, when we remembered Zion (Psalm 137:1). The exiles hung their harps on the willows, because their captors demanded a song, sing us one of the songs of Zion, and the demand felt obscene, like being asked to perform happiness at your own funeral. How shall we sing the LORD's song in a foreign land? (Psalm 137:4). That question is the question of this whole book, and I've lived with it long enough now to know that it admits of more than one answer, and that the answer the psalm itself gives, the bitter one, is not the only faithful one, though it's where we have to start.

Psalm 137 is grief, and grief that curses, and we should not rush past it, because a church that cannot grieve its losses will never be honest enough to sing anything true. The psalm gives us permission to weep over what's gone, to feel the obscenity of being asked to perform contentment in the place of our defeat, even to rage at the empire that brought us low, and the end of that psalm gets so dark, asking for the heads of Babylon's infants against the rocks, that we squirm to read it in church. But God put it in the Bible, the rage and all, because he would rather have our honest fury than our dishonest serenity, and a people who can bring God their rage are closer to him than a people who've buried it under a smile. The church in the West needs to sit by the rivers and weep before it does anything else, and I said as much chapters ago and I'll say it again at the end, because we have a chronic habit of skipping the grief and rushing to the strategy, building on a wound we never cleaned. Grieve first. The harps come down off the willows only after the weeping has been allowed to do its slow work.

But the exiles did learn to sing. Not the old songs of Zion as though nothing had changed, that would have been the denial we've warned against, the pretending the loss wasn't real. And not a permanent defeated silence either, the harp left hanging on the willow forever, which would have been the despair. They learned a new song, the songs that came up out of Babylon itself, the deepening theology, the synagogue gatherings around the open Word, the hope sharpened to a fine point in the dark. They learned to sing the LORD's song in the strange land by discovering the one thing that changes everything, which is that the LORD was in the strange land, that he had not stayed behind in the smoking rubble of the temple, that he had gone with them into Babylon and was waiting for them there. The question how shall we sing turned out to contain a hidden gift, because the answer was, you can, the song is still in you, the God of the song has not abandoned the singers, he came to Babylon ahead of you and he is here.

Ezekiel saw it, and the timing of his visions is no accident. Ezekiel watched, in a vision, the glory of the LORD rise up and leave the temple in Jerusalem (Ezekiel 10), the most devastating thing a Jew could imagine, God moving out of his house, the lights going off in the holiest place on earth. And then, where does Ezekiel receive his great visions of that glory? By the rivers of Babylon. In the land of the captors.
