The heavens opened and he saw visions of God there (Ezekiel 1:1), in the unclean foreign place where God supposedly couldn't be, and the glory that left the temple in Jerusalem appeared to the prophet in Babylon. God was in Babylon before the exiles arrived. He was waiting for them in the place they were sure was godforsaken. He always is. That's the pattern of the whole Bible, God turning up in the place we'd written off, the manger instead of the palace, the cross instead of the throne, the tomb that turned out to be empty. He specializes in being found exactly where we were certain he couldn't be, which means the very godforsakenness of our moment, the emptied churches and the closed frame and the long defeat, is not evidence of his absence. It may be the address where he's waiting.

This is the resolution that doesn't resolve, the ending that leaves weight, and I won't pretend it ties off neatly, because the exile does not tie off neatly and I'd be lying if I gave you a bow. I cannot tell you that the Western church will recover, because I do not know, and the men who tell you they know are the same Hananiahs who promised return in two years. I cannot give you a strategy that ends the exile, because the exile is not a problem to be solved. It's a condition to be inhabited faithfully, for seventy years, by people most of whom will die inside it with the work unfinished. What I can tell you is the thing this whole book has been pressing toward from the first page, which is that the exile was always going to be the truest home the church ever had. We did not choose it. It was given. And it is the condition in which the people of God have always done their deepest and most faithful work, in Babylon, in the catacombs, in the upper room, in the underground churches that are growing right now in the very places where it costs the most, in every dark season when the empire did not love them and the favor of the culture was gone and they had nothing left but the Word and the body and the broken bread and the promise. The church has never been healthier than when it was an exile, and never sicker than when it was an establishment, and if that's true, then what's happening to us is not the disease. It might be the cure.

I think about the people who actually built the synagogue, the unnamed exiles who, with the temple gone and no obvious way to keep the faith alive, simply started gathering on the Sabbath to read the scrolls and remember and pray. There's no command in the Torah to build a synagogue. There's no blueprint. The synagogue is what the exiles improvised when their world fell apart, an act of stubborn, creative faithfulness by people who refused to let the faith die just because the institutions of the faith had been destroyed. And that improvisation, that desperate Sabbath gathering of displaced people around a scroll, became the form that carried the people of God for two and a half millennia and shaped the Christian church itself. Nobody planned it. Nobody had a strategy. It grew up out of necessity, out of love, out of the refusal of ordinary believers to stop being the people of God just because the temple was gone. And I find enormous hope in that, because it means the next form of the faithful church, the form that will carry the gospel through the post-Christendom centuries, is probably not going to be designed by experts at conferences. It's going to be improvised by ordinary faithful believers who refuse to let the faith die, who gather and read and pray and love and bless their cities, and who, without quite meaning to, invent the thing that lasts. The synagogue was not a program. It was a people refusing to quit, and God honored the refusal by building twenty-five centuries on it. He may be doing the same thing right now, in small rooms we'd never think to study, among people we'd never put on a stage.

So I don't actually know what the church on the far side of this exile will look like, and I've made my peace with not knowing, mostly. It may be smaller. It will almost certainly be poorer, less respected, less powerful, less comfortable. It may meet in homes more than in buildings, the way the church began and the way it survives now in the hard places. It may look, to us, like a defeat, the way the synagogue must have looked like a poor substitute to anyone who remembered the temple. But it may also be, like the synagogue, the most durable and portable and faithful form the people of God have had in centuries, stripped down to the things that actually carry the faith, the Word and the table and the gathered people and the presence of God, freed at last from the props that were never the faith and that we mistook for it. I won't see the finished form. I'm planting in a season I won't see completed. But the synagogue tells me that what gets improvised in exile by faithful people refusing to quit can outlast every temple the empire ever built.

Peter called them elect exiles, and we are back where we started in the first chapter, with both words at once and no contradiction (1 Peter 1:1). Elect, chosen, beloved, held by a God who goes with us into Babylon and meets us there ahead of our arrival. Exiles, displaced, foreign, without standing in the empire, which is exactly the condition in which the people of God finally learn to lean on God instead of on their cultural arrangements. Peter wrote that letter to scattered exiles across an empire that would soon enough be lighting them on fire to illuminate its gardens, and he did not tell them to recover their power, did not give them a five-point plan to re-establish Christian influence in the Roman provinces. He told them to be holy, to love one another earnestly from a pure heart, to keep their conduct honorable among the Gentiles so that the watching pagans, who slandered them, might see their good deeds and glorify God on the day he visits (1 Peter 2:11-12). He told them to suffer well, to bless when they were reviled, to always be ready to give a reason for the hope that was in them, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). He told them, in other words, the exact thing this whole book has been trying to say in a hundred thousand more words than Peter needed. Be the church that cannot be explained without God, in the place that does not want you, for as long as it takes, and entrust your souls to a faithful Creator while doing good (1 Peter 4:19), and trust the One who suffered before you and was raised on the third day and is coming back for you.

There's a question that's been running under this whole book, and I want to bring it to the surface before the end, because it's the question that decides everything. The question is whether we actually believe that Jesus is enough. Not whether we'd say so, because of course we'd say so, but whether we believe it down where it counts, in the place that decides what we reach for when we're afraid. Because Christendom let us have Jesus and the census, Jesus and the power, Jesus and the cultural home, and we never had to find out whether Jesus alone was enough, because we never had Jesus alone. We always had Jesus plus. And the exile is taking away the plus. It's taking away the census and the power and the cultural home, one piece at a time, until what's left is Jesus alone, and the terror of the exile, the thing under all the other fears, is the fear that Jesus alone might not be enough, that we might be left with him and find that he doesn't fill the hole the establishment leaves.

And here's the testimony I can offer, after all these years, for whatever it's worth. He is enough. I don't say it triumphantly, because I'm still finding it out, still being pried off the plus, still reaching for the census in my weaker moments. But in the moments when the plus has been genuinely stripped away, when I've stood in the emptied room or sat in the dry season or faced the trend that won't turn, and there's been nothing left but Jesus, I've found, to my surprise, that he's there, and that he's enough, that the thing I was afraid would be a void turns out to be a Presence, that the bottom I was terrified of falling through turns out to be him. The exile is a long, hard, unwanted experiment in whether Jesus alone is enough, and the church has run this experiment before, in Babylon and the catacombs and the underground, and the result has always come back the same. He is enough. He was always enough. The plus was never necessary, and a good deal of the time it was actually in the way, a distraction from the only thing that was ever going to satisfy. We're being given, at great cost, the chance to find out for ourselves what the persecuted church has always known. Jesus is enough. He really is. We just couldn't believe it while we had Jesus plus everything else.

I've been a pastor for the whole span of this collapse, and I have to confess, as the book ends, that I spent too much of it grieving the country I lost instead of loving the city I was sent to. I wanted the old map back. I wanted the borrowed power and the full census and the easy deference, and I called my wanting faithfulness when it was nostalgia for an exile I had not yet accepted, a homesickness for a home that was never really home. The acceptance has come slowly and against my will, the way most true things come to me, late and reluctant and through some pain, and I won't tell you it's made the exile easier, because it hasn't. It's only made it possible to be honest about where I actually am, which is by the rivers of Babylon, with the harp in my hand, deciding, the way every one of us has to decide, whether to hang it on the willow and weep forever or to take it down and sing.

There's a line in this psalm I skip over because the more famous ones crowd it out, and it's the vow in the middle, the one the exiles make to themselves while they're refusing to perform on demand. If I forget you, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill. Let my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth, if I do not remember you, if I do not set Jerusalem above my highest joy (Psalm 137:5-6). Read that as an exile's discipline and it's exactly right. The danger in Babylon was never only the harp on the willow, the silence of despair. The danger was also forgetting, slowly, comfortably, getting so settled in Babylon that you lost the memory of Zion altogether, assimilated until you couldn't remember the song even if someone asked for it. So the exiles bound themselves with a vow. We will not forget. We will sit by these foreign rivers and we will not perform the song on demand for our captors' entertainment, but we will also not let the song die in us, we will keep it alive, we will set Jerusalem above our highest joy even here, especially here, because a people who forget their home will become Babylonians within a generation. That vow is the thin line between the two errors this whole book has named, the despair that hangs the harp on the willow forever and the assimilation that forgets the tune. We will remember, and we will not perform on demand, and we will keep the song alive until the day comes to sing it freely again.

That's the posture I want for the exilic church, and for myself. Not the despair that goes silent, and not the assimilation that forgets, but the stubborn vow of the exile who will not let the song die, who keeps Zion in his memory and the tune in his throat even in a land that mocks both, waiting for the day he can sing it out loud and free. If I forget you, let my right hand forget its skill. That's a pastor's vow for the long exile. Whatever else Babylon takes, it will not take the song, because I will not let it, because the song is the one thing worth more than my own comfort and my own safety and my own standing, the song of the God who went into exile to bring his people home.

I'm going to sing. Badly, probably, and often through tears, and in a strange land that does not know the tune and may not want to hear it. I'll sing it to my five sons and pray the song takes root in them deeper than it took in me. I'll sing it to a congregation that's smaller than the one I started with and dearer to me for being smaller. I'll sing it to the pastors in the Network who are deciding whether their own fires go out. I'll sing it badly and I'll keep singing, because the LORD is here, in Babylon, where he has always been, waiting for his people in the very place they were certain was godforsaken. The temple is ash and the empire holds the whip and the seventy years stretch out past the far edge of my own life, and I will not see the return, and that's all right, because my grandchildren might, and the King is coming regardless, and the song was never really mine anyway. It belongs to the One who went into exile to bring his people home.

I want to leave you with one last image, and it's the one I come back to most, the road to Emmaus, because it's the whole exile in miniature and it tells you how the story ends. Two disciples are walking away from Jerusalem on the afternoon of the resurrection, away from the city, defeated, their hopes in ashes, talking about how they had hoped he was the one to redeem Israel and now he was dead and it was over (Luke 24:21). Their establishment had collapsed. Everything they'd assumed about how God would work had come apart on a Roman cross, and they were walking home in the gray light of total defeat. And a stranger falls in beside them and asks what they're discussing, and they pour out their grief to him, not knowing it's him, not recognizing the risen Christ walking beside them in their disappointment, and he listens to the whole thing, the whole story of their collapsed hope, before he says a word. And then he opens the Scriptures to them, and walks them through the whole story, and shows them that the cross was not the failure of the plan but the plan, that the suffering was not the absence of God but the very means of redemption, and their hearts burn within them though they still don't know who he is. And then they sit down to eat, and he takes the bread and breaks it, and in the breaking of the bread their eyes are opened and they recognize him, and he vanishes, and they get up that very hour and run back to Jerusalem to tell the others he's alive.

That's the exile, and that's the hope. We are the disciples on the road, walking away from the collapse of everything we assumed, grieving a hope that died, certain it's over. And the risen Christ is walking beside us the whole time, in the very disappointment, unrecognized, present in our defeat before we know he's there. He doesn't rebuke our grief; he listens to it. And then he does two things, the two things this whole book has been about. He opens the Scriptures and shows us that the collapse is not the failure of the plan but somehow inside the plan, that the death was the way to the life, that the exile is the school and not the abandonment. And he breaks the bread, and in the breaking, at the table, our eyes are opened and we recognize him. The Word and the table. He meets the exiles on the road through the Word that reinterprets their defeat and the bread that opens their eyes, and those are the same two things he's given us, the Word and the table, the very things the exilic church gathers around when everything else is stripped away. He is on the road with us. He has been the whole time. And he will open our eyes, in the Word and in the breaking of the bread, and we will recognize him, and we will get up that very hour and run.

We did not choose the exile. But it was always going to be the truest home we have. Take the harp down off the willow. The God of the song never stayed behind. He is walking the road beside us in the gray light, unrecognized, patient, and any moment now, in the Word and in the bread, our eyes will open and we'll know him. Sing.
chapters.verdict: We did not choose the exile, but it was always going to be the truest home we have.
reflect: Can you stop grieving the country you lost long enough to love the city you were sent to?
What song is the Lord asking you to sing in this strange land, and have you fallen silent?
If the exile is the church's most native condition, what have you been calling home that was never home at all?
